(8) 1 ⸢KUŠ₃ ana NIM⸣ DIB
quotations.translation: (7) Night of (day) 13, ME (= moonrise to sunset) was 11 (UŠ), measured (despite) clouds; beginning of the night, Sin was 20 fingers above the twins’ star of the shepherd, Sin (8)  having passed 1 cubit to the east.
quotations.publication: Sachs, A. J., Hunger, H. 1988. Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia, Vol. I: Diaries from 652 B.C. to 262 B.C. Vienna: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften.

quotations.original: EN.NUN ša₂ gi-ne₂-e TA GAN EN TIL ŠE MU.12.[KAM₂ mu₂-ma-kuš] ša₂ mar₂-tak-šat-su <LUGAL> MU-šu₂ na-bu-u₂
quotations.translation: Diary from month IX to the end of month XII, year 12 [of Umakuš,] who is called king Artaxerxes.
quotations.publication: Sachs, A. J., Hunger, H. 1988. Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia, Vol. I: Diaries from 652 B.C. to 262 B.C. Vienna: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften.

quotations.original: ina KIN ina še-rim UD.28.KAM MUL₂.BIR meš-ḫu im-šuḫ ZI
quotations.translation: In Month VI, in the morning (which corresponds to) the 28th day, The Kidney expels a flare.
quotations.genre: schematic astronomy: 'three stars each' + rising times
quotations.publication: Horowitz, W., 2014. The Three Stars Each: The Astrolabes and Related Texts (Archiv für Orientforschung, Beiheft 33). Horn/Wien: Berger & Söhne/Institut für Orientalistik der Universität Wien.
quotations.comment: See also: Steele, J. M. (2017). Rising Time Schemes in Babylonian Astronomy (1st ed.). Springer Science. 53-54. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-55221-7

quotations.original: Si Haedus quem fert Auriga in occasu fuerit inventus, et eum Saturnus quadrata vel diametra radiatione respexerit, nati in ipso momento vitae moriuntur, [...] Quodsi Mars cum ipsa stella in occasu fuerit inventus [...]
quotations.translation: If Haedus whom Auriga carries is found on the descendant and Saturn stands in square or opposition to it, the ones born in that moment die, [...] If Mars is found on the descendant with this star [...]
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: εἰδώλοις δ’ ἐν ὑγροῖσι Κρόνον καὶ φοίνιον Ἄρην ξυνὴν ἐξανύοντας ὁδὸν Τιτὰν ὅτε λεύσσῃ
quotations.translation: When the Titan (the Sun) sees (is in aspect with) Saturn and bloody Mars as they complete a common path in watery zodiac signs

quotations.original: Si Saturnus et Luna unum hospitium partis acceperint, et in eodem loco pariter constituti aequabili societatis ratione iungantur, is omnes impetus et omnes animi cogitationes et omnes actus inbecilla timoris trepidatione semper inpugnant.
quotations.translation: If Saturn and the Moon take up the hospitality of one degree and equally located in the same place join in equatable ratio of union [i. e. conjunction], they always attack all impulses and all thoughts of the mind and all actions with the feeble nervousness of fear.
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Si [...], nec renatis luminibus deserto Solis orbe lucescat, faciet humiles deiectos et omni licentiae potestate subiectos, inbecilles viribus, et omni virtutis praesidio destitutos.
quotations.translation: If [the moon is shining] not with reborn light, having left the orb of the Sun behind, it makes [the natives] humble, dejected and subjected to every whim of authority, feeble in power and destitute of the protection of all virtue.
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Si in finibus Mercurii Luna fuerit inventa, et masculini generis sidus acceperit, [...] qui sic has stellas habuerint, nunquam filios sortiuntur.
quotations.translation: If the Moon is found in the terms of Mercury and accepted [or approached (accesserit)] a planet of masculine gender [...], those who have the stars thus will never be allotted children.
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: basis nocte a fortuna ad genium.
quotations.translation: [The lot of] basis [can be calculated by adding to the ascendant the amount of degrees] at night from the lot of fortune until the lot of the daemon
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: GE₆ 29 a-ku₆-ku₆-<<ku₆>>-tu₄ ina ŠU₂ KUR 2 ⸢DANNA⸣ [...]
quotations.translation: Night of the 29th, red glow flared up in the west; 2 bēru [...]
quotations.publication: Sachs, A. J., Hunger, H. 1988. Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia, Vol. I: Diaries from 652 B.C. to 262 B.C. Vienna: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften.

quotations.original: in 20 GU₄.UD ina ŠU₂ ina MAŠ₂ ŠU₂
quotations.translation: Around (day) 20, Mercury set in the west in Capricorn.
quotations.publication: Sachs, A. J., Hunger, H. 1989. Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia, Vol. II: Diaries from 261 B.C. to 165 B.C. Vienna: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften.

quotations.original: (2') ina 30 (3') IZI 30 GU₄.UD ina NIM ina A UŠ
quotations.translation: (2') On (day) 30, (3') month V, (day) 30, Mercury became stationary in the east in Leo.
quotations.genre: astronomical diaries and related texts: planetary excerpt
quotations.publication: Hunger, H. 2001. Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia, Vol. V. Lunar and Planetary Texts. Vienna, Austria: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wis­senschaften.

quotations.original:
(3') ina 22
(4') APIN 24 GU₄.UD ina ŠU₂ ina PA UŠ
quotations.translation: (3') On (day) 22 (4') month VIII, (day) 24, Mercury became stationary in the west in Sagittarius.
quotations.genre: astronomical diaries and related texts: planetary excerpt
quotations.publication: Hunger, H. 2001. Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia, Vol. V. Lunar and Planetary Texts. Vienna, Austria: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wis­senschaften.
quotations.comment: The double date is peculiar and unexplained; perhaps they are ideal date and actual date.

quotations.original: Extra partes Sagittarii oritur Falcis Lupus Aquarius minor et Ara.
quotations.translation: Outside the degrees of Sagittarius rises the Sickle, the Wolf, the Small Waterbearer and the Altar.
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: In Pisce septentrionali oritur Cervus Lepus, in australi Cetus id est marina belua.
quotations.translation: In the Northern Fish rise the Stag, the Hare, in the Southern [Fish rises] Cetus, i. e. the sea monster.
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: quaedam vero aversa esse ab horoscopo et quodam modo aliena, quae non inmerito pigra diximus
quotations.translation: these we call averse [unaspected] to the ascendant and in some way alien, which we rightly call dull
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Oriuntur autem variis temporibus ac diebus et secundum climata;
quotations.translation: But they rise at different times and days also according to the climes
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Sane extra ceteros climacteras etiam septimi anni et noni per omne vitae tempus multiplicata ratione currentes naturali quadam et latenti ratione variis hominem periculorum discriminibus semper afficiunt,
quotations.translation: Aside from other climacteric periods, also every seventh and ninth year and their multiples through all life in some natural and hidden ways affect men with various dangerous crises.
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Deus vero illud signum dicitur, quod contra hoc signum in diametro fuerit constitutum
quotations.translation: That sign is called God which is located opposite this sign in opposition
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Crios autem ideo a Graecis dictum est hoc signum, quod, cum <in> eo Sol fuerit, inter diem et noctem quodammodo iudicat, quod crinein dicitur, et quod in eo signo inter hiemem positus et aestatem ipse rursus iudicetur.
quotations.translation: This sign is called κριός by the Greeks because when the Sun is in it, it judges between day and night, as it were, which is called κρίνειν, and because located in that sign between winter and summer it is judged likewise.
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Quanta autem sit temporum distributio, breviter ostendemus: Sol accipit menses XIX, Luna menses XXV, Saturnus menses XXX, Iuppiter menses XII, Mars menses XV, Venus menses VIII, Mercurius menses XX.
quotations.translation: We will show briefly how the distribution of times works: The Sun takes 19 months, the Moon 25 months, Saturn 30 months, Jupiter 12 months, Mars 15 months, Venus 8 months, Mercury 20 months.
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: [...] quotienscunque Iuppiter post excessum Saturni ad oportuna geniturae venerit loca.
quotations.translation: [...] whenever Jupiter comes to the suitable places of the nativity after the departure of Saturn
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Hae figurae stellarum quando prosint, quando noceant, in libris posterioribus explicabimus;
quotations.translation: We will explain in the later books when these configurations of stars are beneficial, when they are harmful
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Lunaticos vero tunc facit, si figura Lunae vel scema vel similitudinem Saturni comparetur ac Martis, Iove ac Venere <in> alienis existentibus signis;
quotations.translation: But it then makes lunatics if the figure or σχῆμα of the Moon would be united with Saturn and Mars, with Jupiter and Venus being in alien [i. e. unaspected] signs
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Lunaticos vero tunc facit, si figura Lunae vel scema vel similitudinem Saturni comparetur ac Martis, Iove ac Venere <in> alienis existentibus signis;
quotations.translation: But it then makes lunatics if the figure or σχῆμα of the Moon would be united with Saturn and Mars, with Jupiter and Venus being in alien [i. e. unaspected] signs
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Integer itaque horoscopi gnomon ponendus est, ut vera pars sollerti conputatione collecta apotelesma fideli faciat pronuntiatione proferri.
quotations.translation: Therefore the gnomon of the hour-marker is to be placed untouched so that the influence can be deduced by rational computation and pronounced faithfully
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: minuuntur autem etiam haec, si sic positum Solem malivolum sidus impediat
quotations.translation: but this is diminished if a malefic located there hinders the Sun
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: [...] et an benivolarum stellarum testimoniis adornetur an vero malivolarum inpugnatione pulsetur.
quotations.translation: [...] whether well aspected by benefics or badly aspected by malefics.
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Quidam hunc locum volentes suptilius explicare terna numina decanis singulis applicarunt, quos munifices applicandos esse voluerunt id est liturgos ita ut per signa singula novem possint munifices inveniri, ut ternis munificibus decani singuli praeferantur.
quotations.translation: Some who wish to elaborate this in more detail add three divinities each to every decan, which they call munifices i. e. λειτουργοί, so that for every sign nine munifices can be found and every decan is divided into three munifices.
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Si enim aut Mars istam mixtionem minaci radiatione pulsaverit, aut sit nocturna genitura, haec quae diximus minuuntur omnia
quotations.translation: For if either Mars aspects this configuration badly or it is a night-chart, everything we said will be diminished
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: et malivolarum stellarum minaces radii ex loci oportunitate franguntur.
quotations.translation: and the bad aspects of the malefics are broken by the favorable qualities of the place.
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: MUL₂ GAL ša₂ ma-gal KUR u₃ meš-ḫi TUK-u₂
quotations.translation: A meteor which was very bright and had a tail.
quotations.publication: Sachs, A. J., Hunger, H. 1988. Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia, Vol. I: Diaries from 652 B.C. to 262 B.C. Vienna: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften.

quotations.original: ⸢GE₆⸣ 19 a-kam₂ AN DIB
quotations.translation: Night of the 19th, mist crossed the sky.
quotations.publication: Sachs, A. J., Hunger, H. 1988. Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia, Vol. I: Diaries from 652 B.C. to 262 B.C. Vienna: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften.

quotations.original: tunc enim proteguntur, quotienscumque oportuna radiatione praecesserint.
quotations.translation: they will be protected whenever they precede with a favorable aspect
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: ⸢22⸣ ina KIN.SIG bu-tuq TIR.AN id SI u KUR GAL₂-ši
quotations.translation: The 22nd, in the afternoon, there was a section of a rainbow in the direction of north and east.
quotations.publication: Sachs, A. J., Hunger, H. 1988. Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia, Vol. I: Diaries from 652 B.C. to 262 B.C. Vienna: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften.

quotations.original: TIR.AN ina KUR GIB
quotations.translation: A rainbow stretched in the east.
quotations.publication: Sachs, A. J., Hunger, H. 1988. Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia, Vol. I: Diaries from 652 B.C. to 262 B.C. Vienna: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften.

quotations.original: Sed si sic hos omnes positos Saturnus de trigono respexerit vel de exagono vel etiam si pariter fuerit constitutus, perpetua felicitas istis decernitur.
quotations.translation: But if Saturn aspects them all in a trine or in a sextile or even if he stands side-by-side (conjunction), this indicates perpetual felicity.
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Matutinae sunt in ortu, quae praecedentes orbem Solis oriuntur;
quotations.translation: Matutine rising are those which rise preceding the orb of the Sun
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Voluerunt Lunam <ita> constituere, ut primum se Saturno coniungeret eique temporum traderet principatum, nec inmerito
quotations.translation: They wanted to place the moon such that it first joins Saturn and passes on to him the rulership of time, and rightly so
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: cursus regressus stationes societates augmenta ortus occasusque monstravit
quotations.translation: He showed the courses, retrogrades, stations, associations, increases, risings and settings.
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Sed maximas felicitates decernit sic positus, si nulla ei malivola stella in IMC. posita restiterit.
quotations.translation: But he [Jupiter] indicates the utmost fortune in this position if no malefic on the lower midheaven resists him.
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Si Saturnus Marti fuerit trigonica radiatione coniunctus, et in oportunis geniturae locis <sit> ista sociatio, [...]
quotations.translation: If Saturn aspects Mars in trine and this aspect takes place in the fortunate places of the nativity, [...]
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Ideo autem cum horoscopo maxima coniunctione sociatur, quia horoscopum <de trigono respicit et> de trigono ab horoscope videtur.
quotations.translation: Because it aspects the ascendant in an utmost way because it sees it in trine and is seen by it in a trine
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Harum quinque zonarum quae media est, corusci Solis incensa luminibus et sempiterni ardoris adustione torrida ignito colore perpetui ruboris inficitur.
quotations.translation: Of those five zones the one in the middle is always burned by the gleaming sun and parched by the burning of sempiternal heat, is stained by the fire-hot color of perpetual redness
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: et adhuc intra Solis orbem destituta luminibus Luna claudatur, nec renatis luminibus deserto Solis orbe lucescat
quotations.translation: and the Moon is still enclosed in the orb of the Sun, devoid of light, and does not [yet] shine with reborn light after leaving the Sun's orb
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Si [...] Saturnus <vero> et Mars ita sint positi ut unus Solis alter Lunae radiis adhaerescat [...]
quotations.translation: However, if Saturn and Mars are placed such that either one comes into aspect with the Sun, the other with the Moon [...]
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.

quotations.original: Antiscium itaque eius in Ariete constitutum <et> Solis antiscium, quod in Libram fuerat missum, per diametrum sibi facta contraria amplissimi ordinis decreto in exilium mitti fecerunt ob hoc, quod Saturni et Solis antiscia in cosmicis constituta sideribus de diametro se viderunt.
quotations.translation: they do it, because the antiscia of Saturn and the Sun are located in cosmic stars in opposition [to each other?]
quotations.publication: Firmicus Maternus. 1897. Ivlii Firmici Materni Matheseos Libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll, F. Skutsch. Stuttgart: B. G. Teubner.
quotations.comment: "Meaning uncertain, but perhaps Firmicus means that that [sic] actual planets are opposed in the heavens in addition to their shadow-degrees." (Dykes, Benjamin. Firmicus Maternus: Mathêsis. )

quotations.original: σκοπεῖν [...] πότερον ἐνεργῶς τυγχάνουσι διακείμενοι κατά τε αὐτὸ τὸ κοσμικὸν καὶ τὸ κατὰ τὴν γένεσιν ἢ τὸ ἐναντίον
quotations.translation: We must observe [...] whether they are actively situated both in the cosmos itself and in the nativity, or the reverse
quotations.comment: Robbins 1940 (p. 239, fn. 3): "The horoscopic point and other angles change for each nativity; the signs of the zodiac, houses of the planets, terms, etc., are cosmic, as being related to the universe itself and therefore fixed.

quotations.original: ὑφίστανται γάρ τινες μυστικῶς τὸν μὲν καθολικὸν ὡροσκόπον καὶ τὰ τούτου τετράγωνα κοσμικὰ κέντρα, τὸν δε κλῆρον καὶ τὰ τούτου τετράγωνα γενεθλιαλογικὰ κέντρα.
quotations.translation: Some have mystically hypothesized that the common ascendant and its triangles are the cosmic cardines, while the Lot and its triangles are the natal cardines

quotations.original: [ὁ κλῆρος ἔ]ρωτος εὑρέθη Ταύρῳ μοιρῶν δʹ οἴκῳ καὶ ὁρίοις Ἀ[φροδίτης· οὖτος σημαίν]ει τὸν περὶ φ̣ιλίας καὶ συστάσεως
quotations.translation: The lot of desire was found in Taurus at 4 degrees, house and terms of Venus: this signifies the (qualities) relating to affection and association.

quotations.original: Ἀφροδείτης ἐν Τοξότῃ μοι[ρ]ῶν θʹ λεπτο̑ν νδʹ· ἑῷα ἀνατολάς
quotations.translation: Venus in Sagittarius at 9 degrees, 54 minutes—morning rising

quotations.original:
(...), καὶ πλάνα φέγγη 
ἀπλανέων τ᾽ αὐγὰς πυριλαμπέας ἐξονομήνω, 
ζωιδίων τε πόλοιο περίδρομον, (...)
quotations.translation:
(...), of the wandering lights too,
and of the fiery-bright rays of the unwandering ones, let me speak of them by name,
and of the circuit of the sphere of the zodiac signs, (...)
quotations.publication: Lopilato, R., 1998. The "Apotelesmatika" of Manetho. Providence, Rhode Island: Brown University.

quotations.transliteration: šꜥ[ṱ s ẖn 10 sp 4 | ỉw=k ḏd mḥ 4] [pꜣ] ỉp [pꜣ hby ḥꜣṱ=f n-ỉm=f]
quotations.translation: Take [it from 10: remainder 4] | You shall say 4 cubits is [the] number [of lowering its top from it]
quotations.publication: R.A. Parker, 1972, Demotic Mathematical Texts, Brown Egyptological Studies 7, Providence RI/London.

quotations.transliteration: ỉw=w ḏd n=k [fy 15 2/3 r 100] | ỉw=k šꜥṱ 6 ẖ[n 100 sp 94] | iw=k ḏd ḫr-š[m 6 r 94 r1]5 2/3 | my ỉn=f 1/3 r 47
quotations.translation: If it is said to you [carry 15 2/3 to 100,] | you subtract 6 from [100, 94 remains]. | You shall say [6] goes to 94 with the result 1]5 2/3 | Cause it to be brought to 1/3 result 47.
quotations.publication: R.A. Parker, 1972, Demotic Mathematical Texts, Brown Egyptological Studies 7, Providence RI/London.

quotations.transliteration: ỉw=w ḏd n=k [fy 15 2/3 r 100] | ỉw=k šꜥṱ 6 ẖ[n 100 sp 94] | iw=k ḏd ḫr-š[m 6 r 94 r1]5 2/3 | my ỉn=f 1/3 r 47
quotations.translation: If it is said to you [carry 15 2/3 to 100,] | you subtract 6 from [100, 94 remains]. | You shall say [6] goes to 94 with the result 1]5 2/3 | Cause it to be brought to 1/3 result 47.

quotations.original: TA ME.A EN 30 ME 7.30 ZI-šu₂
quotations.translation: From daylight rising until 30 days its displacement is (0);7,30.
quotations.publication: M. Ossendrijver, 2017, New results on a Babylonian scheme for Jupiter's motion along the zodiac, Journal of Near Eastern Studies 76, 231–247

quotations.original: ⸢16  ŠU⸣ 12 ina KUR 19.26.40 ALLA ŠU₂
quotations.translation: (Year)  ⸢16 , (month) IV⸣, (day) 12, in the east, 19;26,40 Cancer, it sets.
quotations.publication: Neugebauer, Otto, 1955, Astronomical Cuneiform Texts

quotations.original: Secure spectat occasus siderum atque ortus et tam diversas concordantium vias; observat ubi quaeque stella primum terris lumen ostendat, ubi columen eius summumque cursus sit, quousque descendat; curiosus spectator excutit singula et quaerit.
quotations.translation: Serenely it looks upon the rising and setting of the stars and the diverse orbits of bodies precisely balanced with one another. The mind observes where each star first shows its light to earth, where its culmination, the highest altitude of its course, lies and how far it descends. As a curious spectator the mind separates details and investigates them.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: At illa regio caelestis per triginta annos velocissimo sideri viam praestat nusquam resistenti sed aequaliter cito.
quotations.translation: But in the heavenly region the swiftest star, which never stops and maintains a constant velocity, has a journey of thirty years.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Nunc, ut ad propositum opus veniam, audi quid de ignibus sentiam quos aer transversos agit. Magna illos vi excuti argumentum est quod obliqui feruntur et praerapida celeritate; apparet illos non ire, sed proici.
quotations.translation: Now to get to my proposed work. Hear what I think about those fires which the atmosphere drives across the sky. They move obliquely at very high speeds, which is proof that they have been driven by a great force. It is obvious that they do not move on their own accord but are hurled.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: GE₆ 17 ina EN dele-bat e MUL₂.ŠUR GIGIR ša₂ ULU₃ 1 KUŠ₃
quotations.translation: Night of (day) 17, first part of the night, Venus was 1 cubit above the southern rein of the chariot.
quotations.publication: Hunger, H. 2014. Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia, Vol. VII: Almanacs and Normal Star Almanacs. Vienna, Austria: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften.

quotations.original: satius erit de re ipsa quaerere quam mirari quid ita Aristoteles globum ignis appellaverit capram. Talis enim fuit forma eius qui bellum adversus Persen Paulo gerente lunari magnitudine apparuit.
quotations.translation: It will be more appropriate to investigate the phenomenon itself rather than to wonder why Aristotle has called a ball of fire a Goat. Actually, that was the shape of a fire which did appear, about the size of the moon, when Paulus was waging war against Perseus.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Vidimus nos quoque non semel flammam ingentis pilae specie, quae tamen in ipso cursu suo dissipata est.
quotations.translation: Also, we have more than once seen a flaming light in the shape of a huge ball which was then dissipated in mid-flight.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Interim illud existimo eiusmodi ignes existere aere vehementius trito, cum inclinatio eius in alteram partem facta est et non cessit, sed inter se pugnavit; ex hac vexatione nascuntur trabes et globi et faces et ardores.
quotations.translation: For the time being, I guess this: fires of this sort come into existence because the atmosphere undergoes severe friction when there has been a tilting of it to one side and there is no yielding, only internal struggle. From this vexation are produced fiery shapes, the so-called Boards, Balls, Torches, and Blazes.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Tunc ignes tenuissimi iter exile designant et caelo producunt.
quotations.translation: Then the extenuated fires make a slender path and draw it out in the sky.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Varia et multa terrarum orbis expirat, quaedam umida, quaedam sicca, quaedam calentia, quaedam concipiendis ignibus idonea.
quotations.translation: the terrestrial globe exhales many different particles, some wet, some dry, some hot, some suitable for starting fires.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: sed acrior sit Caniculae rubor, Martis remissior, Iovis nullus in lucem puram nitore perducto.
quotations.translation: The red of the Dog Star is brighter, that of Mars weaker, while Jupiter has no red, with its gleam extended into pure light.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Necesse est ergo, in magna copia corpusculorum quae terrae eiectant et in superiorem agunt partem, aliqua in nubes pervenire alimenta ignium, quae non tantum collisa possint ardere sed etiam afflata radiis solis;
quotations.translation: In the great quantity of particles which the earth ejects and forces into the upper air it is necessary, therefore, that some nutriments of fire reach the clouds, which not only can burn in colliding but even when breathed on by rays of the sun.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Illud enim stultissimum, existimare aut decidere stellas, aut transilire, aut aliquid illis auferri et abradi.
quotations.translation: Yet it is the stupidest thing to suppose that stars actually fall, or jump across, or that anything is taken or rubbed away from them.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Illud enim stultissimum, existimare aut decidere stellas, aut transilire, aut aliquid illis auferri et abradi.
quotations.translation: Yet it is the stupidest thing to suppose that stars actually fall, or jump across, or that anything is taken or rubbed away from them.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Atqui, quo solet, quaeque [stellae] invenitur loco et magnitudo sua singulis constat;
quotations.translation: Still, each star is found in its usual place and its size remains constant.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Memoriae proditum est, quo die Urbem divus Augustus Apollonia reversus intravit, circa solem visum coloris varii circulum, qualis esse in arcu solet. Hunc Graeci halo vocant, nos dicere coronam aptissime possumus.
quotations.translation: It is recorded in history that the day the deified Augustus entered Rome on his return from Apollonia a circle of varied colours was seen around the sun, colours that usually appear in a rainbow. The Greeks call it a “halo.” We can call it, very appropriately, a “corona.”
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Ob hoc tales splendores Graeci areas vocaverunt quia fere terendis frugibus destinata loca rotunda sunt.
quotations.translation: For this reason the Greeks called such shining lights “threshing-floors” because generally the places set aside for threshing grain are round.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: si a septemtrione discessit, aquilo erit; si ab occidente, favonius.
quotations.translation: If it has parted on the north side, there will be a north wind; if on the west, a west wind.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Hae coronae noctibus fere circa lunam et alias stellas notantur; interdiu raro, adeo ut quidam ex Graecis negaverint omnino eas fieri, cum illos historiae coarguant.
quotations.translation: Such halos will be seen generally at night around10 the moon and other heavenly bodies; but rarely in the daytime. Consequently, some Greeks argue that they do not occur at all during the day.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: At contra arcus nocte non fit aut admodum raro, quia luna non habet tantum virium ut nubes transeat et illis colorem suffundat, qualem accipiunt sole perstrictae. Sic enim formam arcus discoloris efficiunt.
quotations.translation: On the other hand, a rainbow does not occur at1 night, or very rarely, because the moon does not have enough strength to penetrate clouds and suffuse them with colour, such as they receive when touched by the sun’s rays.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Mundum ipsum praecipiti velocitate labentem et ortus occasusque intra momentum temporis revolventem nemo nostrum sentit procedere.
quotations.translation: Not one of us perceives that the universe itself moves, gliding along at headlong speed, unrolling its risings and settings within a moment of time.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Aristoteles ait post autumnale aequinoctium qualibet hora diei arcum fieri; aestate non fieri, nisi aut incipiente aut inclinato die.
quotations.translation: Aristotle says that after the autumnal equinox a6 rainbow occurs at any hour of the day; in the summer it does not occur except at the beginning or end of the day.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Aristoteles ait post autumnale aequinoctium qualibet hora diei arcum fieri; aestate non fieri, nisi aut incipiente aut inclinato die.
quotations.translation: Aristotle says that after the autumnal equinox a6 rainbow occurs at any hour of the day; in the summer it does not occur except at the beginning or end of the day.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: At temporibus aestivis super nostrum verticem fertur; itaque medio die excelsissimus terras rectiore aspicit linea quam ut ullis nubibus possit occurri; omnes enim sub se tunc habe nubibus possit occurri; omnes enim sub se tunc habet.
quotations.translation: But in summertime the sun passes overhead. Thus, it is very high at midday and looks down on the earth in too vertical a line to be able to be met by any clouds. For the sun then has all the clouds beneath it.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Nunc de virgis dicendum est, quas non minus pictas variasque aeque pluviarum signa solemus accipere.
quotations.translation: At this point mention should be made of Streaks, which, no less varicoloured than a rainbow, we commonly accept as equally a sign of rain.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Haec dicitur perfecta defectio, quae stellas quoque ostendit et intercipit lucem, tunc scilicet cum uterque orbis sub eodem libramento stetit.
quotations.translation: A so-called total eclipse also shuts out the daylight and reveals the stars. It occurs, of course, when the centre of both spheres have come to a balance with the earth’s—all on the same straight line.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Ob hoc omnia eiusmodi simulacra candida sunt et similia lunaribus circulis, quia ex percussu oblique accepto sole respondent.
quotations.translation: For this reason all phenomena of this type are white and similar to moon-shaped discs, because they reflect bright light when they are struck obliquely by the sun.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Sunt bothyni, cum velut corona cingente introrsus ingens caeli recessus est similis effossae in orbem specu; sunt pithiae, cum magnitudo vasti rotundique ignis dolio similis vel fertur vel uno loco flagrat; sunt chasmata, cum aliquod spatium caeli desedit et flammam velut dehiscens in abdito ostentat.
quotations.translation: There are bothyni: within a surrounding corona there is a great gap in the sky like a hole dug in a circle. There are pithiai: an enormous round mass of fire, like a barrel, either darts by or blazes in one place. There are chasmata: some area of the sky settles and, gaping in hiding—so to speak—sends out flame.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Quomodo nunc me hoc loco geram? Quid vocem? Imagines solis?2 Historici soles vocant et binos ternosque apparuisse memoriae tradunt.
quotations.translation: Now, how am I to express myself in this section?2 What should I call these things? Images of the sun? Historians call them “suns” and record that they have appeared two and three at a time.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Quomodo nunc me hoc loco geram? Quid vocem? Imagines solis?2 Historici soles vocant et binos ternosque apparuisse memoriae tradunt.
quotations.translation: Now, how am I to express myself in this section?2 What should I call these things? Images of the sun? Historians call them “suns” and record that they have appeared two and three at a time.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Graeci parhelia appellant, quia in propinquo fere a sole visuntur aut quia accedunt ad aliquam similitudinem solis.
quotations.translation: The Greeks call them “parhelia,” either because they are commonly seen near the sun, that is, alongside it, or because they are near to some resemblance to the sun.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Ex his fulgoribus quaedam praeceps eunt similia prosilientibus stellis, quaedam certo loco permanent et tantum lucis emittunt ut fugent tenebras ac diem repraesentent, donec consumpto alimento primum obscuriora sint, deinde flammae modo quae in se cadit per assiduam deminutionem redigantur ad nihilum.
quotations.translation: Some of these flashes pass by abruptly like shooting stars, others remain in a fixed position1 and emit only enough light to dispel the darkness and give the illusion of daylight until, having consumed their fuel, they first become dimmer; then, in the manner of a fire which collapses upon itself, they steadily diminish and are reduced to nothingness.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Haec fulgura dicuntur, quia brevis illorum facies et caduca est nec sine iniuria decidens; saepe enim fulminum noxas ediderunt.
quotations.translation: These are called Flashes, because their appearance is brief and dying. Yet their descent is not without harm, for often they accomplish the damage of lightning-bolts.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Haec fulgura dicuntur, quia brevis illorum facies et caduca est nec sine iniuria decidens; saepe enim fulminum noxas ediderunt. Ab his tacta nos dicimus siderata, id est icta sine fulmine, quae ἀστερόπληκτα Graeci vocant.
quotations.translation: These are called Flashes, because their appearance is brief and dying. Yet their descent is not without harm, for often they accomplish the damage of lightning-bolts. We call objects hit by them “star-struck,” that is, struck but not by an actual lightning bolt. The Greeks have the term asteroplekta.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Haec fulgura dicuntur, quia brevis illorum facies et caduca est nec sine iniuria decidens; saepe enim fulminum noxas ediderunt. Ab his tacta nos dicimus siderata, id est icta sine fulmine, quae ἀστερόπληκτα Graeci vocant.
quotations.translation: These are called Flashes, because their appearance is brief and dying. Yet their descent is not without harm, for often they accomplish the damage of lightning-bolts. We call objects hit by them “star-struck,” that is, struck but not by an actual lightning bolt. The Greeks have the term asteroplekta.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: At quibus longior mora est et ignis fortior motumque caeli sequens aut etiam proprios cursus agunt, cometas nostri putant, de quibus dictum est. Horum genera sunt pogoniae et cyparissiae et lampades et alia omnia quorum ignis in exitu sparsus est.
quotations.translation: But the ones which last a long time, and have a stronger flame, and follow the motion of the sky or even maintain their own course, our Stoics call comets (which have already been discussed). Types of these are: Bearded, Cypress Trees, and Lamps—as well as all the others which have fire scattered behind them as they go out.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Omnis de universo quaestio in caelestia, sublima, terrena dividitur.
quotations.translation: Any study of the universe is divided into uranology [the study of the sky], meteorology, and geography.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Separat, quia medius intervenit; iungit, quia utrique per hunc inter se consensus est; supra se dat quicquid accepit a terris, rursus vim siderum in terrena transfundit.
quotations.translation: [The atmosphere] separates because it intervenes midway; it joins because through it there is a communication between the two. It transmits to the upper region whatever it receives from the earth. On the other hand, it transfuses to earthly objects the influences of the stars.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Ab aethere lucidissimo aer in terram usque diffusus est, agilior quidem tenuiorque et altior terris nec minus aquis, ceterum aethere spissior graviorque, frigidus per se et obscurus.
quotations.translation: Air is diffused from the bright atmosphere down1 to earth. It is thinner, more mobile, and more buoyant than earth and water too but thicker and heavier than upper atmosphere.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Summa pars eius siccissima calidissimaque et ob hoc etiam tenuissima est propter viciniam aeternorum ignium et illos tot motus siderum assiduumque caeli circumactum;
quotations.translation: Its highest region is extremely dry and hot, and for this reason also very thin because of the nearness of the eternal fires, the many movements of the stars, and the continuous revolution of heaven.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: “Vos,” inquit, “dicitis, cum causas stellarum transvolantium redditis, posse aliquas aeris partes ad se trahere ignem ex locis superioribus et sic ardore accendi.”
quotations.translation: “When” says he, “you give an explanation of shooting stars you say that some parts of the atmosphere can draw fire from the upper regions and thus be kindled by the heat.”
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: “Quid ergo? Non aliquando etiam apparentibus stellis et nocte tranquilla fulgurat?”
quotations.translation: “But well! Does it not sometimes flash lightning, even when the stars are visible and the night is clear?”
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Quinque stellarum potestates Chaldaeorum observatio excepit. Quid, tu tot illa milia siderum iudicas otiosa lucere?
quotations.translation: The observation of the Chaldaeans is restricted to the powers of five planets.3 Well! Do you think that those many thousands of stars shine uselessly?
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Quid est porro aliud quod errorem maximum incutiat peritis natalium quam quod paucis nos sideribus assignant, cum omnia quae supra nos sunt partem nostri sibi vindicent?
quotations.translation: Furthermore, what else is there which causes the greatest error on the part of horoscope experts than the fact that they assign us to only a few stars while all the stars above us claim a share of us for themselves?
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Summissiora forsitan propius in nos vim suam dirigunt et ea quae frequentius mota aliter nos aliterque prospiciunt.
quotations.translation: Perhaps the lower stars, and those which look upon us sometimes one way sometimes another because they change position more frequently, influence us more directly.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: “Quid ergo,” inquit, “non potest aliqua ex his transcurrentibus stellis incidere in nubem et extingui?”
quotations.translation: “Well, then,” he says, “is it not possible that some of those shooting stars fall into a cloud and are extinguished?”
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: 29 mul₂.NUN.ki ina NIM ⸢IGI⸣
quotations.translation: (Day) 29, the Eridu (star) appears in the east.
quotations.genre: astronomical diaries and related texts: almanac
quotations.publication: Hunger, H. 2014. Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia, Vol. VII: Almanacs and Normal Star Almanacs. Vienna, Austria: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften.

quotations.original: 10 ŠU.PA ina KUR IGI
quotations.translation: (Day) 10, ŠU.PA appears in the east.
quotations.genre: astronomical diaries and related texts: normal star almanac
quotations.publication: Hunger, H. 2014. Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia, Vol. VII: Almanacs and Normal Star Almanacs. Vienna, Austria: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften.

quotations.original: Puta enim me confiteri verum esse quod dicis, aliquando post tonitrua emicare ignes stellis transversis et cadentibus similes, non ob hoc tonitrua facta sunt, sed, cum hoc fieret, tonitrua facta sunt.
quotations.translation: Consider that I admit what you say is true, that sometimes after thunder fires gleam like shooting and falling stars. Thunder was not caused on this account, but when this happened thunder occurred.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Puta enim me confiteri verum esse quod dicis, aliquando post tonitrua emicare ignes stellis transversis et cadentibus similes, non ob hoc tonitrua facta sunt, sed, cum hoc fieret, tonitrua facta sunt.
quotations.translation: Consider that I admit what you say is true, that sometimes after thunder fires gleam like shooting and falling stars. Thunder was not caused on this account, but when this happened thunder occurred.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Ergo, ut solet aestus aequinoctialis sub ipsum lunae solisque coitum omnibus aliis maior undare, sic hic qui ad occupandas terras emittitur, solitis maximisque violentior, plus aquarum trahit nec, antequam supra cacumina eorum quos perfusurus est montium crevit, devolvitur.
quotations.translation: Therefore, just as the equinoctial tide following the conjunction of the moon and the sun usually rises higher than at any other time, so the tide which is sent to overwhelm the lands is more violent than the greatest of ordinary tides and carries more water and does not ebb before it has risen above the peaks of the mountains which it intends to flood.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Ergo, ut solet aestus aequinoctialis sub ipsum lunae solisque coitum omnibus aliis maior undare, sic hic qui ad occupandas terras emittitur, solitis maximisque violentior, plus aquarum trahit nec, antequam supra cacumina eorum quos perfusurus est montium crevit, devolvitur.
quotations.translation: Therefore, just as the equinoctial tide following the conjunction of the moon and the sun usually rises higher than at any other time, so the tide which is sent to overwhelm the lands is more violent than the greatest of ordinary tides and carries more water and does not ebb before it has risen above the peaks of the mountains which it intends to flood.

quotations.original: Arsura enim terrena contendit, quandoque omnia sidera quae nunc diversos agunt cursus in Cancrum convenerint, sic sub eodem posita vestigio ut recta linea exire per orbes omnium possit; inundationem futuram, cum eadem siderum turba in Capricornum convenerit. Illic solstitium, hic bruma conficitur; magnae potentiae signa, quando in ipsa mutatione anni momenta sunt.
quotations.translation: For earthly things will burn, he contends, when all the planets which now maintain different orbits come together in [...] Cancer, and are so arranged in the same path that a straight line can pass through the spheres of all of them. The deluge will occur when the same group of planets meets in [...] Capricorn. The solstice is caused by Cancer, winter by Capricorn; they are signs of great power since they are the turning-points in the very change of the year.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

Illic solstitium, hic bruma conficitur; magnae potentiae signa, quando in ipsa mutatione anni momenta sunt.

The deluge will occur when the same group of planets meets in the sign of Capricorn. The solstice is caused by Cancer, winter by Capricorn; they are signs of great power since they are the turning-points in the very change of the year.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Nam et caput eius in Germania esse comperimus, et aestate quidem incipit crescere sed, adhuc manente intra mensuram suam Nilo, primis caloribus, cum sol vehementior intra extrema veris nives mollit, quas ante consumit quam tumescere Nilus incipiat; reliquo vero aestatis minuitur et ad hibernam magnitudinem redit atque ex ea demittitur. At Nilus ante exortum Caniculae augetur mediis aestibus ultra aequinoctium.
quotations.translation: For we have found out that the source of the Danube is in Germany. It does begin to rise in the summer but at a time when the Nile is still flowing within its normal limits, when a strong sun between the beginning and the end of spring softens the snows, which the sun melts entirely before the Nile begins to rise. In the rest of the summer the Danube diminishes and returns to its winter level, and even falls below it. But the Nile increases from the middle of the summer, before the rise of the Dog Star, to beyond the equinox.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: At quisquis mundum mensura sua aestimaverit et terram cogitaverit tenere puncti locum, intelleget nihil in illa posse ita eminere ut caelestia magis sentiat, velut in propinquum illis accesserit.
quotations.translation: But anyone who judges the universe by its own measure and reflects that the earth occupies only the position of a pinpoint, will realize that nothing on earth can be so high that it can feel more strongly the influences from the sky as though it had approached close to them.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Hoc falsum esse ex eo apparet quod aura in omnem partem vehit et contra ortum plenis velis navigatur; quod non eveniret, si semper ventus ferretur a sole.
quotations.translation: That this is wrong is obvious from the fact that the breeze blows vessels in every direction and a ship can be navigated with full sails against the sunrise. This would not happen if the wind were always coming from the direction of the sun.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Etesiae, inquiunt, hieme non sunt, quia brevissimis diebus sol desinit, priusquam frigus evincatur;
quotations.translation: The Etesian winds do not exist in the winter, they say, because in a season of very short days the sunshine ends before the cold is overcome.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Et ob hoc a solstitio illis initium est—ultraque ortum Caniculae non valent—quia iam multum e frigida caeli parte in hanc egestum est ac sol mutato cursu in nostram rectior tendit et alteram partem aeris attrahit, alteram vero impellit.
quotations.translation: And for this reason the Etesians have their beginning at the summer solstice. They do not blow strong after the rise of the Dog Star, because by then much of the cold section of the sky has been carried down to this region; and the sun, after changing direction, moves towards our region more directly and attracts one part of the atmosphere while repelling another part.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Iulio enim mense iam despoliata sunt omnia aut certe admodum pauca iacent adhuc sub nive.
quotations.translation: For in the month of July everything is clear of snow, or at least very few places still lie under snow.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Sed ut ad id de quo agitur revertar, venti quattuor sunt, in ortum, occasum, meridiem septemtrionemque divisi
quotations.translation: But to return to the subject which is being discussed: there are four winds, divided amongst the East, the West, the South, and the North.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Ab oriente hiberno eurus exit, quem nostri vocavere vulturnum—T. Livius hoc illum nomine appellat in illa pugna [...]
quotations.translation: Eurus comes from the winter sunrise [S.E.], a wind which our people call Vulturnus. T. Livy calls it by this name in connection with that famous battle [...]
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Qui surgit ab oriente aequinoctiali, subsolanus apud nos dicitur, Graeci illum ἀφηλιώτην vocant.
quotations.translation: The wind which4 rises from the equinoctial sunrise [E.] is called by us Subsolanus; the Greeks call it the Apheliotes.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Non enim eodem semper loco sol oritur aut occidit, sed alius est ortus occasusque aequinoctialis—bis autem aequinoctium est—alius solstitialis, alius hibernus.
quotations.translation: For the sun does not always rise or set in the same place. One rising and setting is the equinoctial [i.e., rising due E., setting due W.]—moreover, the equinox occurs twice a year—another is the summer-solstitial [i.e., rising in the N.E., setting in the N.W.], and still another the winter-solstitial [i.e. rising in the S.E., setting in the S.W.].
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Ab oriente solstitiali excitatum καικίαν Graeci appellant; apud nos sine nomine est.
quotations.translation: The wind which is aroused from the summer-solstitial sunrise [N.E., though in fact Caecias is the E.N.E. wind] the Greeks call Caecias; it has no name in our language.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Aequinoctialis occidens favonium mittit, quem zephyrum esse dicent tibi etiam qui graece nesciunt loqui.
quotations.translation: The equinoctial sunset [W.] sends Favonius, which5 even those who do not know how to speak Greek will tell you is Zephyr.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: A solstitiali occidente corus venit, qui apud quosdam argestes dicitur—mihi non videtur, quia cori violenta vis est et in unam partem rapax, argestes fere mollis est et tam euntibus communis quam redeuntibus—
quotations.translation: From the summer-solstitial setting [N.W.] comes Corus, which is called Argestes by some. This does not seem right to me, because the force of Corus is violent, gusting in one direction, while Argestes is ordinarily gentle and hits travellers the same coming and going.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: ab occidente hiberno africus furibundus et ruens; apud Graecos λίψ dicitur.
quotations.translation: From the winter sunset [S.W.] comes the furious rushing Africus; it is called Lips among the Greeks.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: A septemtrionali latere summus ere summus est aquilo, medius septemtrio, imus θρασκίας; huic deest apud nos vocabulum.
quotations.translation: In the northern section the highest is Aquilo [N.N.E.], the middle Septemtrio [N.], the lowest is Thrascias [N.N.W.], for which there is lacking a word in our language.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: A meridiano axe εὐρόνοτος est; deinde νότος, latine auster; deinde λευκόνοτος, apud nos sine nomine est.
quotations.translation: At the southern axis there is the Euronotus [S.S.E.]; then the Notus [S.], or in Latin the Auster; then the Leuconotus [S.S.W.], which has no Latin name.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Hanc lineam, quae inter aperta et occulta est (id est hunc circulum), Graeci ὁρίζοντα vocant, nostri finitorem esse dixerunt, alii finientem.
quotations.translation: The line (that is, this circle) which exists between the visible and the invisible sector is what the Greeks call the horizon line; some of us call it the limiter line, others call it the limiting line.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Caelum autem dividitur in circulos quinque, qui per mundi cardines eunt: est septemtrionalis, est solstitialis, est aequinoctialis, est brumalis, est contrarius septemtrionali.
quotations.translation: The sky is divided into five circles which pass through the cardinal points of the universe. In these five circles are the northern circle, the summer solstitial circle, the equinoctial circle, the wintry circle, and the one that is opposite to the northern.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Adiciendus est adhuc meridianus circulus, qui ὁρίζοντα rectis angulis secat.

quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Ergo ὁρίζων, sive finiens circulus, quinque illos orbes quos modo dixi fieri scindit et efficit decem partes, quinque ab ortu, quinque ab occasu.
quotations.translation: Accordingly, the horizon, or limiting circle, splits those five belts, whose location I just described, into ten sectors, five in the east and five in the west.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Non religionem incutit mentibus, et quidem publice, sive deficere sol visus est, sive luna (cuius obscuratio frequentior) aut parte sui aut tota delituit?
quotations.translation: Does it not inspire religion in men’s minds, and even on a nationwide scale, if the sun is seen in eclipse, or the moon (whose eclipses are more frequent) is obscured in part or entirely?
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Longeque magis illa, actae in transversum faces et caeli magna pars ardens et crinita sidera et plures solis orbes et stellae per diem visae subitique transcursus ignium multam post se lucem trahentium?
quotations.translation: And this is far more so in the case of torches driven across the scene, much of the sky burning, comets, several suns, stars appearing in the daytime, and the sudden passage of fires dragging a long trail of light after them.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.translation: And this is far more so in the case of torches driven [crosswise], much of the sky burning, comets, several suns, stars appearing in the daytime, and the sudden passage of fires dragging a long trail of light after them.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Horae sunt quas perdimus. Puta dies esse, puta menses, puta annos; perdimus illos nempe perituros.
quotations.translation: They are only hours which we lose. Suppose it is a matter of days, months, years; we lose only what is going to be lost anyway.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Sol spectatorem, nisi deficit, non habet. Nemo observat lunam nisi laborantem; tunc urbes conclamant, tunc pro se quisque superstitione vana strepitat.
quotations.translation: The sun does not have a spectator unless it is in eclipse, no one watches the moon if it is not in eclipse, but then cities cry out and each person makes a din in accordance with inane superstition.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Quanto illa maiora sunt quod sol totidem, ut ita dicam, gradus quot dies habet et annum circuitu suo claudit, quod a solstitio ad minuendos dies vertitur, quod ab aequinoctio statim inclinat et dat noctibus spatium
quotations.translation: How much more important are the following considerations. The sun has as many steps, so to speak, as it has days and it closes the year by its own circuit; from the summer-solstice it turns to make the days shorter; for, from the equinox it immediately inclines and gives more space to the night.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: quod sidera abscondit, quod terras, cum tanto maior sit illis, non urit sed calorem suum intensionibus ac remissionibus temperando fovet, quod lunam numquam implet nisi adversam sibi, nec obscurat nisi obliquam
quotations.translation: t hides the stars. Although the sun is much larger than the earth it does not burn it up but fosters it by controlling its heat in an alternately more intense and more subdued degree. It never causes the moon to be full unless it is opposite, nor dims it by phases unless it is oblique.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Duo certe, qui apud Chaldaeos studuisse se dicunt, Epigenes et Apollonius Myndius, peritissimus inspiciendorum natalium, inter se dissident.
quotations.translation: Certainly, two authorities, who say they studied among the Chaldaeans, disagree with each other, Epigenes and Apollonius of Myndus, the latter highly skilled in casting horoscopes.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Idem in cometis fit: si rarus et insolitae figurae ignis apparuit, nemo non scire quid sit cupit et, oblitus aliorum, de adventicio quaerit, ignarus utrum debeat mirari an timere.
quotations.translation: The same thing happens in the case of comets. If a rare fire, and one of unusual shape, appears everyone wants to know what it is and, ignoring the other celestial phenomena, asks about the newcomer, uncertain whether he ought to admire or fear it.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Huic videtur plurimum virium habere ad omnes sublimium motus stella Saturni. Haec, cum proxima signa Marti premit aut in lunae viciniam transit aut in solis incidit radios, natura ventosa et frigida contrahit pluribus locis aera conglobatque; deinde, si radios solis assumpsit, tonat fulguratque; si Martem quoque consentientem habet, fulminat.
quotations.translation: The planet Saturn seems to Epigenes to exert the greatest power on all the motions of the celestial bodies. When it presses upon the constellation closest to Mars or passes into the moon’s vicinity or encounters the rays of the sun, since it is windy and cold by nature, it attracts and collects air in many places. Then, if Saturn absorbs the rays of the sun there is thunder and lightning flashes. If it also has Mars in conjunction there are lightning bolts.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Huic videtur plurimum virium habere ad omnes sublimium motus stella Saturni. Haec, cum proxima signa Marti premit aut in lunae viciniam transit aut in solis incidit radios, natura ventosa et frigida contrahit pluribus locis aera conglobatque; deinde, si radios solis assumpsit, tonat fulguratque; si Martem 3quoque consentientem habet, fulminat.
quotations.translation: The planet Saturn seems to Epigenes to exert the greatest power on all the motions of the celestial bodies. When it presses upon the constellation closest to Mars or passes into the moon’s vicinity or encounters the rays of the sun, since it is windy and cold by nature, it attracts and collects air in many places. Then, if Saturn absorbs the rays of the sun there is thunder and lightning flashes. If it also has Mars in conjunction there are lightning bolts.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Huic videtur plurimum virium habere ad omnes sublimium motus stella Saturni. Haec, cum proxima signa Marti premit aut in lunae viciniam transit aut in solis incidit radios, natura ventosa et frigida contrahit pluribus locis aera conglobatque; deinde, si radios solis assumpsit, tonat fulguratque; si Martem 3quoque consentientem habet, fulminat.
