When it presses upon the constellation closest to Mars or passes into the moon’s vicinity or encounters the rays of the sun, since it is windy and cold by nature, it attracts and collects air in many places. Then, if Saturn absorbs the rays of the sun there is thunder and lightning flashes. If it also has Mars in conjunction there are lightning bolts.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Talem effigiem ignis longi fuisse Callisthenes tradit, antequam Burin et Helicen mare absconderet. Aristoteles ait non trabem illam sed cometen fuisse; ceterum ob nimium ardorem non apparuisse sparsum ignem sed, procedente tempore, cum iam minus flagraret, redditam suetam cometis faciem.
quotations.translation: Callisthenes reports that a similar likeness of an extended fire appeared just before the sea covered Buris and Helice. Aristotle says that this was not a Beam but a comet. Moreover, he says that because of its excessive brightness the fire did not appear scattered but as time went on and it blazed less it recovered the usual appearance of a comet.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Duo, inquit Epigenes, cometarum genera sunt. Alii ardorem undique effundunt nec locum mutant; alii in unam partem ignem vagum in modum comae porrigunt et stellas praetermeant, quales duo aetate nostra visi sunt.
quotations.translation: There are, Epigenes says, two types of comets. Some pour out fire in all directions and do not change position. Others extend a vague fire like hair in one direction and travel among the stars, like the two seen in our own time.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Cometas autem immixtos stellis videmus per superiora labentes.
quotations.translation: But indeed, we see comets mixed in with the stars, gliding through the upper regions.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Adice nunc quod, etiamsi in summum pertenderet, ubi sideribus iter est, utique ab eo motu qui universum trahit solveretur.
quotations.translation: Add now the fact that even if it reached the highest region, where the stars have their path, a whirlwind would be especially broken up by the motion which carries along the universe.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Vide ne hoc magis deceat magnitudinem mundi ut in multa itinera divisus est nec unam deterat semitam, ceteris partibus torpeat.
quotations.translation: Consider whether this concept is not more in keeping with the size of the universe: that the universe, divided as it is into many routes, does not wear away just one path while it is inactive in other sections.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Atqui quia lunaris illa orbita ceterorumque supra lunam meantium motus irrevocabilis est nec haesitat usquam nec resistit nec dat ullam nobis suspicionem obiectae sibi morae
quotations.translation: And yet the lunar orbit, and the movements of the other bodies travelling above the moon, is invariable. It nowhere hesitates or stops, nor does it give us any indication of an obstacle delaying it.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Quas antequam exponere incipiam, illud imprimis praesumendum est cometas non in una parte caeli aspici nec in signifero tantum orbe sed tam in ortu quam in occasu, frequentissime tamen circa septentrionem.
quotations.translation: Before I undertake to describe them I must first state that comets are seen not in one part only of the sky or only in the one area of the zodiac but they are seen as much in the east as in the west; most frequently, however, towards the north.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Quibusdam antiquorum haec placet ratio. Cum ex stellis errantibus altera se alteri applicuit, confuso in unum duarum lumine facies longioris sideris redditur; nec hoc tunc tantum evenit, cum stella stellam attigit, sed etiam cum appropinquavit; intervallum enim quod inter duas est illustratur ab utraque inflammaturque et longum ignem efficit.
quotations.translation: Some of the ancient scholars favour this explanation: when one of the planets has come into conjunction with another the light of both blends into one and presents the appearance of an elongated star. This happens not only when planet touches planet but even when they only come close. For the space between the two planets lights up and is set aflame by both planets and produces a train of fire.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Quibusdam antiquorum haec placet ratio. Cum ex stellis errantibus altera se alteri applicuit, confuso in unum duarum lumine facies longioris sideris redditur; nec hoc tunc tantum evenit, cum stella stellam attigit, sed etiam cum appropinquavit; intervallum enim quod inter duas est illustratur ab utraque inflammaturque et longum ignem efficit.

This happens not only when planet touches planet but even when they only come close. For the space between the two planets lights up and is set aflame by both planets and produces a train of fire.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

Cum ex stellis errantibus altera se alteri applicuit, confuso in unum duarum lumine facies longioris sideris redditur; nec hoc tunc tantum evenit, cum stella stellam attigit, sed etiam cum appropinquavit; intervallum enim quod inter duas est illustratur ab utraque inflammaturque et longum ignem efficit.

Cum ex stellis errantibus altera se alteri applicuit, confuso in unum duarum lumine facies longioris sideris redditur; nec hoc tunc tantum evenit, cum stella stellam attigit, sed etiam cum appropinquavit; intervallum enim quod inter duas est illustratur ab utraque inflammaturque et longum ignem efficit.

This happens not only when planet touches planet but even when they only come close. For the space between the two planets lights up and is set aflame by both planets and produces a train of fire.

quotations.original: His illud respondebimus certum esse numerum stellarum mobilium, solere autem eodem tempore et has apparere et cometen, ex quo manifestum fit non illarum coitu fieri cometen sed proprium esse et sui iuris.
quotations.translation: We will give this answer to their theory: the number of planets is fixed. Moreover, planets are usually visible when a comet also is seen to appear. Consequently it is obvious that a comet is not produced by a conjunction of planets but has its own existence and in its own right.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: et Saturnus aliquando supra Iovem est et Mars Venerem aut Mercurium recta linea despicit, nec tamen propter hunc illorum concursum, cum alter alterum subit, cometes fit.
quotations.translation: Saturn is often above Jupiter, and Mars looks vertically down on Venus or Mercury. And yet no comet is produced as a result of this coming together of planets, when one passes under the other.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Si cometen faceret stella stellae superveniens, momento esse desineret.
quotations.translation: If a star made a comet by approaching another4 star the comet would cease to exist in a moment.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Summa enim velocitas transeuntium est, ideoque omnis defectio siderum brevis est quia cito illa idem cursus qui admoverat abstrahit.
quotations.translation: For, the velocity of stars in transit is very great. Consequently, every eclipse of stars is brief because the same motion that brought them rapidly together separates them rapidly.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Summa enim velocitas transeuntium est, ideoque omnis defectio siderum brevis est quia cito illa idem cursus qui admoverat abstrahit.
quotations.translation: For, the velocity of stars in transit is very great. Consequently, every eclipse of stars is brief because the same motion that brought them rapidly together separates them rapidly.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Summa enim velocitas transeuntium est, ideoque omnis defectio siderum brevis est quia cito illa idem cursus qui admoverat abstrahit.
quotations.translation: For, the velocity of stars in transit is very great. Consequently, every eclipse of stars is brief because the same motion that brought them rapidly together separates them rapidly.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Videmus solem et lunam intra exiguum tempus, cum obscurari coeperunt, liberari: quanto celerior debet fieri in stellis digressio tanto minoribus?
quotations.translation: We see the sun and the moon separate within a very short time after the eclipse has begun. The separation ought to be much quicker in the case of stars, which are much smaller.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Videmus solem et lunam intra exiguum tempus, cum obscurari coeperunt, liberari: quanto celerior debet fieri in stellis digressio tanto minoribus?
quotations.translation: We see the sun and the moon separate within a very short time after the eclipse has begun. The separation ought to be much quicker in the case of stars, which are much smaller
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Adversus haec ab Artemidoro illa dicuntur: non has tantum stellas quinque discurrere, sed has solas observatas esse;
quotations.translation: Against such theories Artemidorus gives the following arguments: not these five planets only have erratic movements but these five are the only ones seen.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Adversus haec ab Artemidoro illa dicuntur: non has tantum stellas quinque discurrere, sed has solas observatas esse;
quotations.translation: Against such theories Artemidorus gives the following arguments: not these five planets only have erratic movements but these five are the only ones seen.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: ceterum innumerabiles ferri per occultum aut propter obscuritatem luminis nobis ignotas aut propter circulorum positionem talem ut tunc demum cum ad extrema eorum venere visantur.
quotations.translation: However, innumerable planets move in secret, unknown to us either on account of the dimness of their light or because the position of their orbits is such that they are eventually seen only when they reach the extremities of those orbits.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: ceterum innumerabiles ferri per occultum aut propter obscuritatem luminis nobis ignotas aut propter circulorum positionem talem ut tunc demum cum ad extrema eorum venere visantur.
quotations.translation: However, innumerable planets move in secret, unknown to us either on account of the dimness of their light or because the position of their orbits is such that they are eventually seen only when they reach the extremities of those orbits.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Illud etiamnune nemo dicere audebit mundum ferri per immensum et cadere quidem, sed non apparere an cadat, quia praecipitatio eius aeterna est, nihil habens novissimum in quod incurrat.
quotations.translation: Moreover, no one will dare to say that the world is moving through immense space and is actually falling, and that it is not apparent whether it falls or not because its headlong rush is eternal and it has nothing at the end with which it might collide.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Quid est deinde quo probes non quinque tantum stellas moveri sed multas esse et in multis mundi regionibus?
quotations.translation: How next can you prove that not only the five planets move but that there are also many planets in many regions of the universe?
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Primo igneus ac rubicundus orbis fuit clarumque lumen emittens, quanto vinceret noctem; deinde paulatim magnitudo eius districta est et evanuit claritas; novissime totus intercidit.
quotations.translation: At first it was a fiery red disc, emitting a light so bright that it dispelled the night. Then gradually its size diminished and its brightness faded. Finally it disappeared entirely.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Primo igneus ac rubicundus orbis fuit clarumque lumen emittens, quanto vinceret noctem; deinde paulatim magnitudo eius districta est et evanuit claritas; novissime totus intercidit.
quotations.translation: At first it was a fiery red disc, emitting a light so bright that it dispelled the night. Then gradually its size diminished and its brightness faded. Finally it disappeared entirely.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.translation: At first it was a fiery red disc, emitting a light so bright that it dispelled the night. Then gradually its size diminished and its brightness faded. Finally it disappeared entirely.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Attalo regnante initio cometes modicus apparuit; deinde sustulit se diffuditque et usque in aequinoctialem circulum venit, ita ut illam plagam caeli cui lactea nomen est in immensum extentus aequaret.
quotations.translation: In the reign of Attalus a comet appeared, of moderate size at first. Then it rose up and spread out and went all the way to the equator, so that its vast extent equalled the region of the sky which is called the Milky Way.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Non est, inquit, species falsa nec duarum stellarum confinio ignis extentus, sed proprium sidus cometae est, sicut solis ac lunae.
quotations.translation: A comet, he says, is not an illusion or fire extending from the edges of two planets but is a celestial body on its own, like the sun and the moon.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Ceterum non est illi palam cursus; altiora mundi secat et tunc demum apparet cum in imum cursus sui venit.
quotations.translation: On the other hand, its orbit is not clear. A comet cuts through the upper regions of the universe and then finally becomes visible when it reaches the lowest point of its orbit.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Ceterum non est illi palam cursus; altiora mundi secat et tunc demum apparet cum in imum cursus sui venit.
quotations.translation: On the other hand, its orbit is not clear. A comet cuts through the upper regions of the universe and then finally becomes visible when it reaches the lowest point of its orbit.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Talis illi forma est, non in rotundum restricta, sed procerior et in longum producta.
quotations.translation: It has a distinct shape thus: not limited to a disc, but extended and elongated lengthwise
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Deinde, quod adversus priores, etiam adversus hunc dicitur: si erraret cometes essetque sidus, intra signiferi terminos moveretur, intra quos omne sidus cursus suos colligit.
quotations.translation: Then, what is said against previous theorists is also said against this one: if a comet were a planet—that is, if it were a celestial body—it would move within the limits of the zodiac, within which all celestial bodies restrict their orbits.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Hoc loco sunt illa a Posidonio scripta miracula, columnae clipeique flagrantes aliaeque insigni novitate flammae.
quotations.translation: In this group are those marvellous sights described by Posidonius: blazing Columns and Shields, and other flames remarkable for their novelty.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Hoc loco sunt illa a Posidonio scripta miracula, columnae clipeique flagrantes aliaeque insigni novitate flammae.
quotations.translation: In this group are those marvellous sights described by Posidonius: blazing Columns and Shields, and other flames remarkable for their novelty.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Multos cometas non videmus, quia obscurantur radiis solis; quo deficiente quondam cometen apparuisse, quem sol vicinus obtexerat, Posidonius tradit.
quotations.translation: We do not see many comets because they are obscured by the rays of the sun. Posidonius reports that once during an eclipse a comet appeared which the nearness of the sun had concealed.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Placet ergo nostris cometas, sicut faces, sicut tubas trabesque et alia ostenta caeli, denso aere creari.
quotations.translation: Accordingly, our Stoics are pleased to believe that comets, like Torches, Trumpets, and Beams, and other displays of the sky, are created from condensed air.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: In aere quoque non dextram laevamque premit partem—nulla est enim illi via—sed, qua illum vena pabuli sui duxit, illa repit nec ut stella procedit sed ut ignis pascitur.
quotations.translation: Also, in the atmosphere it does not press to the right or left side—for it has no route—but it crawls wherever a vein of its food leads it. It does not proceed as a star does but feeds as a fire does.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Etiamnunc ignis aut it quo illum natura sua ducit, id est sursum, aut eo quo trahit materia cui adhaesit et quam depascitur; nullis ignibus ordinariis et caelestibus iter flexum est.
quotations.translation: Furthermore, fire either goes where its own1 nature leads it, that is, upwards, or in the direction that its fuel attracts it, to which it clings and on which it feeds. None of the ordinary fires in the sky has a curved path.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: “Si erratica,” inquit, “stella esset, in signifero esset.” Quis unum stellis limitem ponit?
quotations.translation: “If a comet were a planet,” someone said, “it would be in the zodiac.” Who places one boundary for planets?
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Quod si iudicas non posse ullam stellam, nisi signiferum attigit, vadere, cometes potest sic alium habere circulum ut in hunc tamen parte aliqua sui incidat;
quotations.translation: But if you are convinced that no planet can have an orbit unless it touches the zodiac, a comet can have such an unusual orbit that it still comes into the zodiac at some point of it.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Quid ergo miramur cometas, tam rarum mundi spectaculum, nondum teneri legibus certis nec initia illorum finesque notescere, quorum ex ingentibus intervallis recursus est?
quotations.translation: Why, then, are we surprised that comets, such a3 rare spectacle in the universe, are not yet grasped by fixed laws and that their beginning and end are not known, when their return is at vast intervals?
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: multaeque hodie sunt gentes quae facie tantum noverunt caelum, quae nondum sciunt cur luna deficiat, quare obumbretur.
quotations.translation: And yet there are many nations today that know the sky only by its face and do not yet understand why the moon lacks fulness and why it is obscured in an eclipse.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Harum quinque stellarum quae se ingerunt nobis, quae alio atque alio occurrentes loco curiosos nos esse cogunt, qui matutini vespertinique ortus sint, quae stationes, quando in rectum ferantur, quare agantur retro, modo coepimus scire;
quotations.translation: The five planets force themselves upon our attention. Occurring in one place or another they compel us to be curious. Recently we have begun to understand what their morning and evening risings mean, their positions, the time of their movement straight forwards, why they move backward.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Harum quinque stellarum quae se ingerunt nobis, quae alio atque alio occurrentes loco curiosos nos esse cogunt, qui matutini vespertinique ortus sint, quae stationes, quando in rectum ferantur, quare agantur retro, modo coepimus scire;
quotations.translation: The five planets force themselves upon our attention. Occurring in one place or another they compel us to be curious. Recently we have begun to understand what their morning and evening risings mean, their positions, the time of their movement straight forwards, why they move backward.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Non licet stare caelestibus nec averti; prodeunt omnia; ut semel missa sunt, vadunt;
quotations.translation: It is not possible for celestial bodies to stand still or turn away. They all move forward. Once they are set in motion they advance.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Non licet stare caelestibus nec averti; prodeunt omnia; ut semel missa sunt, vadunt;
quotations.translation: It is not possible for celestial bodies to stand still or turn away. They all move forward. Once they are set in motion they advance.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Quid est ergo cur aliqua redire videantur? Solis occursus speciem illis tarditatis imponit et natura viarum circulorumque sic positorum ut certo tempore intuentes fallant;
quotations.translation: What is the reason, then, that some celestial bodies appear to move backward? The encounter with the sun imposes upon them the appearance of slowness, as well as the nature of their paths and their orbits which are so placed that at a fixed period they deceive observers.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Dic tu mihi prius quare luna dissimillimum soli lumen accipiat, cum accipiat a sole; quare modo rubeat, modo palleat; quare lividus illi et ater color sit, cum conspectu solis excluditur.
quotations.translation: Tell me first why the moon receives light totally unlike the sun although she receives it from the sun. Why does the moon sometimes grow red, sometimes pale? Why is her colour blue or black when she is cut off from the sun’s view?
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Dic tu mihi prius quare luna dissimillimum soli lumen accipiat, cum accipiat a sole; quare modo rubeat, modo palleat; quare lividus illi et ater color sit, cum conspectu solis excluditur.
quotations.translation: Tell me first why the moon receives light totally unlike the sun although she receives it from the sun. Why does the moon sometimes grow red, sometimes pale? Why is her colour blue or black when she is cut off from the sun’s view?
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Et hoc tamen et illud sidus eiusdem condicionis est, cum effectu et natura dissimile sit. Intra brevissimum tempus Aries extollitur, Libra tardissime emergit;
quotations.translation: Yet both constellations are of the same class even though they are unlike in influence and characteristics. Aries rises within a very short time, Libra emerges quite slowly;
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: sed acrior sit Caniculae rubor, Martis remissior, Iovis nullus in lucem puram nitore perducto.
quotations.translation: The red of the Dog Star is brighter, that of Mars weaker, while Jupiter has no red, with its gleam extended into pure light.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Videamus nunc quemadmodum fiat is fulgor qui sidera circumvenit.
quotations.translation: Now let us see what causes that bright light1 which surrounds stars.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume I: Books 1-3. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 450. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1971.

quotations.original: Adice nunc quod, si causa illis flatus esset spatium diei ac longitudo, et ante solstitium flarent, cum longissimi dies sunt et cum maxime nives tabescunt.
quotations.translation: Add now the fact that if the cause of their blowing were the lengthened space of the day, they would also blow before the solstice when days are longest and when snows are mostly melted.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original:
Eurus ad Auroram Nabataeaque regna recessit
Persidaque et radiis iuga subdita matutinis.
Vesper et occiduo quae litora sole tepescunt
Proxima sunt zephyris. Scythiam septemque triones
Horrifer invasit boreas. Contraria tellus
Nubibus assiduis pluvioque madescit ab austro.
quotations.translation:
Eurus has gone toward the Dawn
And the Nabataean realms
And to Persia
And the ridges lying under
The morning rays.
Evening and the coasts
Which are warmed by the setting sun
Are close to Zephyrus.
The gusty Boreas has possessed
Scythia and the Septemtriones.
The land facing these
Drips
With continuous clouds
From the rainy Auster.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Ex his quidam circuli in transversa currunt et alios interventu suo scindunt.
quotations.translation: Out of these some circles run transversely and split the other circles by intersecting them.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Meridianus circulus, qui in ὁρίζοντα incurrit, regiones duas adicit.
quotations.translation: The meridian circle, which meets the horizon, adds two more sectors.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Non religionem incutit mentibus, et quidem publice, sive deficere sol visus est, sive luna (cuius obscuratio frequentior) aut parte sui aut tota delituit?
quotations.translation: Does it not inspire religion in men’s minds, and even on a nationwide scale, if the sun is seen in eclipse, or the moon (whose eclipses are more frequent) is obscured in part or entirely?
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Atqui quia lunaris illa orbita ceterorumque supra lunam meantium motus irrevocabilis est
quotations.translation: And yet the lunar orbit, and the movements of the other bodies travelling above the moon, is invariable.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: et hoc tamen sidus et illud eiusdem naturae est, cum illud exiguo tempore ascendat, hoc diu proferatur.
quotations.translation: and yet both these constellations are of the same character, although one ascends in a short time and the other appears slowly.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: sed sic quomodo aequinoctium in calorem frigusque flectentis anni, quomodo illa quae Chaldaei canunt, quid stella nascentibus triste laetumve constituat.
quotations.translation: but in the way that the equinox is a sign of the year turning to hot or to cold, or as the things the Chaldaeans predict, the sorrow or joy that is established at people’s birth by a star.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Sed mendacium est ire eos tardius, nam intra sextum mensem dimidiam partem caeli transcurrit hic proximus, prior intra pauciores menses recepit se.
quotations.translation: But it is not true that they move slowly, for this last comet ran across half the sky in only six months. The previous comet withdrew in fewer months.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Sed mendacium est ire eos tardius, nam intra sextum mensem dimidiam partem caeli transcurrit hic proximus, prior intra pauciores menses recepit se.

quotations.original: Deinde hic proximus a septentrione motus sui initium fecit et per occidentem in meridiana pervenit erigensque cursum suum oblituit, alter ille Claudianus, a septentrione primum visus, non desiit in rectum assidue celsior ferri, donec excessit.
quotations.translation: In the second place, this recent comet started its motion in the north and passing through the west it arrived in the southern region and its orbit passed out of sight as it was rising. The other comet, the one in the time of Claudius, was first seen in the north, and was carried continuously straight up and did not stop until it disappeared.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.original: Sideris proprium est ducere orbem.
quotations.translation: It is characteristic of a planet to follow a curve.
quotations.publication: Seneca. Natural Questions, Volume II: Books 4-7. Translated by Thomas H. Corcoran. Loeb Classical Library 457. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1972.

quotations.translation: It is also necessary to investigate the hostile places (topoi) and the planets, not with respect to the others alone, but also to the Ascendant and the Sun and Moon: for when these are in opposition, they signify critical years (klimakteres) and death.

quotations.translation:
You are helpless, despite all your art.
Let them stand up and help you now,
The scanners of heaven, the star-gazers,
Who announce, month by month,
Whatever will come upon you.

quotations.original: נִלְאֵ֖ית בְּרֹ֣ב עֲצָתָ֑יִךְ יַעַמְדוּ־נָ֨א וְיוֹשִׁיעֻ֜ךְ (הברו) [הֹבְרֵ֣י] שָׁמַ֗יִם הַחֹזִים֙ בַּכּ֣וֹכָבִ֔ים מֽוֹדִעִים֙ לֶחֳדָשִׁ֔ים מֵאֲשֶׁ֥ר יָבֹ֖אוּ עָלָֽיִךְ׃
quotations.transliteration: nilʾêt̲ bərōb̲ ʿăṣāt̲āyik̲ yaʿamd̲û-nāʾ wəyôšîʿuk̲ (hb̲rw) [hōb̲ərê] šāmayim haḥōzîm bakkôk̲āb̲îm môd̲iʿîm leḥŏd̲āšîm mēʾăšer yāb̲ōʾû ʿālāyik̲.
quotations.translation:
You are helpless, despite all your art.
Let them stand up and help you now,
The scanners of heaven, the star-gazers,
Who announce, month by month,
Whatever will come upon you.

quotations.original: וְהִשְׁבִּ֣ית אֶת־הַכְּמָרִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֤ר נָֽתְנוּ֙ מַלְכֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֔ה וַיְקַטֵּ֤ר בַּבָּמוֹת֙ בְּעָרֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֔ה וּמְסִבֵּ֖י יְרֽוּשָׁלָ֑͏ִם וְאֶת־הַֽמְקַטְּרִ֣ים לַבַּ֗עַל לַשֶּׁ֤מֶשׁ וְלַיָּרֵ֙חַ֙ וְלַמַּזָּל֔וֹת וּלְכֹ֖ל צְבָ֥א הַשָּׁמָֽיִם׃
quotations.transliteration: wəhišbît̲ ʾet̲-hakkəmārîm ʾăšer nāt̲ənû malk̲ê yəhûd̲āh wayqaṭṭēr babbāmôt̲ bəʿārê yəhûd̲āh ûməsibbê yərûšālā͏im wəʾet̲-hamməqaṭṭərîm labbaʿal laššemeš wəlayyārēaḥ wəlammazzālôt̲ ûlək̲ōl ṣəb̲āʾ haššāmāyim.
quotations.translation: He suppressed the idolatrous priests whom the kings of Judah had appointed to make offerings at the shrines in the towns of Judah and in the environs of Jerusalem, and those who made offerings to Baal, to the sun and moon and constellations—all the host of heaven.

quotations.original: נֹטֶ֣ה שָׁמַ֣יִם לְבַדּ֑וֹ וְ֝דוֹרֵ֗ךְ עַל־בָּ֥מֳתֵי יָֽם׃
quotations.transliteration: nōṭeh šāmayim ləb̲addô wəd̲ôrēk̲ ʿal-bomŏt̲ê yām.
quotations.translation:
Who by Himself spread out the heavens,
And trod on the back of the sea;

quotations.original: עֹֽשֶׂה־עָ֭שׁ כְּסִ֥יל וְכִימָ֗ה וְחַדְרֵ֥י תֵמָֽן׃
quotations.transliteration: ʿōśeh-ʿāš kəsîl wək̲îmāh wəḥad̲rê t̲ēmān.
quotations.translation:
Who made the Bear(?) and Orion,
Pleiades, and the chambers of the south wind;

quotations.original: הֲתֹצִ֣יא מַזָּר֣וֹת בְּעִתּ֑וֹ וְ֝עַ֗יִשׁ עַל־בָּנֶ֥יהָ תַנְחֵֽם׃
quotations.transliteration: hăt̲ōṣîʾ mazzārôt̲ bəʿittô wəʿayiš ʿal-bānêhā t̲anḥēm.
quotations.translation:
Can you lead out Mazzaroth(?) in its season,
Conduct the Bear with her sons?
quotations.comment:
Identified as "most probable of all" with Leo by Halpern (2002: 260).

quotations.original: הַֽ֭תְקַשֵּׁר מַעֲדַנּ֣וֹת כִּימָ֑ה אֽוֹ־מֹשְׁכ֖וֹת כְּסִ֣יל תְּפַתֵּֽחַ׃

quotations.translation:
Can you tie cords to Pleiades
Or undo the reins of Orion?

quotations.original: ⲡⲉⲛⲧⲁϥⲧⲁⲙⲓⲉ ⲧϭⲓⲛⲙⲟⲩⲧ ⲙⲛⲡⲥⲟⲩⲛⲣⲟⲩϩⲉ ⲙⲛⲡϣⲱⲡϣ ⲙⲛⲛⲧⲁⲙⲉⲓⲟⲛ ⲙⲡⲣⲏⲥ
quotations.transliteration: pentaftamie tcinmout mnpsounrouhe mnpšôpš mnntameion mprês
quotations.translation: Who makes Pleiades, and Hesperus, and Ursa Major, and the chambers of the south.

quotations.original: ⲁⲕⲉⲓⲙⲉ ⲇⲉ ⲉⲧⲙⲣⲣⲉ ⲛⲧϭⲓⲙⲙⲟⲩⲧⲉ ⲁⲩⲱ ⲁⲕⲟⲩⲱⲛ ⲙⲡⲉⲕⲧⲟ ⲙⲡⲥⲟⲩⲛϩⲱⲣ
quotations.transliteration: akeime de etmrre ntcimmoute auô akouôn mpekto mpsounhôr
quotations.translation: And dost thou understand the band of Pleiades, and hast thou opened the barrier of Orion?

quotations.original: IZI GE₆ 22 EN e SA₄ ša₂ ABSIN 1 KUŠ₃ 8 SI
quotations.translation: Month V, night of the 22nd, first part of the night, it was 1 cubit 8 fingers above the bright star of the furrow
quotations.genre: astronomical diaries and related texts: planetary excerpt
quotations.publication: Hunger, H. 2001. Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia, Vol. V. Lunar and Planetary Texts. Vienna, Austria: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wis­senschaften.
quotations.comment: EN occurs in two texts from Uruk, A 3456 and IM 44152; there I assumed an abbreviation or variant for USAN "first part of the night." (Hunger ADRT 5, 352; ADRT 6, XI).

quotations.translation: ...] ... in Akhelo, they will constitute 24 evils for him.

quotations.translation: If he (or it) had Me[rcury itsel]f as his (or its) Krahtout | his growth shall be established in its likeness.
quotations.publication: GH 95

quotations.original: τὸν δὲ ὡρονόμον ὡροσκόπον προσδεῖ δι’ ὅλην τὴν [ἀν]αλογίαν ἐκ τοῦ ἀναφορικοῦ πρὸς κλεψύδραν
quotations.translation: One also needs the hour-apportioning Ascendant in complete proportion from the (table) of rising-times according to a water clock
quotations.publication: GH 95

quotations.original:
quis foret humano conatus pectore tantum,
invitis ut dis cuperet deus ipse videri,
sublimis aperire vias imumque sub orbem,
et per inane suis parentia finibus astra?
quotations.translation: Who of but human understanding would have essayed so great a task as to wish against heaven’s wish to appear a god himself; to reveal paths on high and paths beneath the bottom of the earth and stars obedient to appointed orbits through the void?
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original:
iuvat ire per ipsum
aera et immenso spatiantem vivere caelo
et adversos stellarum noscere cursus.
quotations.translation: It is my delight to traverse the very air and spend my life touring the boundless skies, learning of the constellations and the contrary motions of the planets.
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.
quotations.comment: The fixed stars of the sky revolve from east to west, and so do the planets (seven, ineluding the Sun and Moon); but the speed of the latter is somewhat slower, so that their movement appears to be contrary to that of the stars. (Goold 1977)

quotations.original:
postquam omnis caeli species, redeuntibus astris,
percepta, in proprias sedes, et reddita certis
fatorum ordinibus sua cuique potentia formae, 
er varios usus artem experientia fecit
exemplo monstrante viam
quotations.translation: After every aspect of the sky had been observed, as the stars returned to their original positions, and each figuration had assigned to it its powers of influence in accordance with the sure cycles of destiny, by repeated practice and with examples pointing the way experience built up the science;
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original:
postquam omnis caeli species, redeuntibus astris,
percepta, in proprias sedes, et reddita certis
fatorum ordinibus sua cuique potentia formae, 
er varios usus artem experientia fecit
exemplo monstrante viam
quotations.translation: After every aspect of the sky had been observed, as the stars returned to their original positions, and each figuration had assigned to it its powers of influence in accordance with the sure cycles of destiny, by repeated practice and with examples pointing the way experience built up the science;
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original:
speculataque longe
deprendit tacitis dominantia legibus astra
quotations.translation: and from wide observation [they] discovered that by hidden laws the stars wield sovereign power
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original:
quasque vices agerent certa sub sorte notavit
omniaque ad numen mundi faciemque moveri
quotations.translation: what cycles they experienced according to fixed law, and that all things moved to the will and disposition of heaven
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original: summaque complexus stellantis culmina caeli
quotations.translation: compassing the rooftops of the starry sky
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original:
Quod nisi librato penderet pondere tellus,
non ageret currus, mundi subeuntibus astris,
Phoebus ab occasu et numquam remearet ad ortus
quotations.translation: And did not the Earth’s weight hang poised, the Sun would not drive his car past his setting, as the stars of heaven appeared, and would never return to his rising
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original:

quotations.translation: And did not the Earth’s weight hang poised, the Sun would not drive his car past his setting, as the stars of heaven appeared, and would never return to his rising
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original: lunave summersos regeret per inania cursus
quotations.translation: or the Moon pursues through space a path under the horizon
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original:
nec matutinis fulgeret Lucifer horis
Hesperos emenso dederat qui lumen Olympo.
quotations.translation: nor at the hour of dawn would shine the Morning Star, which earlier as the Star of Eve had sent forth its light after traversing the sky.
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original:
nunc, quia non imo tellus deiecta profundo
sed medio suspensa manet, sunt pervia cuncta
quotations.translation: As it is, however, since the Earth has not been cast down to the lowest depth but remains poised in midair, all the space about it affords passage
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original:
nam neque fortuitos ortus surgentibus astris
nec totiens possum nascentem credere mundum
quotations.translation: For I cannot believe that when stars appear to view their risings are the product of chance or that the firmament is so often created anew
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original: cum facies eadem signis per saecula constet
quotations.translation: for centuries the constellations have displayed the same features
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original:
cum suspensus eat Phoebus currusque reflectat
huc illuc agilis, et servet in aethere metas
quotations.translation: the Sun moves unsupported, as it wheels its chariot nimbly now this way and now that, keeping to its turning points in heaven
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original: solisve assiduos partus et fata diurna,
quotations.translation: or that the firmament is so often created anew and the Sun dies daily and is continually reborn
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original:
solisque orbem lunaeque rotundum
aspicimus tumido quaerentis corpore lumen,
quod globus obliquos totus non accipit ignes.
quotations.translation: round, we see, is the orb of the Sun, and round is the orb of the Moon, which looks in vain for light for its rotund body inasmuch as the sun’s oblique rays do not fall on the whole of its globe.
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original: sic tellus glomerata manet mundumque figurat
quotations.translation: So too the Earth is rounded and reflects the shape of the heavens
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.translation: That is why it is impossible to behold all the constellations in every part of the world. You will never find Canopus shining until you have crossed the seas and come to the shores of Rhodes
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.translation: That is why it is impossible to behold all the constellations in every part of the world. You will never find Canopus shining until you have crossed the seas and come to the shores of Rhodes
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original: sed quaerunt Helicen, quibus ille supervenit ignis
quotations.translation: but those who dwell beneath that brilliant star [i.e. Canopus] will look in vain for the Bear,
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original: te testem dat, luna, sui glomeraminis orbis
quotations.translation: [The Earth] makes you, O Moon, a witness to its roundness
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original:
quod si plana foret tellus, semel orta per omnem
deficeres pariter toti miserabilis orbi.
quotations.translation: If the Earth were flat, you would rise for the whole world only once and the failure of your light would be lamented by every land at the same time.
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original:
post illis apparet Delia terris
exoriens simul atque cadens
quotations.translation: the Moon appears to these lands first, and then to those, rising and setting simultaneously
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original: atque alios superat gyros aliosque relinquit
quotations.translation: as it rises above some horizons, leaving others behind
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original: atque alios superat gyros aliosque relinquit

quotations.original: omnia quae possis caelo numerare sereno
quotations.translation: signs all of which you will be able to count in a cloudless sky
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original: tum venit angusto Capricornus sidere flexus
quotations.translation: Next comes Capricorn, curled up within his cramped asterism
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.
quotations.comment: Capricorn does not completely fill up thirty degrees. (footnote Goold 1977)

quotations.original:
At qua fulgentis caelum consurgit ad Arctos,
omnia quae summo despectant sidera mundo
quotations.translation: Now where heaven reaches its culmination in the shining Bears, which from the summit of the sky look down on all the stars
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.

quotations.original:
nec norunt obitus unoque in vertice mutant
in diversa situm caelumque et sidera torquent
quotations.translation: and [the Bears] know no setting and, shifting their opposed stations about the same high point, set sky and stars in rotation
quotations.publication: Manilius. Astronomica. Edited and translated by G. P. Goold. Loeb Classical Library 469. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1977.
