quotations.original: Τὰ κατεστηριγμένα ζῴδια διαιρεῖται εἰς μέρη τρία. Ἅ μὲν γὰρ αὐτῶν ἐπὶ τοῦ ζῳδιακοῦ κύκλου κεῖται, ἃ δὲ λέγεται βόρεια, ἃ δὲ προσαγορεύεται νότια.
quotations.translation: The constellations are divided in three parts. For one of them lies on the zodiac, another is said to be “northern” and another is called “southern”.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Ὁ δὲ λόγος ἐπὶ τῶν δωδεκατημορίων, καὶ οὐκ ἐπὶ τῶν κατεστηριγμένων ζῳδίων.
quotations.translation: The statement is about the zodiac signs, and not about the constellations.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Ὁ δὲ λόγος ἐπὶ τῶν δωδεκατημορίων, καὶ οὐκ ἐπὶ τῶν κατεστηριγμένων ζῳδίων.
quotations.translation: The statement is about the zodiac signs, and not about the constellations.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: εὗρον ἐγὼ τὸν μὲν Δία μοιρικῶς ὡρονομοῦντα καὶ τὴν Ἀφροδίτην κατὰ τοῦ ὡροσκόπου καὶ τῆς Σελήνης καὶ τοῦ Διὸς καὶ τοῦ κλήρου τῆς τύχης ἀγαθοδαιμονοῦσαν καὶ ἑῴαν ἀνατολικὴν, καὶ τοῖς ἀριθμοῖς προσθετικὴν, καὶ δεκατεύουσαν τὴν τριταίαν τῆς Σελήνης, καὶ τὸ δωδεκατημόριον αὐτῆς Σκορπίον τετυχηκότα καὶ τὸν διέποντα τοῦ ὡροσκόπου τὸν Δία κατὰ κάθετον ὡρονομοῦντα.
quotations.translation: I found Jupiter apportioning the hours (i.e, in the Ascendant) in terms of degree, and Venus—with respect to the Ascendant and the Moon and Jupiter and the lot of fortune—being in (the place of) Agathos Daimon, at its eastern rising, additive in its numbers, and in superior (quartile) aspect to the Moon on the third day, and Scorpio happened to be its dodekatemorion, and the hour-ruler of the Ascendant, Jupiter, was apportioning the hours along the perpendicular.

quotations.original: ἔστι δὲ τὸ ζῴδιον (…) ἀμετάβολον
quotations.translation: The zodiac sign (Taurus) is (…) invariable

quotations.original: ἔστι δὲ τὸ ζῴδιον (…) ἐργαστικόν
quotations.translation: The zodiac sign (Taurus) is (…) industrious

quotations.original: Βόρεια δέ ἐστιν, ὅσα τοῦ τῶν ζῳδίων κύκλου πρὸς ἄρκτους κεῖται. Ἔστι δὲ τάδε· ἡ Μεγάλη Ἄρκτος, ἡ Μικρά, Δράκων ὁ διὰ τῶν Ἄρκτων, Ἀρκτοφύλαξ, Στέφανος, Ἐνγόνασιν, Ὀφιοῦχος, Ὄφις, Λύρα, Ὄρνις, Ὀϊστός, Ἀετός, Δελφίς, Προτομὴ Ἵππου καθ’ Ἵππαρχον, Ἵππος, Κηφεύς, Κασσιέπεια, Ἀνδρομέδα, Περσεύς, Ἡνίοχος, Δελτωτὸν καὶ ὁ ὕστερον κατεστηριγμένος ὑπὸ Καλλιμάχου Βερενίκης Πλόκαμος.
quotations.translation: Northern (constellations) there are as many as lie to the north of the zodiac. These are the following: the Great Bear, the Little (Bear), Dragon between the Bears, Bear Keeper, Crown, Kneeling Man, Ophiuchus, Serpent, Lyre, Bird, Arrow, Eagle, Dolphin, Forepart of a Horse according to Hipparchus, Horse, Cepheus, Cassiopeia, Andromeda, Perseus, Charioteer, Triangle and the later by Callimachus established Lock of Berenikē.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Ἰσημερία δέ ἐστι φθινοπωρινή, ὅταν ὁ ἥλιος ἀπ’ ἄρκτων πρὸς μεσημβρίαν παροδεύων πάλιν ἐπὶ τοῦ ἰσημερινοῦ γένηται κύκλου καὶ ἴσην τὴν ἡμέραν τῇ νυκτερινῇ ποιήσηται.
quotations.translation: And it is autumnal equinox, when the sun, in passing from north to south, arrives at the celestial equator again and makes the day equal to the night.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

Ἔστι δὲ τάδε· Ὠρίων καὶ Προκύων, Κύων, Λαγωός, Ἀργώ, Ὕδρος, Κρατήρ, Κόραξ, Κένταυρος, Θηρίον, ὃ κρατεῖ ὁ Κένταυρος, καὶ Θυρσόλογχος, ὃν κρατεῖ ὁ Κένταυρος καθ’ Ἵππαρχον, Θυμιαθήριον, Νότιος Ἰχθύς, Κῆτος, Ὕδωρ τὸ ἀπὸ τοῦ Ὑδροχόου, Ποταμὸς ὁ ἀπὸ τοῦ Ὠρίωνος, Νότιος Στέφανος, ὑπὸ δέ τινων Οὐρανίσκος προσαγορευόμενος, Κηρύκειον καθ’ Ἵππαρχον.
quotations.translation: Southern (constellations) there are as many as lie to the south of the zodiac. These are the following: Orion and Procyon, Dog, Hare, Argo, Hydra, Crater, Raven, Centaurus, Wild Animal, that Centaurus is holding, and Thyrsus-Lance, that Centaurus is holding according to Hipparchus, Censer, Southern Fish, Sea Monster, Water from Aquarius, River from Orion, Southern Crown, but according to some called Canopy, (and) Caduceus according to Hipparchus.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.comment: Aujac omits this constellation.

quotations.original: (...), νοτόθεν δὲ <συνανατέλλει> ὁ Ὠρίων ξίφος ἔχων ἐν τῇ δεξιᾷ χειρὶ ἀνατετακώς, τῇ εὐωνύμῳ κατέχει τὸ λεγόμενον Κηρίκειον, ἐζωσμένος κατὰ μέσον τοῦ σώματος.
quotations.translation: (...), in the south Orion <rises with it (i.e., Taurus)>, having a sword stretched out in his right hand - in his left one he holds the so-called Caduceus -, girdled around the middle of his body.
quotations.publication: Vettius Valens. 1986. Vettii Valentis Antiocheni Anthologarium Libri Novem, ed. D. Pingree. Leipzig: B.G. Teubner.

quotations.original: ἔστι δὲ τὸ ζῴδιον (…) ἀτελές
quotations.translation: The zodiac sign (Taurus) is (…) incomplete

quotations.original: Δίδυμοί εἰσιν … εὔφωνοι
quotations.translation: Gemini is … good-voiced

quotations.original: καὶ ἔστιν ὁ μὲν πρῶτος Χονταρέ, ὁ δὲ δεύτερος Χονταχρέ, ὁ τρίτος Σικέτ
quotations.translation: The first (decan of Aries) is Chontare, the second Chontachre, the third Siket

quotations.original: καὶ ἔστιν ὁ μὲν πρῶτος Χονταρέ, ὁ δὲ δεύτερος Χονταχρέ, ὁ τρίτος Σικέτ
quotations.translation: The first (decan of Aries) is Chontare, the second Chontachre, the third Siket

quotations.original: οἱ δὲ δεκανοὶ αὐτοῦ τρεῖς· Χώου ὁ πρῶτος, Ἔρω ὁ δεύτερος, Ῥομβρόμαρε ὁ τρίτος
quotations.translation: The decans of (Taurus) are three: Chōou is the first, Erō the second, Rhombromare the third

quotations.original: καὶ ἔστιν ὁ μὲν πρῶτος Χονταρέ, ὁ δὲ δεύτερος Χονταχρέ, ὁ τρίτος Σικέτ

quotations.translation: The decans of (Taurus) are three: Chōou is the first, Erō the second, Rhombromare the third

quotations.original: Οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἐπὶ τοῦ Ταύρου ἐπὶ τοῦ νώτου αὐτοῦ κείμενοι ἀστέρες τὸν ἀριθμὸν ϛʹ καλοῦνται Πλειάδες· οἱ δὲ ἐπὶ τοῦ βουκράνου τοῦ Ταύρου κείμενοι ἀστέρες τὸν ἀριθμὸν εʹ καλοῦνται Ὑάδες.
quotations.translation: The stars lying on Taurus, on its back, 6 in number, are called Pleiades; and the stars lying on the bull’s head of Taurus, 5 in number, are called Hyades.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἐπὶ τοῦ Ταύρου ἐπὶ τοῦ νώτου αὐτοῦ κείμενοι ἀστέρες τὸν ἀριθμὸν ϛʹ καλοῦνται Πλειάδες· οἱ δὲ ἐπὶ τοῦ βουκράνου τοῦ Ταύρου κείμενοι ἀστέρες τὸν ἀριθμὸν εʹ καλοῦνται Ὑάδες.
quotations.translation: Thus the stars lying on Taurus, on its back, 6 in number, are called Pleiades; and the stars lying on the bull’s head of Taurus, 5 in number, are called Hyades.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original:
Κύπρις δ’ ἐν Ταύρῳ γάνυται νόον, ἐν δέ νυ Κούρῃ
Ἑρμείας
quotations.translation: The mind of the Cyprian (Venus) rejoices in Taurus, that of Mercury in the Girl (Virgo)

quotations.original: Καρκίνον αὖτε λάχεν (…) ἠματί⟨η⟩ Κύπρις
quotations.translation: The Cyprian (Venus) has been allotted Cancer (and Scorpio and Pisces, as its triangle) by day

quotations.original: Μήνη δὲ περὶ τριτάτην Ταύροιο
quotations.translation: And the Moon (has its exaltation) at the third (degree) of Taurus

quotations.original: Αἰγίοχος δὲ Καρκίνου ἐν δεκαπέντε
quotations.translation: And the Aegis-bearer (Jupiter) (has its exaltation) in fifteen (degrees) of Cancer

quotations.original: ἤν (…) δόμον ἢ ὕψος τύχῃ λελαχυῖα Σελήνη
quotations.translation: If (…) the Moon happens to have been in its house or exaltation

quotations.original: ἢν δ’ ἂρ Ἐνυαλίῳ συνέῃ Κρόνος
quotations.translation: If Saturn is together with the Warlike one (Mars)

quotations.original:
δὴ γὰρ Θοῦρος ἀεὶ σφοδρός τε καὶ ὠκὺς 
εἰς ὁρμὰς ἄσκεπτον ἀεὶ τάχος ἠδ’ ἀλόγιστον
θερμὸς ἐὼν ἤνεγκεν
quotations.translation: For the Furious one (Mars), always forceful and quick in impulse, being hot, has brought a haste always unconsidered and unreasoned

quotations.original: οἱ δὲ τρεῖς δεκανοί εἰσιν οὗτοι· Θοσόλκ ὁ πρῶτος, Οὔαρε ὁ δεύτερος, Φούορι ὁ τρίτος
quotations.translation: The three decans (of Gemini) are these: Thosolk is the first, Ouare the second, Phouori the third

quotations.translation: The decans are three: the first, Souchōe, the second, Ptēchout, the third, Chontare

quotations.original: Ὁ δὲ προηγούμενος τῶν ποδῶν τῶν Δίδυμων ἀστὴρ προσαγορεύεται Πρόπους.
quotations.translation: The leading star of the feet of Gemini is called Propus.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.
quotations.comment: Some manuscripts have the variant Τρόπους or Τρίπους, probably resulting from a wrong copying of Π into T as the name Πρόπους (“forward foot”) is fitting in the context.

quotations.original: Οἱ δὲ ἐν τῳ Καρκίνῳ νεφελοειδεῖ συστροφῇ ἐοικότες καλοῦνται Φάτνη· οἱ δὲ πλησίον αὐτῆς δύο ἀστέρες κείμενοι Ὄνοι προσαγορεύεται.
quotations.translation: The ones (i.e. stars) in Cancer looking like a nebulous mass are named Manger; and the two stars lying close to it are called Asses.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Ὁ δὲ ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ τοῦ Λέοντος κείμενος λαμπρὸς ἀστὴρ ὁμωνύμως τῷ τόπῳ, ἐφ’ ᾧ κεῖται, Καρδία Λέοντος προσαγορεύεται· ὑπὸ δέ τινων Βασιλίσκος καλεῖται, ὅτι δοκοῦσιν οἱ περὶ τὸν τόπον τοῦτον γεννώμενοι βασιλικὸν ἔχειν τὸ γενέθλιον.
quotations.translation: The bright star lying in the heart of the Lion is called equally in name to the place, in which it lies, Heart of Lion; but according to some it is named Basiliskos, because those born around this place are reputed to have a royal nativity.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Ὁ δὲ ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ τοῦ Λέοντος κείμενος λαμπρὸς ἀστὴρ ὁμωνύμως τῷ τόπῳ, ἐφ’ ᾧ κεῖται, Καρδία Λέοντος προσαγορεύεται· ὑπὸ δέ τινων Βασιλίσκος καλεῖται, ὅτι δοκοῦσιν οἱ περὶ τὸν τόπον τοῦτον γεννώμενοι βασιλικὸν ἔχειν τὸ γενέθλιον.

quotations.original:
Κερόεσσα, τό τε πλάτος ἐμβαίνουσα
ᾧ τε βορειοτάτον ζώνης πλινθήιόν ἐστιν
quotations.translation: The Horned one (Moon), approaching both in latitude and to the part of its zone in which the northernmost border is

quotations.original: ἢ Διὸς ἢ Παφίης ἐν σχήμασι μαρτυρεόντων ἢ καὶ συνεσσομένων
quotations.translation: With Jupiter or the Paphian (Venus) witnessing in configurations or even being together (in the same sign)

quotations.original: οἱ δὲ δεκανοὶ τρεῖς· ὁ πρῶτος Στωχνῆε, ὁ δὲ δεύτερος Σεσμέ, ὁ τρίτος Σισιεμέ
quotations.translation: The decans are three: the first is Stōchnēne, the second Sesme, the third Sisieme

quotations.translation: The three decans of (Sagittarius) are: the first, Rhēouō; the second, Sesme; the third, Komme

quotations.translation: The three decans of (Capricorn) are: Smat, the first; Srō, the second; Isrō, the third

quotations.original: ἔχει δὲ δεκανοὺς γ'· καὶ τῷ μὲν πρώτῳ δεκανῷ παρανατέλλουσιν ἡ Άθηνᾶ καὶ ἡ οὐρὰ τοῦ Κήτους καὶ τὸ γ' τοῦ Δελτωτοῦ καὶ ὁ Κυνοκέφαλος ὁ τὰ λύχνα φέρων καὶ ἡ κεφαλὴ τοῦ Αἰλούρου τῆς δωδεκαώρου.
quotations.translation: [Aries] has 3 decans. And together with the first decan rise Athena, the tail of Cetus, the 3[rd star of] the Triangle and the Dog-headed One who carries the lamps and the head of the Cat from the dodecaoros.
quotations.publication: CCAG VII

quotations.original: ἐπεὶ οὖν ἡ Σελένη ἐν τῷ κέντρῳ εὑρέθη, ἐξετράπη ἠ γένεσις δι' ἡμερῶν σπ' καὶ ὡρῶν ιβ'.
quotations.translation: Since the moon is at a cardinal point [IC], the nativity will occur in 280 days and 12 hours.
quotations.publication: Vettius Valens. 1986. Vettii Valentis Antiocheni Anthologarium Libri Novem, ed. D. Pingree. Leipzig: B.G. Teubner.

quotations.original: νῦν γὰρ ἐν μὲν τοῖς κατὰ μῆνα σχηματισμοῖς πάσας λαμβάνει τὰς διαιρέσεις (καὶ γὰρ εὐθεῖα γίνεται καὶ ἀμφίκυρτος καὶ κοίλη)
quotations.translation: As it is, the shapes which the moon itself each month shows are of every kind straight, gibbous, and concave-but in eclipses the outline is always curved;

quotations.original: κζʹ. Τὰ κυνοκαύματα· καὶ ἡ σταφυλὴ ἄρχεται περκάζειν.
quotations.translation: 27. The dog-days: and the grapes begin to turn dark.
quotations.publication: L. Bianchi, 1914: Sitzungsberichte der Heidelberger Akademie der Wissenschaften, Philosophisch-Historische Klasse (1914, 3. Abhandlung): Griechische Kalender: IV. Der Kalender des sogenannten Clodius Tuscus

quotations.original:
7. de ydromelli
inchoantibus canicularibus diebus aquam puram pridie sumis ex fonte.
quotations.translation:
7. On Honey-water.
At the beginning of the dog days, the day before you take
pure water from a spring.
quotations.publication: Brodersen, K. (Ed.). (2016). Das Bauernjahr: Lateinisch-deutsch. Walter de Gruyter GmbH & Co KG.

quotations.original: Οἱ Λεοντιανοὶ καὶ Παρθενιανοὶ καὶ Σκορπιανοὶ καὶ Τοξιανοὶ φαλακροὶ γίνονται ἢ ἀναφαλαντιαῖοι·
quotations.translation: Those born under Leo, Virgo, Scorpio, and Sagittarius become bald or develop receding hairlines.
quotations.publication: CCAG VII

quotations.translation: For those born under Capricorn become more prone to receding hairlines.

quotations.original: Ὁ μὲν γὰρ ἀνὰ μέσον τῶν σκελῶν τοῦ Ἀρκτοφύλακος κείμενος ἐπίσημος ἀστὴρ Ἀρκτοῦρος ὀνομάζεται.
quotations.translation: The notable star lying in the midst of the legs of the Bear Keeper is named Arcturus.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: (5) 26 ina ŠU₂ ina SAG R1N₂ IGI ma-diš (6) TUR
quotations.translation: (5) (Day) 26, it (Jupiter) appears in the West in the beginning of Libra, it is very (6) faint.
quotations.genre: astronomical diaries and related texts: planetary excerpt
quotations.publication: Hunger, H. 2001. Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia, Vol. V. Lunar and Planetary Texts. Vienna, Austria: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wis­senschaften.

quotations.original: ina 30 MU.MEŠ 7.20 KI-šu₂ ana GIŠ.NIM DIB
quotations.translation: In 30 years its (Saturn's) position passes to the east by 7;20 (UŠ).
quotations.publication: Brack-Bernsen & Hunger 2005/6, AfO 51, 96-107

quotations.original: οἱ δὲ τρεῖς αὐτοῦ δεκανοί· Πτιαῦ ὁ πρῶτος, Ἀεὺ ὁ δεύτερος, Πτηβυοὺ ὁ τρίτος

quotations.translation: In the second decan (of Aries), called Sentachor

quotations.original: δεκανῶι δευτέρωι καλουμένῳ Αρωθ
quotations.translation: In the second decan (of Taurus), called Arōth

quotations.original: ὁ δ’ οἴαξ τῶν ὅλων ὡροσκόπος Σκορπίου ἀπ̣έτεμνε μοίρας δέκα ὀκτώι (…) δεκανὸν Θουμου̣θ̣
quotations.translation: The rudder of all, the Ascendant, cut off eighteen degrees of Scorpio (…) the decan Thoumouth

quotations.translation: The Shining one (Saturn) wards off raging fire (from houses) with its strength when in aspect, but the Furious one (Mars) provokes it

quotations.original: συνδέσμῳ δ’ ἀνάγοντι Σεληναίης παρεούσης
quotations.translation: When the Moon is present in the ascending lunar node

quotations.original: dil-bat ina MAŠ₂ TUR

quotations.original: κόρην ἂν φράσσαιο καὶ ἠυκόμου Κυθερείης
quotations.translation: You would declare (the prospects for) a wife (lit. “girl”) (from the Descendant) and the fair-haired one from Cythera (Venus)

Ἠέλιος φαυλοῖσι βεβλαμμένος, Ἀφρογενής τε 
(…)
ἀνέρι πῆμα φέρουσιν
quotations.translation: The Sun, when injured by bad ones (malefics), and the Foam-born (Venus) (…) bring pain to a husband

quotations.translation: when Zeus (Jupiter) has rushed at (approached) or is even present (in the same zodiac sign) with her (Venus)

quotations.original: Ὁ δὲ ἐν ἄκρᾳ τῇ ἀριστερᾷ χειρὶ τῆς Παρθένου κείμενος λαμπρὸς ἀστὴρ Στάχυς προσαγορεύεται· ὁ δὲ παρὰ τὴν δεξιὰν τῆς Παρθένου πτέρυγα κείμενος ἀστερίσκος Προτρυγητὴρ ὀνομάζεται.
quotations.translation: The bright star lying on the tip of the left hand of Virgo is called Wheat Ear; and the little star lying near the right wing of Virgo is named Harbinger of the Vintage.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Ὁ δὲ ἐν ἄκρᾳ τῇ ἀριστερᾷ χειρὶ τῆς Παρθένου κείμενος λαμπρὸς ἀστὴρ Στάχυς προσαγορεύεται· ὁ δὲ παρὰ τὴν δεξιὰν τῆς Παρθένου πτέρυγα κείμενος ἀστερίσκος Προτρυγητὴρ ὀνομάζεται.

quotations.original: Οἱ δὲ ὲν ἄκρᾳ τῇ δεξιᾷ χειρὶ κείμενοι τοῦ Ὑδροχόου δʹ ἀστέρες Κάλπις καλοῦνται.
quotations.translation: The 4 stars lying on the tip of the right hand of Aquarius are called Pitcher.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.
quotations.comment: Some manuscripts have the variant Κάλπεις or Κάλπη.

quotations.original:
α. ἀρχαίης ὦ θινὸς ἐπεστηλωμένον ἄχθος,
εἴποις ὅντιν’ ἔχεις, ἢ τίνος, ἢ ποδαπόν.
β. Φίντων’ Ἑρμιονῆα Βαθυκλέος, ὃν πολὺ κῦμα
ὤλεσεν, Ἀρκτούρου λαίλαπι χρησάμενον.
quotations.translation:
A. “O stone standing a burden on the ancient beach, tell me whom thou holdest, whose son and whence.”
B. “Phinto the son of Bathycles of Hermione, who perished in the heavy sea, encountering the blast of Arcturus.”
quotations.publication: Anth. Gr. 7.503

quotations.original: Οἱ δὲ ἀπὸ τῶν οὐραίων μερῶν τῶν Ἰχθύων κατὰ τὸ ἑξῆς κείμενοι ἀστέρες Λίνοι προσαγορεύεται· εἰσί δὲ ἐν μὲν τῷ νοτίῳ λίνῳ ἀστέρες θʹ, ἐν δὲ τῷ βορείῳ λίνῳ ἀστέρες εʹ· ὁ δὲ ἐν ἄκρῳ τῷ λίνῳ κείμενος λαμπρὸς ἀστὴρ Σύνδεσμος προσαγορεύτεται.
quotations.translation: The stars lying from the tail parts of Pisces in a row are called Cords; in the southern cord there are 9 stars, in the northern cord there are 5 stars; the bright star lying on the tip of the cord is called Knot.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.
quotations.comment: Some manuscripts have the variant Λίνον or Λήνον, thus not taking both cords together as a constellation but distinguishing them into two constellations immediately, as two separate cords from two separate fish.

quotations.original: Οἱ δὲ ἀπὸ τῶν οὐραίων μερῶν τῶν Ἰχθύων κατὰ τὸ ἑξῆς κείμενοι ἀστέρες Λίνοι προσαγορεύεται· εἰσί δὲ ἐν μὲν τῷ νοτίῳ λίνῳ ἀστέρες θʹ, ἐν δὲ τῷ βορείῳ λίνῳ ἀστέρες εʹ· ὁ δὲ ἐν ἄκρῳ τῷ λίνῳ κείμενος λαμπρὸς ἀστὴρ Σύνδεσμος προσαγορεύτεται.

quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Ὁ δὲ παρὰ τὴν Λύραν κείμενος λαμπρὸς ἀστὴρ ὁμωνύμως ὅλῳ τῷ ζῳδίῳ Λύρα προσαγορεύεται.
quotations.translation: The bright star lying by the Lyre is called with the same name as the whole constellation, Lyre.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Ὁ δὲ παρὰ τὴν Λύραν κείμενος λαμπρὸς ἀστὴρ ὁμωνύμως ὅλῳ τῷ ζῳδίῳ Λύρα προσαγορεύεται.

quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Ὁ δὲ μέσος τῶν ἐν τῷ Ἀετῷ τριῶν ἀστέρων ὁμωνύμως τῷ ζῳδίῳ Ἀετὸς προσαγορεύεται.
quotations.translation: The one (i.e., star) in the middle of the three stars in the Eagle is called with the same name as the whole constellation, Eagle.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Ὁ δὲ μέσος τῶν ἐν τῷ Ἀετῷ τριῶν ἀστέρων ὁμωνύμως τῷ ζῳδίῳ Ἀετὸς προσαγορεύεται.

quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Οἱ δὲ ἐν ἄκρᾳ τῇ ἀριστερᾷ χειρὶ τοῦ Περσέως κείμενοι ἀστέρες Γοργόνιον καλοῦνται· οἱ δὲ ἐν ἄκρᾳ τῇ δεξιᾷ χειρὶ τοῦ Περσέως κείμενοι ἀστερίσκοι πυκνοὶ καὶ μικροὶ εἰς τὴν Ἅρπην καταστηρίζονται.
quotations.translation: The stars lying on the tip of the left hand of Perseus are called Gorgon’s Head; the close-packed tiny little stars lying on the tip of the right hand of Perseus are fixed into the Sickle.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.
quotations.comment: Some manuscripts have the variant Γοργώνιον or Γοργόνιοι.

quotations.original: Ὁ δὲ ἐν τῷ εὐωνύμῳ ὤμῳ τοῦ Ἡνιόχου κείμενος λαμπρὸς ἀστὴρ Αἴξ προσαγορεύεται· οἱ δὲ ἐν ἄκρᾳ τῇ αὐτοῦ χειρὶ κείμενοι ἀστερίσκοι δύο Ἔριφοι καλοῦνται.
quotations.translation: The bright star lying on the left shoulder of the Charioteer is called Goat; the two little stars lying on the tip of his hand are called Kids.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Ὁ δὲ ἐν τῷ εὐωνύμῳ ὤμῳ τοῦ Ἡνιόχου κείμενος λαμπρὸς ἀστὴρ Αἴξ προσαγορεύεται· οἱ δὲ ἐν ἄκρᾳ τῇ αὐτοῦ χειρὶ κείμενοι ἀστερίσκοι δύο Ἔριφοι καλοῦνται.

quotations.original: Ὁ μὲν γὰρ ἐν τῷ Πρόκυνι ὢν λαμπρὸς ἀστὴρ Προκύων καλεῖται.
quotations.translation: The bright star which is in Procyon is called Procyon.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Ὁ μὲν γὰρ ἐν τῷ Πρόκυνι ὢν λαμπρὸς ἀστὴρ Προκύων καλεῖται.
quotations.translation: The bright star which is in Procyon is called Procyon.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Ὁ δὲ ἐν τῷ στόματι τοῦ Κυνὸς λαμπρὸς ἀστὴρ, ὃς δοκεῖ τὴν ἐπίτασιν τῶν καυμάτων ποιεῖν, ὁμωνύμως ὅλῳ τῷ ζῳδίῳ Κύων προσαγορεύεται.
quotations.translation: The bright star in the mouth of the Dog, which seems to cause the intensification of the heat, is called with the same name as the whole constellation, Dog.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Ὁ δὲ ἐν τῷ στόματι τοῦ Κυνὸς λαμπρὸς ἀστὴρ, ὃς δοκεῖ τὴν ἐπίτασιν τῶν καυμάτων ποιεῖν, ὁμωνύμως ὅλῳ τῷ ζῳδίῳ Κύων προσαγορεύεται.
quotations.translation: The bright star in the mouth of the Dog, which seems to cause the intensification of the heat, is called with the same name as the whole constellation, Dog.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Ὁ δὲ ἐν ἄκρῳ τῷ πηδαλίῳ τῆς Ἀργοῦς κείμενος λαμπρὸς ἀστὴρ Κάνωβος ὀνομάζεται· οὗτος μὲν ἐν Ῥόδῳ δυσθεώρητός ἐστιν ἢ παντελῶς ἀφ’ ὑψηλῶν τόπων ὀρᾶται· ἐν Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ δέ ἐστι παντελῶς ἐκφανής· σχεδόν γὰρ δʹον μέρος ζῳδίου ἀπὸ τοῦ ὁρίζοντος μετεωρισμένος φαίνεται.
quotations.translation: The bright star lying on the topmost rudder of the Argo is named Canopus; it is hard to observe in Rhodes or completely seen from high places (only); but in Alexandria it is completely showing itself: for it appears almost a 4th part of a zodiac sign (i.e., 7.5 degrees) elevated from the horizon.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.
quotations.comment: Some manuscripts have the variant Κάνοβος or Κάνωπος.

quotations.original: LUL.LA : AL.LUL
quotations.translation: The false star is the Crab.
quotations.publication: Reiner, E., Pingree, D. 1998. Babylonian Planetary Omens: Part Three.

quotations.original: MUL₄ sar-ru [...] : MUL₄ ṣal-bat-a-nu 7 MU-šú
quotations.translation: The false star [...] : Mars its 7 names
quotations.publication: Reiner, E., Civil, M. 1974. The Series HAR-ra = hubullu: Tablets XX-XXIV (Materials for the Sumerian Lexicon XI). Pontificium Institutum Biblicum: Rome.

quotations.original: χαίρει δὲ ὁ Ἑρμῆς ἀεὶ συνὼν κακοποιοῖς καὶ καλοποιοῖς
quotations.translation: Mercury always rejoices when with malefics and benefics

quotations.original: τῶν ἀγαθοποιῶν ἀποστρόφων ὄντων

quotations.original:
ἐπ̣[ὶ] δὲ ζ̣ῳ̣δίων ἃ μέν ἐσ[τι]ν̣ ἀκ[ο]ύ̣ο̣ντα

quotations.translation: As for the zodiac-signs, some are hearers of each other, some are seers of each other, some are sensers of each other.

quotations.original: ἀμφοτέροις εἴη κεν ἀπαίσιος ἥδε καταρχή
quotations.translation: This inception (of marriage) would be childless for both (husband and wife)
quotations.publication: p. 392 Pingree

quotations.original: ἐν ζῴῳ Μήνην κακοδαιμονέοντι
quotations.translation: (has) the Moon in a sign that is in the Place of Kakos Daimōn

quotations.original: ὅς κεν ἔχῃσι δωδέκατον μετὰ χῶρον ἀφ’ ὡρονόμοιο Σελήνην
quotations.translation: whoever has the Moon in the twelfth place from the Ascendant
quotations.publication: p. 393 Pingree

quotations.original: Τοῦ δὲ κόσμου σφαιροειδοῦς ὑπάρχοντος ἄξων καλεῖται ἡ διάμετρος τοῦ κόσμου, περὶ ἣν στρέφεται ὁ κόσμος. Τὰ δὲ πέρατα τοῦ ἄξονος πόλοι λέγονται τοῦ κόσμου.
quotations.translation: Since the cosmos is spherical, the diameter of the cosmos around which the cosmos turns, is called “axis”. The extremities of the axis are called “poles of the cosmos”.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Τῶν δὲ πόλων [τοῦ κόσμου] ὁ μὲν λέγεται βόρειος, ὁ δὲ νότιος, βόρειος μὲν ὁ διὰ παντὸς φαινόμενος ὡς πρὸς τὴν ἡμετέραν οἴκησιν, νότιος δὲ ὁ διὰ παντὸς ἀόρατος ὡς πρὸς τὸν ἡμέτερον ὁρίζοντα.
quotations.translation: Of the [celestial] poles, one is called “northern”, the other one “southern”, northern the one that is continually visible at our home, southern the one that is continually invisible on our horizon.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Εἰσὶ μέντοι τόποι τινὲς ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, ὅπου συμβαίνει τὸν μὲν παρ’ ἡμῖν πόλον τὸν ἀεὶ φανερὸν ἐκείνοις ἀόρατον εἶναι, τὸν δὲ παρ’ ἡμῖν ἀόρατον ἐκείνοις φανερὸν εἶναι.
quotations.translation: There are some places on the earth though, where it happens that the pole always visible for us is invisible to them, but that the invisible one for us is visible to them.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Τῶν δὲ ἐν τῇ σφαίρᾳ κύκλων οἱ μὲν εἰσι παράλληλοι, οἱ δὲ λοξοί, οἱ δὲ διὰ τῶν πόλων.
quotations.translation: Of the circles on the sphere, some are parallel, some are oblique, and some are [passing] through the poles.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Παράλληλοι μὲν οἱ τοὺς αὐτοὺς πόλους ἔχοντες τῷ κόσμῳ. Εἰσί δὲ παράλληλοι κύκλοι εʹ· ἀρκτικός, θερινὸς τροπικός, ἰσημερινός, χειμερινὸς τροπικός, ἀνταρκτικός.
quotations.translation: Parallel are those that have the same poles as the cosmos. There are 5 parallel circles: the arctic circle, the summer tropic, the celestial equator, the winter tropic, the antarctic circle.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Ἀρκτικὸς μὲν οὖν ἐστι κύκλος ὁ μέγιστος τῶν ἀεὶ θεωρουμένων κύκλων, ὁ ἐφαπτόμενος τοῦ ὁρίζοντος καθ’ ἓν σημεῖον καὶ ὅλος ὑπὲρ γῆν ἀπολαμβανόμενος, ἐν ᾧ τὰ κείμενα τῶν ἄστρων οὔτε δύσιν οὔτε ἀνατολὴν ποιεῖται, ἀλλὰ δι’ ὅλης τῆς νυκτὸς περὶ τὸν πόλον στρεφόμενα θεωρεῖται. Οὗτος δὲ ὁ κύκλος ἐν τῇ καθ’ ἡμᾶς οἰκουμένῃ ὑπὸ τοῦ ἐμπροσθίου ποδὸς τῆς Μεγάλης Ἄρκτου περιγράφεται.
quotations.translation: The arctic circle is the biggest of the always visible circles, the one touching the horizon in one point and as a whole taken aside above the earth, in which the stars lying in it never perform a setting nor a rising, but are observed during the whole night turning around the pole. This circle is delineated  in the inhabited region among us by the front foot of the Great Bear.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.
quotations.comment: The circle is delineated by the forefoot of Μεγάλη Ἄρκτος (Megalē Arktos), hence it is named the arctic circle after it.

quotations.original: Ἀρκτικὸς μὲν οὖν ἐστι κύκλος ὁ μέγιστος τῶν ἀεὶ θεωρουμένων κύκλων, ὁ ἐφαπτόμενος τοῦ ὁρίζοντος καθ’ ἓν σημεῖον καὶ ὅλος ὑπὲρ γῆν ἀπολαμβανόμενος, ἐν ᾧ τὰ κείμενα τῶν ἄστρων οὔτε δύσιν οὔτε ἀνατολὴν ποιεῖται, ἀλλὰ δι’ ὅλης τῆς νυκτὸς περὶ τὸν πόλον στρεφόμενα θεωρεῖται.
quotations.translation: The arctic circle is the biggest of the always visible circles, the one touching the horizon in one point and as a whole taken aside above the earth, in which the stars lying in it never perform a setting nor a rising, but are observed during the whole night turning around the pole.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Οὗτος δὲ ὁ κύκλος ἐν τῇ καθ’ ἡμᾶς οἰκουμένῃ ὑπὸ τοῦ ἐμπροσθίου ποδὸς τῆς Μεγάλης Ἄρκτου περιγράφεται.
quotations.translation: This circle (i.e., the arctic circle) is delineated  in the inhabited region among us by the front foot of the Great Bear.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Οὗτος δὲ ὁ κύκλος ἐν τῇ καθ’ ἡμᾶς οἰκουμένῃ ὑπὸ τοῦ ἐμπροσθίου ποδὸς τῆς Μεγάλης Ἄρκτου περιγράφεται.
quotations.translation: This circle (i.e., the arctic circle) is delineated  in the inhabited region among us by the front foot of the Great Bear.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.
quotations.comment: The circle is delineated by the forefoot of Μεγάλη Ἄρκτος (Megalē Arktos), hence it is named the arctic circle after it.

quotations.original: Θερινὸς δὲ τροπικὸς κύκλος ἐστὶν ὁ βορειότατος τῶν ὑπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου γραφομένων κύκλων κατὰ τὴν τοῦ κόσμου γινομένην περιστροφήν, ἐφ’ οὗ γενόμενος ὁ ἥλιος τὴν θερινὴν τροπὴν ποιεῖται, ἐν ῇ μεγίστη μὲν πασῶν τῶν ἐν τῷ ἐνιαυτῷ ἡμέρα, ἐλαχίστη δὲ ἡ νύξ γίνεται.
quotations.translation: The summer tropic is the northernmost of the circles described by the sun during the rotation that the cosmos is performing, on which the sun, when it is on it, makes the summer solstice, on which [the] longest day of all the [days] in the year and the shortest night fall.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Μετὰ μέντοι γε τὴν θερινὴν τροπὴν οὐκέτι πρὸς τὰς ἄρκτους παροδεύων ὁ ἥλιος θεωρεῖται, ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ τὰ ἕτερα μέρη τρέπεται τοῦ κόσμου, διὸ καὶ κέκληται τροπικός.
quotations.translation: Since after the summer solstice though the sun is no longer observed travelling to the north, but it turns itself to the other parts of the cosmos, for this reason it (i.e., the summer tropic) has been named “tropical” too.
quotations.publication: Geminus. 1975. Géminos, Introduction aux Phénomènes, ed. G. Aujac. Paris: Les Belles Lettres.

quotations.original: Mundum et hoc—quocumque nomine alio caelum appellare libuit cuius circumflexu teguntur cuncta, numen esse credi par est, aeternum, inmensum, neque genitum neque interiturum umquam.
quotations.translation: The world and this—whatever other name men have chosen to designate the sky whose vaulted roof encircles the universe, is fitly believed to be a deity, eternal, immeasurable, a being that never began to exist and never will perish.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Formam eius in speciem orbis absoluti globatam esse nomen in primis et consensus in eo mortalium orbem appellantium
quotations.translation: Its shape has the rounded appearance of ashape of world. perfect sphere. This is shown first of all by the name of ‘orb’ which is bestowed upon it by the general consent of mankind.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Hanc ergo formam eius aeterno et inrequieto ambitu, inenarrabili celeritate, viginti quattuor horarum spatio circumagi solis exortus et occasus haut dubium reliquere.
quotations.translation: The world thus shaped then is not at rest but eternally revolves with indescribable velocity, each revolution occupying the space of 24 hours: the rising and setting of the sun have left this not doubtful.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Nec de elementis video dubitari quattuor esse ea: igneum summum, inde tot stellarum illos conlucentium oculos;
quotations.translation: As regards the elements also I observe that they are accepted as being four in number: topmost the element of fire, source of yonder eyes of all those blazing stars;
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: obliquitatem eius intellexisse, hoc est rerum fores aperuisse, Anaximander Milesius traditur primus Olympiade quinquagesima octava, signa deinde in eo Cleostratus, et prima arietis ac sagittarii, sphaeram ipsam ante multo Atlas.
quotations.translation: Tradition says that Anaximander of Miletus in the fifty-eighth Olympiad was the first person to discover the obliquity of the zodiac, that is, to open the portals of science; and that next Cleostratus explained the signs in it, beginning with the Ram and the Archer; the firmament itself having been explained long before by Atlas.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: summum esse quod vocant Saturni sidus ideoque minimum videri et maximo ambire circulo ac tricesimo anno cum brevissime ad sedis suae principia regredi certum est;
quotations.translation: The star called Saturn’s is the highest and consequently looks the smallest and revolves in the largest orbit, returning in thirty years at the shortest to its initial station.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Saturni autem sidus gelidae ac rigentis esse naturae, multumque ex eo inferiorem Iovis circulum et ideo motu celeriore duodenis circumagi annis
quotations.translation: Saturn is of a cold and frozen nature. The orbit of Jupiter is much below it and therefore revolves much faster, completing one rotation every twelve years
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: tertium Martis, quod quidam Herculis vocant, igne ardens solis vicinitate, binis fere annis converti, ideoque huius ardore nimio et rigore Saturni interiectum ambobus ex utroque temperari Iovem salutaremque fieri;
quotations.translation: The third star is Mars, called by some Hercules; owing to the proximity of the sun it has a fiery glow; it revolves once in about two years, and consequently, owing to its excessive heat and Saturn’s frost, Jupiter being situated between them combines the influence of each and is rendered healthy.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: tertium Martis, quod quidam Herculis vocant, igne ardens solis vicinitate, binis fere annis converti, ideoque huius ardore nimio et rigore Saturni interiectum ambobus ex utroque temperari Iovem salutaremque fieri;
quotations.translation: The third star is Mars, called by some Hercules; owing to the proximity of the sun it has a fiery glow; it revolves once in about two years, and consequently, owing to its excessive heat and Saturn’s frost, Jupiter being situated between them combines the influence of each and is rendered healthy.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: praeveniens quippe et ante matutinum exoriens Luciferi nomen accipit ut sol alter diemque maturans, contra ab occasu refulgens nuncupatur Vesper ut prorogans lucem vicemque lunae reddens.
quotations.translation: when in advance and rising before dawn it receives the name of Lucifer, as being another sun and bringing the dawn, whereas when it shines after sunset it is named Vesper, as prolonging the daylight, or as being a deputy for the moon.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: itaque et in magno nominum ambitu est: alii enim Iunonis, alii Isidis, alii Matris Deum appellavere.
quotations.translation: Consequently there is a great competition to give it a name, some having called it Juno, others Isis, others the Mother of the Gods.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: itaque et in magno nominum ambitu est: alii enim Iunonis, alii Isidis, alii Matris Deum appellavere.
quotations.translation: Consequently there is a great competition to give it a name, some having called it Juno, others Isis, others the Mother of the Gods.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: itaque et in magno nominum ambitu est: alii enim Iunonis, alii Isidis, alii Matris Deum appellavere.
quotations.translation: Consequently there is a great competition to give it a name, some having called it Juno, others Isis, others the Mother of the Gods.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: ideo et peculiaris horum siderum ratio est neque communis cum supra dictis; nam ea et quarta parte caeli a sole abesse et tertia, et adversa soli saepe cernuntur, maioresque alios habent cuncta plenae conversionis ambitus in magni anni ratione dicendos.
quotations.translation: Consequently the course of these stars also is peculiar, and not shared by those above-mentioned: those are often observed to be a quarter or a third of the heaven away from the sun and travelling against the sun, and they all have other larger circuits of full revolution, the specification of which belongs to the theory of the Great Year.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: defectus autem suos et solis, rem in tota contemplatione naturae maxime miram et ostento similem, magnitudinum umbraeque indices exsistere.
quotations.translation: but that her eclipses and those of the sun, the most marvellous and indeed portentous occurrence in the whole of our observation of nature, serve as indications of their dimensions and shadow.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: quippe manifestum est solem interventu lunae occultari lunamque terrae obiectu
quotations.translation: It is in fact obvious that the sun is hidden by the passage across it of the moon, and the moon by the interposition of the earth
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: quippe manifestum est solem interventu lunae occultari lunamque terrae obiectu
quotations.translation: It is in fact obvious that the sun is hidden by the passage across it of the moon, and the moon by the interposition of the earth
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: ac vices reddi, eosdem solis radios luna interpositu suo auferente terrae terraque lunae: hac subeunte repentinas obduci terrae tenebras rursumque illius umbra sidus hebetari
quotations.translation: they retaliate on one another, the same rays of the sun being taken away from the earth by the moon intervening and from the moon by the earth: at the transit of the former a sudden shadow passes over the earth, and in return the shadow of the latter dims the heavenly body (the moon)
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: ac vices reddi, eosdem solis radios luna interpositu suo auferente terrae terraque lunae: hac subeunte repentinas obduci terrae tenebras rursumque illius umbra sidus hebetari

quotations.original: macti ingenio este, caeli interpretes rerumque naturae capaces, argumenti repertores quo deos hominesque vicistis! quis enim haec cernens et statos siderum (quoniam ita appellare placuit) labores non suae necessitati mortales genitos ignoscat?
quotations.translation: all hail to your genius, ye that interpret the heavens and grasp the facts of nature, discoverers of a theory whereby you have vanquished gods and men! for who beholding these truths and the regularity of the stars’ periods of trouble (for so it has pleased you to call them), would not forgive his own destiny for the generation of mortals?
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Defectus CCXXIII mensibus redire in suos orbis certum est, solis defectus non nisi novissima primave fieri luna, quod vocant coitum, lunae autem non nisi plena, semperque citra quam proxime fuerint;
quotations.translation: It is certain that eclipses recur in cycles of 223 months—eclipses of the sun only when the moon is in her last or first phase (this is called their ‘conjunction’), eclipses of the moon only at full moon—and always within the period of their last occurrence;
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Defectus CCXXIII mensibus redire in suos orbis certum est, solis defectus non nisi novissima primave fieri luna, quod vocant coitum, lunae autem non nisi plena, semperque citra quam proxime fuerint;
quotations.translation: It is certain that eclipses recur in cycles of 223 months—eclipses of the sun only when the moon is in her last or first phase (this is called their ‘conjunction’), eclipses of the moon only at full moon—and always within the period of their last occurrence;
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Lunam semper aversis a sole cornibus, si crescat, ortus spectare, si minuatur, occasus, haut dubium est
quotations.translation: It is unquestionable that the moon’s horns are always turned away from the sun, and that when waxing she faces east and when waning west;
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: postea a radiorum eius contactu regrediuntur, et in triquetro a partibus centum viginti stationes matutinas faciunt, quae et primae vocantur, mox in adverso a partibus centum octoginta exortus vespertinos, iterumque in centum viginti ab alio latere appropinquantes stationes vespertinas quas et secundas vocant, donec assecutus sol in partibus duodenis occultet illas, qui vespertini occasus appellantur.
quotations.translation: Afterwards they retire from contact with his rays, and make their morning or ‘first’ stations in a triangle 120 degrees away, and subsequently their evening risings opposite 180 degrees away, and again approaching from the other side, make their evening or ‘second’ stations 120 degrees away, till the sun overtaking them at 12 degrees obscures them—this is called their evening setting.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: postea a radiorum eius contactu regrediuntur, et in triquetro a partibus centum viginti stationes matutinas faciunt, quae et primae vocantur, mox in adverso a partibus centum octoginta exortus vespertinos, iterumque in centum viginti ab alio latere appropinquantes stationes vespertinas quas et secundas vocant, donec assecutus sol in partibus duodenis occultet illas, qui vespertini occasus appellantur.

quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: terra a verticibus duobus quos appellaverunt polos centrum caeli est, nec non et signiferi oblique inter eos siti.
quotations.translation: the earth between the two vertices, named in Greek poles, is the centre of the sky, and also of the zodiac, which is situated on a slant between the poles.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Pluribus de causis haec omnia accidunt. prima circulorum quos Graeci ἀψίδας in stellis vocant (etenim Graecis utendum erit vocabulis).
quotations.translation: All these occurrences are due to a plurality ofdue to three causes. causes. The first is the factor of the circles which in the case of the stars the Greeks designate apsides or arcs (it will be necessary to employ Greek terms).
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Huic conexa latitudinum signiferi obliquitatisque causa est. per hunc stellae quas diximus feruntur, nec aliud habitatur in terris quam quod illi subiacet, reliqua a polis squalent. Veneris tantum stella excedit eum binis partibus, quae causa intellegitur efficere ut quaedam animalia et in desertis mundi nascantur.
quotations.translation: Linked with this is the cause of the latitudes of the zodiac and of its obliquity. The stars we have mentioned travel through the zodiac, and the only habitable part of the earth is what lies beneath it—all the other parts towards the poles are frost-bound. Only the planet Venus goes two degrees outside the zodiac; this is understood to be the reason that causes some animals to be born even in the desert places of the world.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: ab his Mercuri stella laxissime, ut tamen e duodenis partibus (tot enim sunt latitudinis) non amplius octonas pererret, neque has aequaliter, sed duas medio eius et supra quattuor infra duas.
quotations.translation: The planet Mercury diverges very widely from these, but without wandering over more than 8 of the 12 degrees of latitude of the zodiac, and these 8 not uniformly but two in the middle of the zodiac, four above it and two below it.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: ab his Mercuri stella laxissime, ut tamen e duodenis partibus (tot enim sunt latitudinis) non amplius octonas pererret, neque has aequaliter, sed duas medio eius et supra quattuor infra duas.
quotations.translation: The planet Mercury diverges very widely from these, but without wandering over more than 8 of the 12 degrees of latitude of the zodiac, and these 8 not uniformly but two in the middle of the zodiac, four above it and two below it.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Convenit stellas in occasu vespertino proximas esse terrae et altitudine et latitudine, exortusque matutinos in initio cuiusque fieri, stationes in mediis latitudinum articulis, quae vocant ecliptica.
quotations.translation: It is agreed that the planets are nearest to the earth in both altitude and latitude at their evening setting, and that their morning risings occur at the beginning of both altitude and latitude, while their stations occur in the middle sections of the altitudes, called ‘ecliptics.’
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Convenit stellas in occasu vespertino proximas esse terrae et altitudine et latitudine, exortusque matutinos in initio cuiusque fieri, stationes in mediis latitudinum articulis, quae vocant ecliptica.
quotations.translation: It is agreed that the planets are nearest to the earth in both altitude and latitude at their evening setting, and that their morning risings occur at the beginning of both altitude and latitude, while their stations occur in the middle sections of the altitudes, called ‘ecliptics.’
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Primum igitur dicatur, cur Veneris stella numquam longius XLVI partibus, Mercurii XXIII ab sole abscedant, saepe citra eas ad solem reciprocent.
quotations.translation: First therefore let us state the reason why Venus never departs more than 46 degrees and Mercury never more than 23 degrees from the sun, and why they often retire and return towards the sun within those limits.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Primum igitur dicatur, cur Veneris stella numquam longius XLVI partibus, Mercurii XXIII ab sole abscedant, saepe citra eas ad solem reciprocent.
quotations.translation: First therefore let us state the reason why Venus never departs more than 46 degrees and Mercury never more than 23 degrees from the sun, and why they often retire and return towards the sun within those limits.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: superiores enim celerrime feruntur in occasu vespertino, hae tardissime, illae a terra altissime absunt cum tardissime moventur, hae cum ocissime
quotations.translation: For the higher planets travel most quickly in their evening setting, whereas these travel most slowly, and the former are farthest from the earth when their pace is slowest but the latter are highest when their pace is quickest
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: incipit autem ab exortu matutino latitudinem scandere, altitudinem vero subire ac solem insequi a statione matutina, ocissima in occasu matutino et altissima, degredi autem latitudine motumque minuere ab exortu vespertino, retro quidem ire simulque altitudine degredi a statione vespertina;
quotations.translation: But she begins to climb her latitude after her morning rise, but after her morning station to ascend her altitude and follow the sun, being swiftest and highest at her morning setting; whereas she begins to descend in latitude and decelerate after her evening rising, and to turn back and simultaneously to descend in altitude after her evening station;
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: exempli gratia in Martis sidere (cuius est maxime inobservabilis cursus) numquam id stationem facere Iovis sidere triquetro
quotations.translation: for example, in the case of the planet Mars (whose course it is very difficult to observe) that it never makes its station with Jupiter at an angle of 120°
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: raro admodum sexaginta partibus discreto (qui numerus sexangulas mundi efficit formas,)
quotations.translation: and very seldom with Jupiter separated 60° (which amounts to ⅙th of the celestial sphere),
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Colores ratio altitudinum temperat, siquidem earum similitudinem trahunt in quarum aera venere subeundo, tinguitque adpropinquantes utralibet alieni meatus circulus, frigidior in pallorem, ardentior in ruborem, ventosus in livorem, sol atque commissurae apsidum, extremaeque orbitae, atram in obscuritatem. suus quidem cuique color est, Saturno candidus, Iovi clarus, Marti igneus, Lucifero candens, Vesperi refulgens, Mercurio radians, lunae blandus, soli cum oritur ardens, post radians
quotations.translation: The colours of the planets vary with their altitudes, inasmuch as they are assimilated to the stars into whose atmosphere they come in rising, and the circuit of another’s path modifies their colour in either direction as they approach, a colder circuit to pallor, a hotter one to redness, a windy one to a leaden colour, the sun and the intersection of its orbit with theirs, and also the extremities of their paths, changing them to black darkness. It is true that each has its own special hue—Saturn white, Jupiter transparent, Mars fiery, Lucifer bright white, Vesper glaring, Mercury radiant, the moon soft, the sun when rising glowing and afterwards radiant
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Colores ratio altitudinum temperat, siquidem earum similitudinem trahunt in quarum aera venere subeundo, tinguitque adpropinquantes utralibet alieni meatus circulus, frigidior in pallorem, ardentior in ruborem, ventosus in livorem, sol atque commissurae apsidum, extremaeque orbitae, atram in obscuritatem. suus quidem cuique color est, Saturno candidus, Iovi clarus, Marti igneus, Lucifero candens, Vesperi refulgens, Mercurio radians, lunae blandus, soli cum oritur ardens, post radians
quotations.translation: The colours of the planets vary with their altitudes, inasmuch as they are assimilated to the stars into whose atmosphere they come in rising, and the circuit of another’s path modifies their colour in either direction as they approach, a colder circuit to pallor, a hotter one to redness, a windy one to a leaden colour, the sun and the intersection of its orbit with theirs, and also the extremities of their paths, changing them to black darkness. It is true that each has its own special hue—Saturn white, Jupiter transparent, Mars fiery, Lucifer bright white, Vesper glaring, Mercury radiant, the moon soft, the sun when rising glowing and afterwards radiant
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.
