quotations.original: namque modo multitudo conferta inest circa dimidios orbes lunae, placida nocte leniter inlustrante eas, modo raritas, ut fugisse miremur, plenilunio abscondente aut cum solis suprave dictarum radii visus praestrinxere nostros.
quotations.translation: For at one time there is a dense crowd of stars in the sky round the circle of the half-moon, a fine night giving them a gentle radiance, but at another time they are scarce, so that we wonder at their flight, when the full moon hides them or when the rays of the sun or the planets above-mentioned dim our sight.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Sol autem ipse quattuor differentias habet, bis aequata nocte diei, vere et autumno, in centrum incidens terrae octavis in partibus arietis ac librae, bis permutatis spatiis, in auctum diei bruma octava in parte capricorni, noctis vero solstitio totidem in partibus cancri. inaequalitatis causa obliquitas signiferi cum pars aequa mundi super subterque terras omnibus fiat momentis; sed quae recta in exortu suo consurgunt signa longiore tractu tenent lucem, quae vero obliqua ociore transeunt spatio.
quotations.translation: The sun itself has four differences, as there are two equinoxes, in spring and autumn, when it coincides with the centre of the earth at the eighth degree of Aries and Libra, and two changes of its course, in the eighth degree of Capricorn at midwinter when the days begin to lengthen and in the same degree of Cancer at the summer solstice. The variation is due to the slant of the zodiac, as at every moment an equal part of the firmament is above and below the earth; but the planets that follow a straight path at their rising keep their light for a longer tract and those that follow a slanting path pass in a swifter period.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Intervalla quoque siderum a terra multi indagare temptarunt, et solem abesse a luna undeviginti partes quantam lunam ipsam a terra prodiderunt.
quotations.translation: Many people have also tried to discover the distances of the planets from the earth, and have given out that the distance of the sun from the moon is 19 times that of the moon itself from the earth.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: ceterum aeterna caelestibus est natura intertexentibus mundum intextoque concretis, potentia autem ad terram magnopere eorum pertinens, quae propter effectus claritatemque et magnitudinem in tanta subtilitate nosci potuerunt
quotations.translation: But the heavenly bodies have a nature that is eternal—they interweave the world and are blended with its weft; yet their potency has a powerful influence on the earth, indeed it is owing to the effects that they produce and to their brilliance and magnitude that it has been possible for them to become known with such a degree of precision, as we shall show in the proper place.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: interque ea solis et lunae, contrarium mundo agere cursum, id est laevom, illo semper in dextram praecipiti;
quotations.translation: among them the sun and moon, follow a course contrary to that of the world, namely to the left, the world always running to the right.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: proximum illi Mercurii sidus, a quibusdam appellatum Apollinis
quotations.translation: The star next to Venus is Mercury, by some called Apollo
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: inferiore circulo fertur novem diebus ociore ambitu, modo ante solis exortum modo post occasum splendens, numquam ab eo XXII partibus remotior
quotations.translation: It travels in a lower circle, with a revolution nine days quicker, shining sometimes before sunrise and sometimes after sunset
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: inferiore circulo fertur novem diebus ociore ambitu, modo ante solis exortum modo post occasum splendens, numquam ab eo XXII partibus remotior
quotations.translation: It travels in a lower circle, with a revolution nine days quicker, shining sometimes before sunrise and sometimes after sunset
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: signiferi autem ambitum peragit trecenis et duodequinquagenis diebus, a sole numquam absistens partibus sex atque quadraginta longius, ut Timaeo placet.
quotations.translation: It completes the circuit of the zodiac every 348 days, and according to Timaeus is never more than 46 degrees distant from the sun.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: iterumque in centum viginti ab alio latere appropinquantes stationes vespertinas quas et secundas vocant
quotations.translation: and again approaching from the other side, make their evening or ‘second’ stations 120 degrees away
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: eadem stationalis senis mensibus conmoratur in signis
quotations.translation: At the same time Mars remains stationary in the signs of the zodiac for periods of six months
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Stadium centum viginti quinque nostros efficit passus, hoc est pedes sexcentos viginti quinque.
quotations.translation: A stade is equivalent to 125 Roman paces, that is 625 feet.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Stadium centum viginti quinque nostros efficit passus, hoc est pedes sexcentos viginti quinque.
quotations.translation: A stade is equivalent to 125 Roman paces, that is 625 feet.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: sextam fere partem huius inmensi spatii quod circa terram circuli solaris animo conprehenditur inesse altitudinis spatio, lunae vero duodecimam, quoniam tanto breviore quam sol ambitu currit;
quotations.translation: the measure of the sun‘s altitude comprises about 1/6th of this conjecturally estimated immense space of the solar circle round the earth, and the moon‘s altitude 1/12th, since the moon runs in a circuit that is much shorter than the sun‘s;
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: namque et in ipso caelo stellae repente nascuntur. plura earum genera.
quotations.translation: There are also stars that suddenly come to birth in the heaven itself; of these there are several kinds.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: cometas Graeci vocant, nostri crinitas
quotations.translation: The Greeks call them ‘comets,’ in our language ‘long-haired stars,’
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: easdem breviores et in mucronem fastigatas xiphias vocavere, quae sunt omnium pallidissimae et quodam gladii nitore ac sine ullis radiis
quotations.translation: The same stars when shorter and sloping to a point have been called ‘Daggers’; these are the palest of all in colour, and have a gleam like the flash of a sword,
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: acontiae iaculi modo vibrantur, atrocissimo significatu;
quotations.translation: ‘Javelin-star’ quiver like a dart; these are a very terrible portent.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: sine ullis radiis, quos et disceus, specie nomini similis, colore autem electro, raros e margine emittit.
quotations.translation: and no rays, which even the Quoit-star, which resembles its name in appearance but is in colour like amber, emits in scattered form from its edge.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: lampadias ardentes imitatur faces
quotations.translation: The ‘Torch-star’ resembles glowing torches
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: ceratias cornus speciem habet, qualis fuit cum Graecia apud Salamina depugnavit.
quotations.translation: The ‘Horned star’ has the shape of a horn, like the one that appeared when Greece fought the decisive battle of Salamis.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: hippeus equinas iubas celerrimi motus atque in orbem circa se euntes.
quotations.translation: the ‘Horse-star’ horses’ manes in very rapid motion and revolving in a circle.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: fiunt et hirci villorum specie et nube aliqua circumdati.
quotations.translation: There also occur ‘Goat comets,’ enringed with a sort of cloud resembling tufts of hair.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: semel adhuc iubae effigies mutata in hastam est, Olympiade CVIII, urbis anno CCCCVIII.
quotations.translation: Once hitherto it has happened that a ‘Mane-shaped’ cometc changed into a spear; this was in the 108thd Olympiad, a.u.c. 408.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: semel adhuc iubae effigies mutata in hastam est, Olympiade CVIII, urbis anno CCCCVIII.
quotations.translation: Once hitherto it has happened that a ‘Mane-shaped’ cometc changed into a spear; this was in the 108thd Olympiad, a.u.c. 408.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Moventur autem aliae errantium modo, aliae inmobiles haerent, omnes ferme sub ipso septentrione, aliqua eius parte non certa, sed maxime in candida quae lactei circuli nomen accepit.
quotations.translation: Some comets move, like the planets, but others are fixed and stationary, almost all of them towards the due North, not in any particular part of it, though chiefly in the luminous region called the Milky Way.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Idem Hipparchus numquam satis laudatus, ut quo nemo magis adprobaverit cognationem cum homine siderum animasque nostras partem esse caeli, novam stellam in aevo suo genitam deprehendit
quotations.translation: Hipparchus before-mentioned, who can never be sufficiently praised, no one having done more to prove that man is related to the stars and that our souls are a part of heaven, detected a new star that came into existence during his lifetime;
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: ut facile discerni posset ex eo non modo an obirent ac nascerentur sed an omnino aliquae transirent moverenturque, item an crescerent minuerenturque, caelo in hereditate cunctis relicto, si quisquam qui cretionem eam caperet inventus esseus esset.
quotations.translation: in order that from that time onward it might be possible easily to discern not only whether stars perish and are born, but whether some are in transit and in motion, and also whether they increase and decrease in magnitude—thus bequeathing the heavens as a legacy to all mankind, supposing anybody had been found to claim that inheritance!
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: ut facile discerni posset ex eo non modo an obirent ac nascerentur sed an omnino aliquae transirent moverenturque, item an crescerent minuerenturque, caelo in hereditate cunctis relicto, si quisquam qui cretionem eam caperet inventus esseus esset.
quotations.translation: in order that from that time onward it might be possible easily to discern not only whether stars perish and are born, but whether some are in transit and in motion, and also whether they increase and decrease in magnitude—thus bequeathing the heavens as a legacy to all mankind, supposing anybody had been found to claim that inheritance!
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: alterum lampadas vocant, plane faces, alterum bolidas, quale Mutinensibus malis visum est.
quotations.translation: one sort are called lampades, which means ‘torches,’ the other bolides (missiles),—that is the sort that appeared at the time of the disasters of Modena.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Emicant et trabes simili modo, quas δοκοὺς vocant, qualis cum Lacedaemonii classe victi imperium Graeciae amisere. fit et caeli ipsius hiatus, quod vocant chasma,
quotations.translation: Other similar meteoric lights are ‘beams.’ in Greek dokoi, for example one that appeared when the Spartans were defeated at sea and lost the empire of Greece. There also occurs a yawning of the actual sky, called chasma
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Cernuntur et stellae cum sole totis diebus, plerumque et circa solis orbem ceu spiceae coronae et versicolores circuli
quotations.translation: Stars are also seen throughout the daytime  in company with the sun, usually actually surrounding the sun’s orb like wreaths made of ears of corn and rings of changing colour—
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Quod plerique appellaverunt soles nocturnos, lumen de caelo noctu visum est C. Caecilio Cn. Papirio consulibus et saepe alias, ut diei species nocte luceret.
quotations.translation: A light from the sky by night, the phenomenon usually called ‘night-suns,’ was seen in the consulship of Gaius Caecilius and Gnaeus Papirius and often on other occasions causing apparent daylight in the night.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Fieri videntur et discursus stellarum, numquam temere ut non ex ea parte truces venti cooriantur.
quotations.translation: Also stars appear to shoot to and fro; this invariably portends the rise of a fierce hurricane from the same quarter.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: geminae autem salutares et prosperi cursus praenuntiae, quarum adventu fugari diram illam ac minacem appellatamque Helenam ferunt, et ob id Polluci ac Castori iis nomina adsignant, eosque in mari deos invocant.
quotations.translation: If there are two of them, they denote safety and portend a successful voyage; and their approach is said to put to flight the terrible star called Helena: for this reason they are called Castor and Pollux, and people pray to them as gods for aid at sea.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: geminae autem salutares et prosperi cursus praenuntiae, quarum adventu fugari diram illam ac minacem appellatamque Helenam ferunt, et ob id Polluci ac Castori iis nomina adsignant, eosque in mari deos invocant.
quotations.translation: If there are two of them, they denote safety and portend a successful voyage; and their approach is said to put to flight the terrible star called Helena: for this reason they are called Castor and Pollux, and people pray to them as gods for aid at sea.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: namque et hoc caelum appellavere maiores quod alio nomine aera, omne quod inani simile vitalem hunc spiritum fundit.
quotations.translation: for the name ‘heaven’ was also given by our ancestors to this which is otherwise designated ‘air’—the whole of that apparently empty space which pours forth this breath of life.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: quotiens errantium accessu inpulsa aut coniectu radiorum exstimulata sunt, qualiter in suculis sentimus accidere, quas Graeci ob id pluvio nomine hyadas appellant.
quotations.translation: by the approach of the planets or goaded on by the impact of their rays, as we observe occurring in the case of the Little Pigs, the Greek name for which is consequently the Hyades, a word denoting rain.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Veteres quattuor omnino servavere per totidem mundi partes (ideo nec Homerus plures nominat) hebeti, ut mox iudicatum est, ratione;
quotations.translation: The ancients noticed four winds in all,Designation of winds. corresponding to the four quarters of the world (this is the reason why even Homer mentions no more)—a dull-witted system, as it was soon afterwards considered;
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: numerosior ratio quattuor his interiecerat, Thrascian media regione inter Septentrionem et occasum solstitialem, itemque Caecian media inter Aquilonem et exortum aequinoctialem ab ortu solstitiali
quotations.translation: The more numerous scheme had inserted four between these: Thrascias (N.N.W.) in the space between Septentrio (N.) and the sunset at the solstice (N.W.) and also Caecias (E.N.E.) in the space between Aquilo (N.E.) and the equinoctial sunrise (E.) on the side of the sunrise at the solstice
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: numerosior ratio quattuor his interiecerat, Thrascian media regione inter Septentrionem et occasum solstitialem, itemque Caecian media inter Aquilonem et exortum aequinoctialem ab ortu solstitiali
quotations.translation: The more numerous scheme had inserted four between these: Thrascias (N.N.W.) in the space between Septentrio (N.) and the sunset at the solstice (N.W.) and also Caecias (E.N.E.) in the space between Aquilo (N.E.) and the equinoctial sunrise (E.) on the side of the sunrise at the solstice
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: numerosior ratio quattuor his interiecerat, Thrascian media regione inter Septentrionem et occasum solstitialem, itemque Caecian media inter Aquilonem et exortum aequinoctialem ab ortu solstitiali
quotations.translation: The more numerous scheme had inserted four between these: Thrascias (N.N.W.) in the space between Septentrio (N.) and the sunset at the solstice (N.W.) and also Caecias (E.N.E.) in the space between Aquilo (N.E.) and the equinoctial sunrise (E.) on the side of the sunrise at the solstice
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: a septentrionibus Septentrio, interque eum et exortum solstitialem Aquilo (Aparctias et Boreas dicti).
quotations.translation: Septentrio from the North and Aquilo between him and sunrise at the solstice (N.E.)—called in Greek Aparctias and Boreas.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: pitheus doliorum cernitur figura in concavo fumidae lucis.
quotations.translation: The ‘Tub-star’ presents the shape of a cask, with a smoky light all round it.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: fiunt et hibernis mensibus et in austrino polo, sed ibi citra ullum iubar.
quotations.translation: Comets also occur in the winter months and at the south pole, but comets in the south have no rays.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: ab oriente brumali Volturnus ([...] hunc Graeci Eurum appellant);
quotations.translation: Vulturnus from the winter sunrise (S.E.)—[...] designated by the Greeks [...] Eurus;
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: nam nisi in medio esset, aequales dies noctesque habere non posse deprehendere est, dioptraeque vel maxime confirmant
quotations.translation: For if the earth were not at the centre, it can be realized that it could not have the days and nights equal: and binoculars confirm this very powerfully
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Tres autem circuli supra dictis zonis inplexi inaequalitates temporum distingunt, solstitialis a parte signiferi excelsissima nobis ad septentrionalem plagam versus, contraque ad alium polum brumalis, item medio ambitu signiferi orbis incedens aequinoctialis.
quotations.translation: But the three circles intertwined between the zones aforesaid are the cause of the differences of the seasons: the Tropic of Cancer on the side of the highest part of the zodiac to the northward of us, and opposite to it the Tropic of Capricorn towards the other pole, and also the equator that runs in the middle circuit of the zodiac.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Tres autem circuli supra dictis zonis inplexi inaequalitates temporum distingunt, solstitialis a parte signiferi excelsissima nobis ad septentrionalem plagam versus, contraque ad alium polum brumalis, item medio ambitu signiferi orbis incedens aequinoctialis.
quotations.translation: But the three circles intertwined between the zones aforesaid are the cause of the differences of the seasons: the Tropic of Cancer on the side of the highest part of the zodiac to the northward of us, and opposite to it the Tropic of Capricorn towards the other pole, and also the equator that runs in the middle circuit of the zodiac.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Septentriones non cernit Trogodytice et confinis Aegyptus, nec Canopum Italia et quem vocant Berenices Crinem item quem sub divo Augusto cognominavere Caesaris Thronon, insignes ibi stellas.
quotations.translation: Cave-dweller Country and Egypt which is adjacent to it do not see the Great and Little Bear, and Italy does not see Canopus and the constellation called Berenice’s Hair, also the one that in the reign of his late Majesty Augustus received the name of Caesar’s Throne, constellations that are conspicuous there.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Septentriones non cernit Trogodytice et confinis Aegyptus, nec Canopum Italia et quem vocant Berenices Crinem item quem sub divo Augusto cognominavere Caesaris Thronon, insignes ibi stellas.
quotations.translation: Cave-dweller Country and Egypt which is adjacent to it do not see the Great and Little Bear, and Italy does not see Canopus and the constellation called Berenice’s Hair, also the one that in the reign of his late Majesty Augustus received the name of Caesar’s Throne, constellations that are conspicuous there.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: verum haec eadem quibusque proximis sublimiora creduntur eademque demersa longinquis
quotations.translation: but these stars are believed to be higher the nearer people are to them, while they seem low to those far away
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Vasaque horoscopica non ubique eadem sunt usui, in trecenis stadiis, aut ut longissime in quingentis, mutantibus semet umbris solis.
quotations.translation: Travellers’ sundials are not the same for reference everywhere, because the shadows thrown varies by the sun as they alter alter the readings at every 300 or at farthest 500 stades.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: itaque umbilici (quem gnomonem appellant) umbra in Aegypto meridiano tempore aequinocti die paulo plus quam dimidiam gnomonis mensuram efficit
quotations.translation: Consequently in Egypt at midday on the day of the equinox the shadow of the pin or ‘gnomon’ measures a little more than half the length of the gnomon itself
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Sic fit ut vario lucis incremento in Meroe longissimus dies XII horas aequinoctiales et octo partes unius horae colligat
quotations.translation: Thus it comes about that owing to the varied lengthening of daylight the longest day covers 12 8/9 equinoctial hours at Meroe
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Umbrarum hanc rationem et quam vocant gnomonicen invenit Anaximenes Milesius, Anaximandri (de quo diximus) discipulus, primusque horologium quod appellant sciothericon Lacedaemone ostendit.
quotations.translation: This theory of shadows and the science called gnomonics was discovered by Anaximenes of Miletus, the pupil of Anaximander of whom we have spoken; he first exhibited at Sparta the time-piece they call ‘Hunt-the-Shadow.’
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Umbrarum hanc rationem et quam vocant gnomonicen invenit Anaximenes Milesius, Anaximandri (de quo diximus) discipulus, primusque horologium quod appellant sciothericon Lacedaemone ostendit.
quotations.translation: This theory of shadows and the science called gnomonics was discovered by Anaximenes of Miletus, the pupil of Anaximander of whom we have spoken; he first exhibited at Sparta the time-piece they call ‘Hunt-the-Shadow.’
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Umbrarum hanc rationem et quam vocant gnomonicen invenit Anaximenes Milesius, Anaximandri (de quo diximus) discipulus, primusque horologium quod appellant sciothericon Lacedaemone ostendit.
quotations.translation: This theory of shadows and the science called gnomonics was discovered by Anaximenes of Miletus, the pupil of Anaximander of whom we have spoken; he first exhibited at Sparta the time-piece they call ‘Hunt-the-Shadow.’
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: quia positio signiferi circa media sui obliquior est, iuxta solstitium autem rectior.
quotations.translation: because the position of the zodiac is more slanting around its middle points but straighter near the solstice.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Babyloniorum placita et motus terrae hiatusque qua cetera omnia siderum vi existimant fieri, sed illorum trium quibus fulmina adsignant, fieri autem meantium cum sole aut congruentium et maxime circa quadrata mundi.
quotations.translation: The theory of the Babylonians deems that even earthquakes and assures in the ground are caused by the force of the stars that is the cause of all other phenomena, but only by that of those three starsa to which they assign thunderbolts; and that they occur when these are travelling with the sun or are in agreement with him, and particularly about the quadratures of the world.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: ingens argumentum plenumque lucis, ac vocis etiam diuinae, hebetes esse qui negent suptermeare sidera ac rursus eadem exsurgere
quotations.translation: It is a vast and illuminating proof, and one of even divine utterance, that those are dull of wit who deny that the same stars pass below the earth and rise up again
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Multiplex etiamnum lunaris differentia, primumque septenis diebus
quotations.translation: Moreover, the lunar difference is manifold, and to begin with, its period is seven days:
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Multiplex etiamnum lunaris differentia, primumque septenis diebus: quippe modici a nova ad dividuam aestus pleniores ab ea exundant plenaque maxime fervent
quotations.translation: Moreover, the lunar difference is manifold, and to begin with, its period is seven days: inasmuch as the tides, which are moderate from new moon to half-moon, therefrom rise higher and at full moon are at their maximum
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: nec tamen in ipsis quos dixi temporum articulis, sed paucis post diebus, sicuti neque in plena aut novissima sed postea
quotations.translation: Nevertheless this does not occur at the exact points of time I have specified, but a few days after, just as it is not at full or new moon but afterwards
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Hesiodus, qui princeps hominum de agricultura praecepit, unum tempus serendi tradidit a vergiliarum occasu;
quotations.translation: Hesiod, the leader of mankind in imparting agricultural instruction, gave only one date for sowing, to begin at the setting of the Pleiads;
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: prius tamen sideralis difficultas, quam sensere etiam periti, subicienda contemplationi est, quo deinde laetior mens discedat a caelo et facta sentiat quae futura praenosci non possint.
quotations.translation: Nevertheless we must first submit to contemplation the difficulties of astronomy, which even experts have been conscious of, in order that subsequently our minds may more happily pass on from the study of the heavens and discern the actual events of the past whose future occurrence cannot be known in advance.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Primum omnium dierum ipsorum anni solisque motus prope inexplicabilis ratio est, ad ccclxv adiciente anno intercalario diei noctisque quadrantes
quotations.translation: First of all it is almost impossible to explain the system of the actual days of the year and that of the movement of the sun, because to the 365 days an intercalary year adds a quarter of a day and of a night
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: admonens observandum frigidae Saturni stellae transitum
quotations.translation: warning us to watch the transit of the cold star Saturn
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: aut enim adventu solis occultantur stellae et conspici desinunt, aut eiusdem abscessu proferunt se (ut emersum hoc melius quam exortum consuetudo dixisset et illud occultationem potius quam occasum);
quotations.translation: the stars are either hidden by the arrival of the sun and cease to be visible, or they present themselves to the view on the sun’s departure (so that custom would have done better to designate the latter as the stars’ ‘emergence’ rather than ‘rising’, and the former as their ‘occultation’ rather than ‘setting’);
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: aut enim adventu solis occultantur stellae et conspici desinunt, aut eiusdem abscessu proferunt se (ut emersum hoc melius quam exortum consuetudo dixisset et illud occultationem potius quam occasum);
quotations.translation: the stars are either hidden by the arrival of the sun and cease to be visible, or they present themselves to the view on the sun’s departure (so that custom would have done better to designate the latter as the stars’ ‘emergence’ rather than ‘rising’, and the former as their ‘occultation’ rather than ‘setting’);
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: aut illo modo, quo die incipiunt apparere vel desinunt oriente sole aut occidente, matutini vespertinive cognominati, prout alteruter eorum mane vel crepusculo contingit.
quotations.translation: or by means of the following mode—by the day on which the risings and settings of the stars begin or cease to be visible at the rising or setting of the sun, these being designated their morning or evening risings and settings according as each of them occurs at dawn or at dusk.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: aut illo modo, quo die incipiunt apparere vel desinunt oriente sole aut occidente, matutini vespertinive cognominati, prout alteruter eorum mane vel crepusculo contingit.
quotations.translation: or by means of the following mode—by the day on which the risings and settings of the stars begin or cease to be visible at the rising or setting of the sun, these being designated their morning or evening risings and settings according as each of them occurs at dawn or at dusk.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Cardines temporum quadripertita anni distinctione constant per incrementa ac decrementa lucis.
quotations.translation: The divisions of the seasons are fixed by the fourfold distribution of the year corresponding with the increases and decreases of daylight.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: inter solstitium et aequinoctium autumni fidiculae occasus autumnum inchoat die xlvi, ab aequinoctio eo ad brumam vergiliarum matutinus occasus hiemem die xliv
quotations.translation: between the solstice and the autumnal equinox the setting of the Lyre on the 46th day marks the beginning of autumn, and from that equinox to midwinter the morning setting of the Pleiads on the 44th day marks that of winter
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: hoc ipso vergiliarum occasu fieri putant aliqui a. d. iii idus Novembris, ut diximus, servantque id sidus etiam vestis institores, et est in caelo notatu facillimum:
quotations.translation: Some think that this occurs exactly at the setting of the Pleiads on November 10, as we have said, and even clothes-dealers go by that constellation, and it is very easy to identify in the sky;
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: viii kal. stella regia appellata Tuberoni in pectore leonis occidit matutino et pridie nonas Feb. fidicula vespere occidit
quotations.translation: On January 25 the star in the breast of the Lion called according to Tubero the Royal Star sets in the morning and the Lyre sets in the evening of February 4.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: maior pars auctorum vindemitoris inmersu—viii idus aquilonii piscis exortu et postero die Orionis;
quotations.translation: the majority of the authorities put it at the setting of the Vintager—on March 8 at the rising of the northern part of the Fish, and on the next day at the rising of Orion;
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Caesar et idus Mart. ferales sibi notavit scorpionis occasu, xv kal. vero April. Italiae milvum ostendi, xii kal. equum occidere matutino.
quotations.translation: Gaesar also noted March 15—the day that was fatal to him—as marked by the setting of the Scorpion, but stated that on March 18 the Kite becomes visible in Italy and on March 21 the Horse sets in the morning.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: in Attica vergiliae vesperi occultantur, eaedem postridie in Boeotia, Caesari autem et Chaldaeis nonis, Aegypto Orion et gladius eius incipiunt abscondi.
quotations.translation: The Pleiads set on the evening of April 3 in Attica and on the day after in Boeotia, but for Caesar and the Chaldaeans on April 5, when for Egypt Orion and his sword begin to set.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: hoc est vulgo appellatum sidus Pariliciurn, quoniam xi kal. Mai. urbis Romae natalis, quo fere serenitas redditur, claritatem observationi dedit
quotations.translation: This constellation is commonly called Parilicium, because April 21, the birthday of the city of Rome, on which fine weather usually returns, has given a clear sky for observing the heavens
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Caesari et viii kal. notatur dies. vii kal. Aegypto haedi exoriuntur, vi Boeotiae et Atticae canis vesperi occultatur, fiidicula mane oritur. v kal. Assyriae Orion totus absconditur, iv autem canis. vi non. Mai. Caesari suculae matutino exoriuntur et viii id. capella pluvialis, Aegypto autem eodem die canis vesperi occultatur. sic fere in vi id. Mai., qui est vergiliarum exortus, decurrunt sidera.
quotations.translation: In Caesar’s calendar April 24 is also a marked day. On April 25 the Kids rise for Egypt, and on April 26 the Dog sets in the evening and the Lyre rises in the morning for Boeotia and Attica. On April 27 Orion entirely disappears for Assyria, and on the 28th the Dog. On May 2 the Little Pigs rise in the morning for Caesar, and on May 8 the She-goat, portending rain, while the Dog sets for Egypt in the evening of the same day. That is a fairly precise account of the movements of the constellations down to May 10, which is the date of the rising of the Pleiads.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Ab solstitio ad fidiculae occasum vi kal. Iul. Caesari Orion exoritur, zona autem eius iv non. Assyriae;
quotations.translation: Between the solstice and the setting of the Lyre, on June 26 by Caesar’s reckoning, Orion rises, and Orion’s Belt on July 4, in the region of Assyria
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: id manifestum fiet adtendentibus; nam primum omnium non hoc evenire nisi noctibus et ante solis ardorem deprehenditur, totumque lunari ratione constat, quoniam talis iniuria non fit nisi interlunio plenave luna, hoc est praevalente—utroque enim habitu plena est, ut saepius diximus, sed interlunio omne lumen quod a sole accepit caelo regerens.
quotations.translation: Close attention to the facts will make this clear; for first of all blight is never found to occur except at night and before the sun gives any heat, and it depends entirely on the phases of the moon, since damage of this sort only takes place at the moon’s conjunction or at full moon, that is, when the moon’s influence is powerful—for the moon is at the full at both phases, as we have often said, but at the point of its conjunctionII. 46. it reflects hack to the sky all the light it has received from the sun.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: differentia utriusque habitus magna, sed manifesta: namque interlunio aestate calidissima est, hieme gelida, e diverso in plenilunio aestate frigidas facit noctes, hieme tepidas.
quotations.translation: The difference between the two phases is great, but it is obvious: the moon is hottest in summer and cold in winter at the conjunction, whereas on the contrary when full it makes the nights cold in summer and warm in winter.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: haec ab horridis sideribus exeunt, ut saepius diximus, veluti arcturo, Orione, haedis.
quotations.translation: these take their origin from certain noxious constellations, as we have said more than once, for instance Arcturus, Orion, the Kids.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: ipse circulus fertur per sagittarium atque geminos, solis centro bis aequinoctialem circulum secans
quotations.translation: The Milky Way itself passes through§ 268. the Archer and the Twins, cutting the equinoctial orbit twice at the sun’s centre-point
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: hoc silente luna seri iubent.
quotations.translation: it is recommended that this [sowing] should take place when the moon is silent.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Omnia quae caeduntur, carpuntur, tondentur innocentius decrescente luna quam crescente fiunt. stercus nisi decrescente luna ne tangito, maxime autem intermenstrua dimidiaque stercorato.
quotations.translation: All cutting, gathering and trimming is done with less injury to the trees and plants when the moon is waning than when it is waxing. Manure must not be touched except when the moon is waning, but manuring should chiefly be done at new moon or at half moon.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Omnia quae caeduntur, carpuntur, tondentur innocentius decrescente luna quam crescente fiunt. stercus nisi decrescente luna ne tangito, maxime autem intermenstrua dimidiaque stercorato.
quotations.translation: All cutting, gathering and trimming is done with less injury to the trees and plants when the moon is waning than when it is waxing. Manure must not be touched except when the moon is waning, but manuring should chiefly be done at new moon or at half moon.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Omnia quae caeduntur, carpuntur, tondentur innocentius decrescente luna quam crescente fiunt. stercus nisi decrescente luna ne tangito, maxime autem intermenstrua dimidiaque stercorato.
quotations.translation: All cutting, gathering and trimming is done with less injury to the trees and plants when the moon is waning than when it is waxing. Manure must not be touched except when the moon is waning, but manuring should chiefly be done at new moon or at half moon.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: si quartam orbis rutilus cinget, et ventos et imbres praemonebit.
quotations.translation: If the moon on her fourth night is surrounded by a bright ring, this will be a warning of both wind and rain.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Sunt et ipsius lunae viii articuli, quotiens in angulos solis incidat, plerisque inter eos tantum observantibus praesagia eius, hoc est iii, vii, xi, xv, xix, xxiii, xxvii et interlunium.
quotations.translation: There are also eight periodic points of the moon herself, corresponding to her angles of incidence with the sun, and most observers only notice the moon’s prognostics between those points; they are the 3rd, 7th, 11th, 15th, 19th, 23rd and 27th days of the moon, and the day of her conjunction.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: sunt in signo cancri duae stellae parvae aselli appellatae, exiguum inter illas spatium obtinente nubecula quam praesepia appellant;
quotations.translation: In the constellation of the Crab there are two small stars called the Little Asses, with a small gap between them containing a little nebula called the Manger;
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: sunt in signo cancri duae stellae parvae aselli appellatae, exiguum inter illas spatium obtinente nubecula quam praesepia appellant;
quotations.translation: In the constellation of the Crab there are two small stars called the Little Asses, with a small gap between them containing a little nebula called the Manger;
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: sunt in signo cancri duae stellae parvae aselli appellatae, exiguum inter illas spatium obtinente nubecula quam praesepia appellant;
quotations.translation: In the constellation of the Crab there are two small stars called the Little Asses, with a small gap between them containing a little nebula called the Manger;
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: namque et in duodecim signa digessere eam sole transmeante iterumque luna
quotations.translation: For they have actually divided the art according to the passing of the sun, and also that of the moon, through the twelve signs of the Zodiac.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: Martis stella ut propior etiam ex quadrato sentit radios, a nonaginta partibus, unde et nomen accepit motus primus et secundus nonagenarius dictus ab utroque exortu.
quotations.translation: The planet Mars being nearer feels the sun’s rays even from its quadrature, at an angle of 90 degrees, which has given to his motion after each rising the name of ‘first’ or ‘second ninety-degree.’
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: solis fulgore eam ut reliqua siderum regi, siquidem in totum mutuata ab eo luce fulgere
quotations.translation: that she is governed by the sun’s radiance as are the rest of the stars, as in fact she shines with a light entirely borrowed from him
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: ideo et inaequali lumine adspici quia ex adverso demum plena reliquis diebus tantum ex se terris ostendat quantum ex sole ipsa concipiat;
quotations.translation: also that the reason why she is seen to vary in her light is that she is full only when opposite to the sun, and on the remaining days shows as much light from herself to the earth as she herself conceives from the sun;
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: ergo ut e flagrante ligno carbo cum crepitu, sic a sidere caelestis ignis exspuitur praescita secum adferens, ne abdicata quidem sui parte in divinis cessante operibus. idque maxime turbato fit aeres quia collectus umor abundantiam stimulat aut quia turbatur quodam ceu gravidi sideris partu.
quotations.translation: Consequently heavenly fire is spit forth by the planet as crackling charcoal flies from a burning log, bringing prophecies with it, as even the part of himself that he discards does not cease to function in its divine tasks. And this is accompanied by a very great disturbance of the air, because moisture collected causes an overflow, or because it is disturbed by the birth-pangs so to speak of the planet in travail.
quotations.publication: Pliny. Natural History, Volume I: Books 1-2. Translated by H. Rackham. Loeb Classical Library 330. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1938.

quotations.original: ἡ δὲ θεὰ καὶ σελασφόρος Σελήνη (…) ὀξυγώνιος
quotations.translation: The goddess and light-bearing Moon (…) being in crescent (phase) …

quotations.original: ἡ δὲ θεὰ καὶ σελασφόρος Σελήνη (…) χρυσῷ ὁμοία
quotations.translation: The goddess and light-bearing Moon (…) being golden (in color) …

quotations.original: φωσφώρος ὁ τῆς Ἀφροδίτηι̣ ἐ̣ν̣ Αἰγ̣όγερωι
quotations.translation: The light-bearer, the (star) of Aphrodite (Venus) (was) in Capricorn …

quotations.original: Εἰ δὲ μὴ εὑρεθῇ ὁ αὐτὸς κύριος τῆς τε ἐκλείψεως καὶ τοῦ κέντρου, ἀλλὰ δύο, τὸν τὰς τῶν ἀμφοτέρων πλείονας ἔχοντα συνοικειώσεις ἑλόμεθα προκρίνοντες τὸν τῆς ἐκλείψεως κύριον·
quotations.translation: But if the same ruler should not be found for the eclipse and the pivot point, but there are two, then we will choose the one having the greater number of affiliations with both, giving preference to the ruler of the eclipse.

quotations.original: Τὸ δὲ μεσεμβόλημα ποιεῖ ἐκβολιμαίους ὑπὸ τῶν γονέων, ἐὰν δὲ ὁ τοῦ Διὸς ἐπιθεωρήσῃ παρασκευάζει ἀνακάμψαι πρὸς τοὺς γονεῖς ἢ πρὸς ἑτέρους οἳ τούτους τεκνοποιοῦνται.
quotations.translation: The interstice makes for expulsion by the parents. And if the star of Zeus should look on, it will bring about a return to the parents or to others who adopt them.

quotations.original: Δορυφορίας δὲ γένη ἐστὶ τρία. Πρῶτον ἐάν τινα ἐν οἴκῳ ὄντα ἰδίῳ ἢ ὑψώματι ἐπίκεντρον ἕτερος ἐν οἴκῳ ἰδίῳ κείμενος ἢ ὑψώματι κατοπτεύῃ ἐπὶ τὴν προαναφερομένην αὐτοῦ μοῖραν τὴν ἀκτῖνα βαλών, οἷον ἐὰν ἐν Λέοντι τὸν Ἥλιον ὄντα ὁ Κρόνος ἐν Ὑδροχόῳ ἴδῃ κατὰ διάμετρον ἢ Ζεὺς ἐν Τοξότῃ κατὰ τρίγωνον ἢ πάλιν Δία ἐν Καρκίνῳ Ἄρης ὢν ἐν Αἰγόκερῳ ἴδῃ.
quotations.translation: There are three kinds of spear-bearing. The first is if, for a certain planet that is in its own house or exaltation while being upon a pivot point, another planet lying in its own house or exaltation should scrutinize the degree pre-ascending it while hurling its rays. For example, if Kronos in Aquarius should see the Sun diametrically when it is in Leo, or Zeus in Sagittarius should see it triangularly; or again, if Ares being in Capricorn should see Zeus in Cancer.

quotations.original: ἐὰν δὲ ὁ τοῦ Διὸς ἐπιμαρτυρήσῃ τῷ δεκανῷ ἀγαθοὺς χρόνους ἕξει καὶ εὑρέματα εὑρήσει καὶ κυριεύσει πολλῶν καὶ ἐσχάτης καλῆς τεύξεται.
quotations.translation:
But if Zeus should testify to this decan, he will have good times and make
 discoveries,  and he will rule over many, and he will meet with a fine end.

quotations.original: Ὁ δὲ καθυπερτερῶν καὶ ἐπιδεκατεύων ὁ αὐτός ἐστιν· ὁ γὰρ ἐν Κριῷ καθυπερτερεῖ καὶ ἐπιδεκατεύει τὸν ἐν τῷ Καρκίνῳ.
quotations.translation:
The one superior and the one [tithing] are the same. For, a planet in
Aries is superior to, and tithes, a planet in Cancer.’

quotations.original: ἐν μὲν γὰρ τοῖς ἀπ’ ἀνατολῆς μέχρι μεσουρανήσεως ἢ ἀπὸ δύσεως μέχρι τῆς ὑπὸ γῆν ἀντιμεσουρανήσεως σχηματισμοῖς ὡς ἀπηλιωτικοῖς ἀρρενοῦσθαι σημαίνει, ἐν δὲ τοῖς λοιποῖς δυσὶ τεταρτημορίοις ὡς λιβυκοῖς θηλύνεσθαι.
quotations.translation: Furthermore, they become masculine and feminine because of their figurations with the Sun. That is, in the figurations from rising up to culminating, or from setting up to culminating under the earth, it signifies becoming masculine since they are in eastern figurations. But in the remaining two quadrants, it signifies becoming feminine, since they are in western ones.

quotations.original: ἐν μὲν γὰρ τοῖς ἀπ’ ἀνατολῆς μέχρι μεσουρανήσεως ἢ ἀπὸ δύσεως μέχρι τῆς ὑπὸ γῆν ἀντιμεσουρανήσεως σχηματισμοῖς ὡς ἀπηλιωτικοῖς ἀρρενοῦσθαι σημαίνει, ἐν δὲ τοῖς λοιποῖς δυσὶ τεταρτημορίοις ὡς λιβυκοῖς θηλύνεσθαι.
quotations.translation: Furthermore, they become masculine and feminine because of their figurations with the Sun. That is, in the figurations from rising up to culminating, or from setting up to culminating under the earth, it signifies becoming masculine since they are in eastern figurations. But in the remaining two quadrants, it signifies becoming feminine, since they are in western ones.

quotations.original: Ὁ γὰρ τοὺς πλείστους λόγους ἔχων πρὸς ἀμφοτέρους τοὺς ἐκκειμένους τόπους τόν τε τῆς ἐκλείψεως καὶ τὸν τοῦ ἑπομένου αὐτῷ κέντρου κατά τε τὰς ἔγγιστα φαινομένας συναφὰς ἢ ἀπορροίας καὶ σχηματισμοὺς καὶ ἔτι κατὰ τὴν κυρίαν τῶν οἴκων καὶ τριγώνων καὶ ὑψωμάτων καὶ ὁρίων, ἐκεῖνος λήψεται μόνος τὴν οἰκοδεσποτείαν.
quotations.translation: The one having the greatest number of relationships to both the places set out, that of the eclipse and that of the pivot point following it, both in accordance with the applications or separations and figurations that appear closest,’ and furthermore in accordance with the ruler of the houses and trigons and exaltations and boundaries, that planet will take the sole rulership.

quotations.original: Λέγεται δὲ ἐμπερίσχεσις καὶ οὕτως, ὅταν δύο ἀστέρες ἀνὰ μέσον ἔχωσι τὴν Σελήνην ἢ τὸν ὡροσκόπον μηδενὸς ἄλλου εἰς τὸ μεταξὺ παρεμβάλλοντος ἀκτῖνα, χαλεπὴ δέ ἐστιν αὕτη ἡ ἐμπερίσχεσις ὅταν ὑπὸ κακοποιῶν γένηται.
quotations.translation: And containment is said thus, whenever two stars should have the Moon or the Hōroskopos between them while no other planet interposes rays in the intermediate interval. But the containment itself is difficult whenever it is made by malefics.’

quotations.original: Εἰ δὲ μὴ εὑρεθῇ ὁ αὐτὸς κύριος τῆς τε ἐκλείψεως καὶ τοῦ κέντρου, ἀλλὰ δύο, τὸν τὰς τῶν ἀμφοτέρων πλείονας ἔχοντα συνοικειώσεις ἑλόμεθα προκρίνοντες τὸν τῆς ἐκλείψεως κύριον·
quotations.translation: But if the same ruler should not be found for the eclipse and the pivot point, but there are two, then we will choose the one having the greater number of affiliations with both, giving preference to the ruler of the eclipse.

quotations.original: Λέγονται δὲ καὶ ἰδιοπροσωπεῖν ὅταν ἕκαστος αὐτῶν τὸν αὐτὸν διασώσῃ πρὸς Ἥλιον ἢ καὶ Σελήνην σχηματισμὸν ὅνπερ καὶ ὁ οἶκος αὐτοῦ πρὸς τοὺς ἐκείνων οἴκους, οἷον ὅταν ὁ τῆς Ἀφροδίτης λόγου ἕνεκεν ἑξάγωνον ποιῇ πρὸς τὰ φῶτα διάστασιν, ἀλλὰ πρὸς Ἥλιον μὲν ἑσπέριος ὤν, πρὸς Σελήνην δὲ ἑῷος ἀκολούθως τοῖς οἴκοις.
quotations.translation: They say that [the stars], are in : their own faces whenever each of them should maintain the, figuration to. the Sun or else the Moon that its house has to.their houses. For example, whenever the star of Aphrodite (for the sake of argument) should make an hexagonal interval to the lights while being west relative to the Sun and east relative to the Moon, in keeping with their houses.’

quotations.original: Λέγονται δὲ καὶ ἰδιοπροσωπεῖν ὅταν ἕκαστος αὐτῶν τὸν αὐτὸν διασώσῃ πρὸς Ἥλιον ἢ καὶ Σελήνην σχηματισμὸν ὅνπερ καὶ ὁ οἶκος αὐτοῦ πρὸς τοὺς ἐκείνων οἴκους, οἷον ὅταν ὁ τῆς Ἀφροδίτης λόγου ἕνεκεν ἑξάγωνον ποιῇ πρὸς τὰ φῶτα διάστασιν, ἀλλὰ πρὸς Ἥλιον μὲν ἑσπέριος ὤν, πρὸς Σελήνην δὲ ἑῷος ἀκολούθως τοῖς οἴκοις.
quotations.translation: They say that [the stars], are in : their own faces whenever each of them should maintain the, figuration to. the Sun or else the Moon that its house has to.their houses. For example, whenever the star of Aphrodite (for the sake of argument) should make an hexagonal interval to the lights while being west relative to the Sun and east relative to the Moon, in keeping with their houses.’

quotations.original: Αἱ δὲ κατὰ μέρος ἀνέσεις καὶ ἐπιτάσεις ληφθήσονται ἀπό τε τῶν ἀνὰ μέσον συζυγιῶν ὅταν κατὰ τῶν τὸ αἴτιον ἐμποιούντων ἢ τῶν σχηματιζομένων αὐτοῖς συμπίπτωσιν, καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν ἄλλων παρόδων ὅταν οἱ ποιητικοὶ τοῦ προτελέσματος ἀστέρες ἀνατολὰς ἢ δύσεις ἢ στηριγμοὺς ἢ ἀκρονύκτους φάσεις ποιῶνται συσχηματιζόμενοι τοῖς τὴν αἰτίαν ἔχουσι δωδεκατημορίοις, ἐπειδήπερ ἀνατέλλοντες μὲν ἢ στηρίζοντες ἐπιτάσεις ποιοῦνται τῶν συμπτωμάτων, δύνοντες δὲ καὶ ὑπὸ τὰς αὐγὰς ὄντες ἢ ἀκρονύκτους ποιούμενοι φάσεις ἄνεσιν ἐμποιοῦσι τῶν ἀποτελουμένων.
quotations.translation: The particular relaxations and intensifications will be taken from conjunctions during the event* whenever they should occur upon the [twelfth-parts] that introduce the cause or the ones figured with them, and from the other passages whenever those stars productive of the prognostication make risings or settings or stations or acronycal phases while being configured with the twelfth-parts that have the cause, since indeed when they are rising or stationing they make intensifications of the events, but when they are setting and under the rays or when they make acronycal phases they cause relaxations of the effects.

quotations.original: Αἱ δὲ κατὰ μέρος ἀνέσεις καὶ ἐπιτάσεις ληφθήσονται ἀπό τε τῶν ἀνὰ μέσον συζυγιῶν ὅταν κατὰ τῶν τὸ αἴτιον ἐμποιούντων ἢ τῶν σχηματιζομένων αὐτοῖς συμπίπτωσιν, καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν ἄλλων παρόδων ὅταν οἱ ποιητικοὶ τοῦ προτελέσματος ἀστέρες ἀνατολὰς ἢ δύσεις ἢ στηριγμοὺς ἢ ἀκρονύκτους φάσεις ποιῶνται συσχηματιζόμενοι τοῖς τὴν αἰτίαν ἔχουσι δωδεκατημορίοις, ἐπειδήπερ ἀνατέλλοντες μὲν ἢ στηρίζοντες ἐπιτάσεις ποιοῦνται τῶν συμπτωμάτων, δύνοντες δὲ καὶ ὑπὸ τὰς αὐγὰς ὄντες ἢ ἀκρονύκτους ποιούμενοι φάσεις ἄνεσιν ἐμποιοῦσι τῶν ἀποτελουμένων.
quotations.translation: The particular relaxations and intensifications will be taken from conjunctions during the event* whenever they should occur upon the [twelfth-parts] that introduce the cause or the ones figured with them, and from the other passages whenever those stars productive of the prognostication make risings or settings or stations or acronycal phases while being configured with the twelfth-parts that have the cause, since indeed when they are rising or stationing they make intensifications of the events, but when they are setting and under the rays or when they make acronycal phases they cause relaxations of the effects.

quotations.original: Καὶ πάντας ἁπλῶς τοὺς καθ’ ὁποιουσδήποτε συσχηματισμοὺς διεξελθεῖν οὕτω πολυμερῶς νοουμένους εἰκότως ἂν καταληφθείη τὸ τοιοῦτον εἶδος ἐπὶ τῇ τοῦ μαθηματικοῦ πρὸς τὰς κατὰ μέρος διακρίσεις ἐπιβολῇ καὶ ἐπινοίᾳ.
quotations.translation:
But since it limitless and impossible to distinguish in an articulate manner the particular effect for each commixture as well as absolutely all the configurations  of whatever kind, it would be reasonable  to leave  such
a form to the apprehensions and conceptions of the mathematician for
the particular distinctions.

quotations.original: Τῶν δὲ ἀπλανῶν ἐπιλεξόμεθα τὸν λαμπρὸν τόν τε αὐτῷ τῷ ἐκλειπτικῷ τόπῳ συγκεχρηματικότα ἐπὶ τῷ παρῳχηκότι κέντρῳ κατὰ τοὺς σχηματισμοὺς τῶν ἐννέα τρόπων καὶ τὸν ἐν τῇ ὥρᾳ τῆς ἐκλείψεως ἢ συνανατείλαντα ἢ συμμεσουρανήσαντα τῷ κατὰ τὰ ἑπόμενα κέντρῳ τοῦ τόπου τῆς ἐκλείψεως.
quotations.translation: Of the fixed stars, we will select the bright one that has conducted business with the place of the eclipse itself upon the pivot point gone by, in accordance with the figurations of the nine ways, and the one that has either co-risen or co-culminated at the hour of the eclipse with the pivot point following the place of the eclipse.

quotations.original: नानाविधाकारकवर्णरूपैः शुभाशुभैर्द्वादशभिर्गृहाख्यैः ॥११॥
quotations.transliteration: nānāvidhākārakavarṇarūpaiḥ śubhāśubhairdvādaśabhirgṛhākhyaiḥ ||11||
quotations.translation: These twelve zodiac houses that have various vidhās (types), kārakas (agents), varṇas (colors), and rūpas (forms) are of benefic and malefic qualities.
quotations.publication: Pingree, David. The Yavanajātaka of Sphujidhvaja. Harvard Oriental Series, vol. 48. Cambridge: Harvard University Press

quotations.original: ἀπέχουσα σεληνιακ[ὰ] μεγέθη δύο
quotations.translation: (Venus) being two lunar sizes distant (from a fixed star)

quotations.original: οἰκοδεσποτεῖ Ἀφροδ[ίτη]
quotations.translation: The house-master  is Venus

quotations.original: Τούτοις δὲ ὡς ἔοικε συνεγνωκότες οἱ παλαιοὶ Αἰγύπτιοι οὕτως ἔχουσι συνῆψαν πανταχῇ τῷ δι’ ἀστρονομίας προγνωστικῷ τὴν ἰατρικὴν διὰ τῶν καλουμένων παρ’ αὐτοῖς ἰατρομαθηματικῶν συντάξεων ἐξ ὧν προσφόρως ἑκάστῳ τὰ βοηθήματα προσφέρουσιν.
quotations.translation: Having come (so it seems) to these same conclusions, the ancient Egyptians completely bound medicine to astronomical prognostic through what they call iatromathematical, systems, by means of which they apply the remedies fittingly.

quotations.original: Ἀρχὴν δὲ ἐποιήσαντο ἀπὸ τοῦ Κριοῦ ἐαρινοῦ τμήματος διὰ τὸ ἐκ τοῦ νοτίου ἡμισφαιρίου ἐπὶ τὸ βόρειον τότε τοῦ Ἡλίου μετερχομένου
quotations.translation: They made the beginning be from the spring section Aries, [...], when the Sun passes from the southern to the northern hemisphere to which our inhabited world is subordinated

quotations.original: Ὡς δὲ Ἵππαρχος καὶ οἱ παλαιοὶ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων κατὰ μέρος διώρισαν οὕτως· κατὰ μὲν τὸν ἀριστερὸν ὦμον Βαβυλωνία, κατὰ δὲ τὸν δεξιὸν Θρᾴκη, κατὰ δὲ τὸ στῆθος Ἀρμενία, κατὰ δὲ πλευρὰς Ἀραβία ἡ πρὸς Αἴγυπτον, κατὰ τὴν ῥάχιν καὶ κοιλίαν Περσὶς καὶ Καππαδοκία, Μεσοποταμία, Συρία, Ἐρυθρὰ θάλασσα
quotations.translation: But like Hipparchus, the ancient Egyptians also made distinctions according to parts, thus: for the left shoulder, Babylonian; for the right shoulder, Thrace; for the breast, Armenia; for the spine, both the vale of Persia and Cappadocia, Mesopotamia, Syria, the Red Sea.

quotations.original: Ὡς δὲ Ἵππαρχος καὶ οἱ παλαιοὶ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων κατὰ μέρος διώρισαν οὕτως· κατὰ μὲν τὸν ἀριστερὸν ὦμον Βαβυλωνία, κατὰ δὲ τὸν δεξιὸν Θρᾴκη, κατὰ δὲ τὸ στῆθος Ἀρμενία, κατὰ δὲ πλευρὰς Ἀραβία ἡ πρὸς Αἴγυπτον, κατὰ τὴν ῥάχιν καὶ κοιλίαν Περσὶς καὶ Καππαδοκία, Μεσοποταμία, Συρία, Ἐρυθρὰ θάλασσα

quotations.original: Ὡς δὲ Ἵππαρχος καὶ οἱ παλαιοὶ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων κατὰ μέρος διώρισαν οὕτως· κατὰ μὲν τὸν ἀριστερὸν ὦμον Βαβυλωνία, κατὰ δὲ τὸν δεξιὸν Θρᾴκη, κατὰ δὲ τὸ στῆθος Ἀρμενία, κατὰ δὲ πλευρὰς Ἀραβία ἡ πρὸς Αἴγυπτον, κατὰ τὴν ῥάχιν καὶ κοιλίαν Περσὶς καὶ Καππαδοκία, Μεσοποταμία, Συρία, Ἐρυθρὰ θάλασσα
quotations.translation: But like Hipparchus, the ancient Egyptians also made distinctions according to parts, thus: for the left shoulder, Babylonian; for the right shoulder, Thrace; for the breast, Armenia; for the spine, both the vale of Persia and Cappadocia, Mesopotamia, Syria, the Red Sea.

quotations.original:
ἓξ δ’ ὁρίων ἐπέχει μοίρας Φαέθων ἐνὶ τούτῳ
τὰς πρώτας, μετέπειτα δ’ ἴσας λάχεν ἡ Κυθέρεια,
ὀκτὼ δὲ Στίλβων τρίτατος, Πυρόεις δέ τε πέντε,
τὰς δ’ ὑπολειπομένας ἔλαχεν Φαίνων ἴσα Θούρῳ.
quotations.translation:
Of boundaries, does Phaethon’ occupy the six degrees the first
In this, thereafter was allotted Cythereia an equal number,
Stilbon eight the third, and Pyroeis five as well,
The remaining ones to equal Thouros’ Phainōn got as lot.

quotations.original: εἰσὶν οὖν αἱ τούτου λαμπραὶ μοῖραι τρίτη, ἐννεακαιδεκάτη, ἕκτη καὶ εἰκοστή, ἑβδόμη καὶ εἰκοστή, τριακοστή.
quotations.translation: The bright degrees of this zōidion, then, are the third, nineteenth, twenty-sixth, and twenty-seventh, thirtieth.

quotations.original: Τὸ δὲ μεταξὺ Κριοῦ καὶ Ταύρου, ὅπερ μεσεμβόλημα καλεῖται, εἴ τις ἔχει ὡροσκόπον, οὗτος ἄλαλος καὶ κωφὸς καὶ ἄσημος· τελευτήσει ἐπὶ τῶν αὐτῶν κλιμακτήρων τῶν τοῦ τρίτου δεκανοῦ τοῦ Κριοῦ.
quotations.translation: And if someone should have as his Hōroskopos the interval between Ares and Taurus, which is called the interstice, he will be mute and obtuse and unintelligible. He will die at the same critical periods as for the third decan of Ares.

quotations.original: Ἑξῆς τὸ τοῦ Ταύρου δωδεκατημόριόν ἐστιν, ὃ εἰς τράχηλον τοῦ κόσμου ἀναφέρεται
quotations.translation: Next is the twelfth-part Taurus, which ascends as far as the neck of the cosmos,

quotations.original: Κατὰ δὲ μέρος τῷ μὲν βορείῳ Διδύμων ὑπόκειται κατὰ τοὺς πόδας Βοιωτία, παρὰ τὴν χεῖρα Θρᾴκη, ὑπὸ τὸν νῶτον Γαλατία, τοῦ δὲ νοτίου ὑπὸ τὸν γλουτὸν Πόντος, κατὰ νῶτον Κιλικία, κατὰ τὴν ὠμοπλάτην Φοινίκη, κατὰ τὴν κορυφὴν Ἰνδική.
quotations.translation: But by part, in the northern twin of Gemini, for the foot, Boeotia; along the hands, Thrace; under the back, Galatia; in the southern twin, under the buttocks, Pontos; for the back, Cilicia; for the shoulder blade, Phoenicia; for the top of the head, Indica.

quotations.original: Κατὰ δὲ μέρος τῷ μὲν βορείῳ Διδύμων ὑπόκειται κατὰ τοὺς πόδας Βοιωτία, παρὰ τὴν χεῖρα Θρᾴκη, ὑπὸ τὸν νῶτον Γαλατία, τοῦ δὲ νοτίου ὑπὸ τὸν γλουτὸν Πόντος, κατὰ νῶτον Κιλικία, κατὰ τὴν ὠμοπλάτην Φοινίκη, κατὰ τὴν κορυφὴν Ἰνδική.

quotations.original: Ὁ ἔχων τὸν πρῶτον ὡροσκοποῦντα ἔσται ἀγχίνους καὶ πεπαιδευμένος, φιλευφρόσυνος, ἐρωτικός, μισοπόνηρος, μικρόλυπος, τὸ ζῆν ἐν παρύγροις τόποις ἔχων, καὶ ἀκαταστατήσει κατὰ γυναῖκα καὶ ἐξ ἔρωτος ἢ φιλίας λήψεται γυναῖκα καὶ οὐρανίων μαθημάτων ἅψεται.
quotations.translation: He who has the first decan marking the hour will be ready of wit and learned, fond of good cheer, erotic, with a hatred of work, irritated by trifles, making a living in places near the sea, and he will have a hard time settling down with a wife, and he will take a wife out of love or friendship, and he will engage in celestial learning.

quotations.original: οἱ δὲ ἀγαθοὶ ἐπιθεωρήσαντες σίνος ποιοῦσι καὶ πάθος.
quotations.translation: but when the good planets are looking on, they cause injury and suffering.

quotations.original: Κατὰ δὲ Πτολεμαῖον Ἰταλία, Γαλλία, Ἀπουλία, Φοινίκη, Χαλδαία, Ὀρχηνία. Κατὰ δὲ μέρος, ὡς ἄλλοι ἱστοροῦσιν, κατὰ μὲν κεφαλὴν Προποντίς, κατὰ τὸ στῆθος Ἑλλάς, ὑπὸ τὴν κοιλίαν Μακεδονία, τὰ δὲ πρὸς τῇ οὐρᾷ Φρυγία.
quotations.translation: According to Ptolemy: Italy, Gaul, Apulia, Phoenicia, Chaldaea, Orchenia. But by parts, according to the inquiries of others: for the head, Propontis; for the breast, Hellas; under the belly, Macedonia; the parts near the tail, Phrygia.

quotations.original: Κατὰ δὲ Πτολεμαῖον Ἰταλία, Γαλλία, Ἀπουλία, Φοινίκη, Χαλδαία, Ὀρχηνία. Κατὰ δὲ μέρος, ὡς ἄλλοι ἱστοροῦσιν, κατὰ μὲν κεφαλὴν Προποντίς, κατὰ τὸ στῆθος Ἑλλάς, ὑπὸ τὴν κοιλίαν Μακεδονία, τὰ δὲ πρὸς τῇ οὐρᾷ Φρυγία.
quotations.translation: According to Ptolemy: Italy, Gaul, Apulia, Phoenicia, Chaldaea, Orchenia. But by parts, according to the inquiries of others: for the head, Propontis; for the breast, Hellas; under the belly, Macedonia; the parts near the tail, Phrygia.

quotations.original: Κατὰ δὲ Πτολεμαῖον Βαβυλωνία, μέση Αἰθιοπία, Μέση ποταμῶν, Ἀσσυρία, Ἑλλάς, Ἀχαΐα, Κρήτη. Κατὰ μέρος δὲ κατὰ μὲν τὸν νῶτον Ἰωνία, κατὰ δὲ τὰ μέσα ἐξ ἀριστερῶν Ῥόδος, Πελοπόννησος, κατὰ δὲ τὸ Σύρμα ἐξ ἀριστερῶν Ἀρκαδία, Κυρήνη, κατὰ τὴν δεξιὰν χεῖρα Δωρίς, κατὰ τὴν εὐώνυμον Σικελία, κατὰ τὸν Στάχυν Περσική.
quotations.translation: According to Ptolemy: Babylonia, middle Ethiopia, Mesopotamia, Assyria, Hellas, Achaia, Crete. But by parts: for the back, Ionia; for the middle of the left side, Rhodes, Peloponnesus; for the train of the robe on the left side, Arcadia, Cyrene; for the right hand, Doris; for the left, Sicily; for Spica, Persia.

quotations.original: ἐὰν δὲ Ἀφροδίτη συμπαθήσῃ τῷ δεκανῷ διὰ μουσικῆς καὶ ἁρμονίας εὐεργετεῖται καὶ φιλεῖται
quotations.translation: And if Aphrodite should be sympathetic to this decan, he is shown kindness with music and harmony, and he is loved.

quotations.original: κατὰ μὲν τὸ μέτωπον Ῥώμη καὶ τὰ περὶ αὐτήν, μέσα Ἀραβία, Αἴγυπτος, Αἰθιοπία, Καρχηδών, ὀπίσθια Λιβύη, Κυρήνη καὶ οἱ συνεχεῖς τόποι, δεξιὰ Σπάρτη καὶ Λιβύη, Σμύρνης ὄρος, κατὰ τὴν κεφαλὴν Τύρος, νῆσος Θρᾳκῶν ἡ πάγκαρπος ἡ κατὰ τὴν Ἀραβίαν κειμένη, κατὰ τὸ στῆθος Κιλικία, κατὰ τὴν κοιλίαν Σινώπη.
quotations.translation: for the forehead, Rome and the surrounding regions; the middle, Arabia, Egypt, Ethiopia, Carthage; the hindparts, Libya, Cyrene and the contiguous places; the right side, Sparta and Libya, the boundary of Smyrna; for the head, Tyre, the fruited island of Thrace lying against Arabia; for the breast, Cilicia; for the belly, Sinope.

quotations.original: κατὰ μὲν τὸ μέτωπον Ῥώμη καὶ τὰ περὶ αὐτήν, μέσα Ἀραβία, Αἴγυπτος, Αἰθιοπία, Καρχηδών, ὀπίσθια Λιβύη, Κυρήνη καὶ οἱ συνεχεῖς τόποι, δεξιὰ Σπάρτη καὶ Λιβύη, Σμύρνης ὄρος, κατὰ τὴν κεφαλὴν Τύρος, νῆσος Θρᾳκῶν ἡ πάγκαρπος ἡ κατὰ τὴν Ἀραβίαν κειμένη, κατὰ τὸ στῆθος Κιλικία, κατὰ τὴν κοιλίαν Σινώπη.

quotations.original: κατὰ δὲ τὴν κεφαλὴν Ἰταλία καὶ ὁ τοῦ Ἀδρία κόλπος καὶ οἱ περὶ αὐτὸν οἰκοῦντες, κατὰ δὲ τὸ στῆθος Συρία, κατὰ δὲ τὴν φαρέτραν Ἀτλαντικὸν πέλαγος, κατὰ δὲ τὴν κοιλίαν Τριβαλλοί, Βακτριανή, Σικελία, ἐπὶ τοῖς ἐμπροσθίοις ποσὶν Αἴγυπτος καὶ οἱ συνεχεῖς τόποι.
quotations.translation: for the head, Italy and the hollow of Adria and those who dwell around it; for the breast, Syria; for the quiver, the Atlantic Sea; for the belly, the Triballi, Bactriana, Sicily; for the forefeet, Egypt and the contiguous regions.

quotations.original: Κατὰ μέρος δὲ ὑπόκειται αὐτῷ κατὰ μὲν τὴν ἀριστερὰν χεῖρα καὶ τὸ στῆθος Συρία, ὑπὸ δὲ τὴν δεξιὰν Εὐφράτης καὶ Τίγρις, κατὰ τὴν ὑδροχόην Τάναϊς καὶ οἱ πρὸς νότον καὶ ζέφυρον ῥέοντες.
quotations.translation: By part, there is subject to it: for the left hand and the breast, Syria; under the right hand, Euphrates and Tigris; for the pitcher, Tanais and those rivers [flowing] to the south and west.

quotations.original: ἔσται δὲ ταῦτα ἐὰν καὶ ἀγαθοποιοὶ ἐπιμαρτυρήσωσι τῷ τόπῳ ἄνευ κακῶν παρουσίας
quotations.translation: These things will obtain if benefics should bear witness to this place without the presence of evil ones.

quotations.original: ἔσται δὲ ταῦτα ἐὰν καὶ ἀγαθοποιοὶ ἐπιμαρτυρήσωσι τῷ τόπῳ ἄνευ κακῶν παρουσίας
quotations.translation: These things will obtain if benefics should bear witness to this place without the presence of evil ones.

quotations.original: εἰ δὲ ἀγαθὸς ἐπίδῃ ἀστὴρ γαμήσει καλὴν γυναῖκα καὶ εὐσταθὴς ἔσται καὶ καλοῦ τέλους τεύξεται.
quotations.translation: But if a good star should look upon, he will marry a fine woman, and he will be tranquil and meet with a good end.

quotations.original: Ἀκόλουθον ἂν εἴη προσλαβεῖν περὶ τῆς τῶν ζ′ πλανωμένων δυνάμεως·
quotations.translation: It would be in order to receive in addition [teachings] concerning the power of the 7 wandering stars;

quotations.original: Ὁ μὲν οὖν Ἥλιος κατείληπται θερμαίνων ἅμα καὶ ξηραίνων. Ἡ δὲ Σελήνη ὑγραίνει καὶ πεπαίνει ὥσπερ τὰ σώματα μετὰ τοῦ ἠρέμα θερμαίνειν. Ὁ δὲ Κρόνος καταψύχει καὶ ἠρέμα ξηραίνει. Ὁ δὲ Ἄρης ξηραίνει μάλιστα καὶ καίει. Ὁ δὲ Ζεὺς εὔκρατον τὸ ποιητικὸν ἔχει, θερμαίνων ἅμα καὶ ὑγραίνων. Καὶ ὁ τῆς Ἀφροδίτης δὲ τῶν αὐτῶν ἐστι κατὰ τὸ εὔκρατον ποιητικός. Ὁ δὲ τοῦ Ἑρμοῦ ποτε μὲν ξηραντικός, ποτὲ δὲ ὑγραντικός.
quotations.translation: The Sun, then, is taken as heating and drying at the same time. The Moon moistens and, as it were, ripens bodies, along with slightly heating. Kronos chills and slightly dries. Ares chiefly dries and burns. Zeus has a productive power that is temperate, heating and moistening at the same time. And the star of Aphrodite is temperately productive of the same things. The star of Hermes is sometimes drying, other times moistening.
